s: 2026-09-14-startweek-保健品卖的不是疗效-是替你承受不确定性
h: the supplement industry isn't selling efficacy, it's selling relief from uncertainty the world spends $6 billion a year on menopause supplements while the uk spent only £60 million on menopause research in the same year; collagen went from slaughterhouse waste at £15 a kilo to a £300 beauty product on the shelf. medium information density, but three things are worth the price: the collagen cost accounting, the billion-dollar failed vitamin d trials, and the funding gap in menopause research; the novel discussion in the back half can be skipped. anyone who has bought collagen, a multivitamin, or a private health check, plus founders and investors in health consumer and supplement brands — the first half has hard material on cost structure and evidence quality. start the week start the week living with uncertainty health consumer supplements evidence quality questioning uncertainty collagen is slaughterhouse scraps zand van tulleken gives the mechanism directly: collagen is the waste of meat and fishing processing — fish heads, fish bones, oxtail, cow ears, cow hooves, all of it otherwise destined for disposal. ground up, boiled in hydrochloric acid, turned into a beauty product, the wholesale price goes from £15 a kilo to £300 a kilo on the high street, a markup he describes as the kind you'd get selling cocaine. so his conclusion is not ‘collagen doesn't work’ but: even if you believe it works, you're being fleeced — boiling chicken bones yourself gets you the same thing. zand van tulleken remove the industry-funded studies and the effect disappears there are two ways to read whether collagen works. put all the studies together and the conclusion is that it helps joint pain, skin appearance and elasticity; but strip out the industry-funded studies and the effect disappears. zand says that in itself should be a very large clue. the methodology doesn't only apply to collagen — when he gets to multivitamins he also stresses that even if you believe the pill in the bottle works, ‘what's actually in the bottle’ is a separate question, and adulteration, contamination and damage to the scientific literature are harms independent of efficacy. zand van tulleken the billion-dollar failed vitamin d trials when zand was in medical school, every doctor believed vitamin d had those exciting effects on the heart and the brain, and a mass of research suggested as much. but when vitamin d was tested as a drug, roughly a billion dollars was spent over the past decade, by people who badly wanted to find those benefits, and nothing was found. the nhs now advises considering a low-dose supplement, especially in winter, which is good advice; but high doses may be harmful, and it won't give you the kind of ‘sparkle’ you were expecting. he adds that many people's approach back then was widely accepted, and they shouldn't feel like fools — the evidence has changed a great deal in just a few years. zand van tulleken menopause: $6 billion on supplements, $60 million on research zand says the menopause chapter was the hardest to write, because in the other chapters he is a victim alongside the reader, whereas in this one ‘nothing is coming for me’: the medical profession lets you down first, and then you're pushed into the arms of the wellness industry, in a very insidious way. the numbers he gives are $6 billion a year globally on menopause supplements, while the uk spent only about $60 million on menopause research last year — the uk doesn't even record how much is spent on menopause research, because the sum is too small. his judgment: the industry is selling doubt and hope, and the first emotion people want to resolve is ‘i don't want to have this problem’, and the second is hope. zand van tulleken the brain rewards the question, not the answer the neuroscience lani watson cites is counterintuitive: when a question sparks curiosity, reward circuits connected to the hippocampus become active, the brain enters a state of ‘ready to learn’, and information acquired afterwards is easier to encode and easier to recall — and it doesn't have to be the answer to that particular question; in this state the brain doesn't distinguish. more crucially, the research shows we don't get the same reward when we find the answer. in other words, the brain rewards asking and staying in curiosity, not hunting the answer down. lani watson socrates would go after the wellness gurus lani holds socrates up as the model for a 21st-century questioning mindset: he deliberately sought out people who claimed certainty and dragged them into a state called aporia — confusion, blankness, uncertainty. she says socrates would have adored the wellness gurus, and would walk into the city square (today, the digital square) and ask them: how can you be certain what health is? what wellness is? what a vitamin is? she concedes socrates had flaws, was famously annoying, and was ultimately put to death for being an annoying questioner and for challenging authority and the s

s: 2026-09-14-decoder-youtube-不是新平台-是比电视网更狠的守门人
h: youtube isn't a new platform — it's a gatekeeper harsher than the tv networks comedian adam conover says hollywood, chasing netflix, destroyed cable with its own hands and handed 60% of television to youtube for free — and youtube's algorithmic gatekeeper is less negotiable than cbs, because no one is accountable for it. someone who has worked at college humor, trutv, netflix and youtube does the platform-economy math out loud. high information density, but entirely an industry-insider view. founders and investors building in content, platforms or media; anyone who wants to understand platform take-rate structures, the algorithmic-gatekeeper mechanism, and the real ledger of the creator economy. decoder decoder adam conover explains how youtube ruined everything creator economy youtube streaming platform gatekeepers labor organizing "creator" is an exploitation script invented by the platforms conover refuses the word "creator," and not out of pedantry: he says it was coined by social media companies to trick people into signing a wildly unequal economic contract — promising "mr. beast made a billion, so can you," then getting you to work for them nearly free for the rest of your life in hopes of one day receiving a sliver of ad revenue. he compares it to avon or mary kay calling their salespeople "entrepreneurs": you think you're building a business, when the label actually conceals what the platform has done to your entire industry. he'd rather call himself a writer, a performer, hollywood labor. adam conover hollywood handed 60% of television to youtube for free conover says that for the past two years, every conversation he's had in hollywood has started with the same line: did you know youtube is now the biggest streaming service on television? his mechanism: after netflix hit television directly, every company assumed it needed its own little $15-a-month hbo, a model that was never going to work. in the chase for netflix, they destroyed cable — and never solved, on streaming, roughly 60% of television content: news, talk shows, lifestyle programming, travel shows, weather. those categories were ceded to youtube, and now when people want to watch someone talk about renovating a house, or about the knicks, or about the news, their first instinct is youtube — and it's all free. adam conover game shows died on the metric of "binge a season in a weekend" conover tells the story of his own pitch: he brought a big ip to a streaming platform to sell a game show, and was turned down with "we can get someone to watch one episode, but we can't get them to watch a whole season over a weekend." he realized on the spot that the platform's entire business model rests on "binge a season in a weekend," and that is not how people watch game shows. what makes this point valuable is that it shows how streaming's metrics systematically eliminate whole content categories: the show isn't bad, it just doesn't fit the subscription-retention model. the result is that game shows, along with other formats, were ceded to youtube — and comedy-variety writers like him, people doing non-fiction comedy in the vein of the daily show, no longer have those jobs produced by the networks at all. adam conover the cable ledger used to add up conover breaks down why the old model could support a middle class: everyone in the country paid for cable, mtv got a cut no matter what it aired, so it could afford writers' rooms, camera crews, union contracts, accountants, health insurance, and a highly paid ceo. his own show was "on the profitability line" — what it cost to make, how much advertising it sold, at what ad rate, what share came back from the cable company; the math came out black, so it ran for five years. he raises two questions: first, streaming no longer knows how to make a show profitable, and can only do strange math like "how many people subscribed to apple tv to watch a certain series"; second, they threw away decades of business-development accumulated in the advertising business — cbs could command a certain rate because it had been negotiating with johnson & johnson for a hundred years. netflix convinced the entire industry that advertising was gone forever, everyone tore that business down, and now they're rebuilding it on peacock. adam conover the algorithm is the gatekeeper, and worse than a person to the counterargument that platforms let a kid in the midwest be seen, conover's response is: then you are the gatekeeper, and the algorithm is the gatekeeper. it used to be nbc, cbs and abc; now it's youtube, instagram and tiktok — and because youtube's business model is different, it barely competes with the other two on long-form, so if you want to make broadly appealing content, you effectively have one option: youtube. he thinks this is worse than the old gatekeepers, not because it's more concentrated, but because no one is accountable: you go tell netflix a show is a good idea, and they say the algorithm says it isn't. i

s: 2026-09-14-macromusings-稳定币每增一美元-只带来六毛美债需求
h: every new stablecoin dollar brings only sixty cents of treasury demand stablecoins are not a new currency but another return of private money; they bring net new demand for the dollar and for treasuries, but each stablecoin dollar corresponds to only about sixty cents of treasury demand, because the money may simply have moved out of a money market fund. a former treasury and fed official walks through stablecoins after the genius act item by item: reserve assets, illicit finance, treasury demand and bank disintermediation, at high information density. founders, investors and financial regulators focused on stablecoins, payments and treasury demand, especially those working on cross-border payments or corporate cash management. macro musings with david beckworth macro musings nellie liang on stablecoins after genius, private money, and the global dollar stablecoins genius act treasuries dollar hegemony regulation genius is more important than its own promoters expected nellie liang says the genius act is ‘possibly more important than i realized at the time’, even though she had argued for legislation for years. in november 2021, when she released the first treasury report on stablecoins, stablecoins were only $25 billion to $30 billion in size; today they are $250 billion to $275 billion. the act does not just give stablecoin issuers clarity, it also got banks seriously considering bringing digital assets and distributed ledger technology into their own systems. she says the degree of innovation the act ignited is ‘quite remarkable’, but the outcome is still unknown. nellie liang the features that make stablecoins useful also make them good for money laundering this is the core tension of the paper: stablecoins are like cash, a bearer instrument, and after initial issuance the issuer has neither insight into nor records of transactions. so the very features that make them faster and cheaper for payments also make them highly attractive for illicit finance. the challenge is that stablecoins were originally designed for trading crypto assets, and regulators now have to refit them for the mainstream payments world while still controlling illicit finance risk. she says this is also why no one really knows how big stablecoins can get, with forecasts ranging from $500 billion to $5 trillion. nellie liang stablecoins could weaken america's sanctions leverage the dollar's global role gives the us two benefits: one, it lowers us borrowing costs; two, it enforces sanctions and aml/cft rules through the correspondent banking network — because the dollar is so widely used, the threat of cutting an institution off from us correspondent banks has teeth. if stablecoins bypass those correspondent relationships and compress settlement onto the blockchain, they weaken the effectiveness of that tool. liang says the economic benefits will persist, but there is tension on the national security side, and it is the same kind of tension as ‘the more efficient the payment, the better suited to illicit finance’. nellie liang each stablecoin dollar brings only sixty cents of treasury demand of the reserve assets of the two largest stablecoins, 79% is treasuries or treasury repos, so each dollar of stablecoins creates roughly 80 cents of t-bill demand. but to see net new demand you have to look at where the money comes from: banks, money market funds, currency in circulation, and overseas demand, four categories. money market funds themselves hold at least 80% of assets in t-bills, so if the new demand all comes from money market funds, it is a net wash, zero new. overseas demand and banks are net new, and banks actually do not hold much in treasuries. under three scenarios, low, medium and high ($0.9 trillion, $1.9 trillion, $4 trillion), a first-round estimate puts each new stablecoin dollar at about 60 cents of treasury demand. nellie liang most of the new treasury demand comes from deposits banks lose this calculation puts the trade-off on the table: to get more t-bill demand, you have to let banks lose deposits, or rely on overseas demand, and those two are the main sources of net new. liang acknowledges that if the deposits lost are at small community banks, and those banks serve small businesses' credit needs, there could be disruption. but she judges this to be more of a transitional disturbance than a permanent replacement of credit — capital markets have not yet fully reached down to small businesses, but will adjust over time. nellie liang paying no interest on deposits is not legally banned, just habit david mentions theoretical papers arguing that cbdc or stablecoins would force banks to pay interest on deposits and stop enjoying permanently cheap funding. liang says she sympathizes with the argument: reg q did not allow banks to pay interest on deposits, which spawned money market funds; after reg q was repealed, interest was allowed on some accounts, but still not on transaction accounts, until dodd-frank finally killed

norway nonviolent resistance education oral history teachers fought a war by not cooperating during the occupation of norway, teachers did not sabotage anything and did not take up weapons; their resistance was refusing to teach nazi propaganda to their students. the norwegian teacher rolf hansen, interviewed by the bbc in 1944, had by then escaped to britain. he recalled that the occupation authorities demanded schools adopt a so-called "positive national policy": denigrating the king, proving to students that the constitution was worthless, and glorifying quisling. his words were, "we never did that." this passive resistance lasted four years, until norway's liberation on 8 may 1945. rolf hansen on the day of the invasion he was still at the school gate telling students to go home germany invaded norway on 9 april 1940, and the capital, oslo, fell almost immediately. hansen remembered standing outside the school that day, watching norwegian anti-aircraft guns try to shoot down german bombers. three or four boys stood in the empty schoolyard, walked over confused and asked: "teacher, is there no school today?" he couldn't help laughing at their stubbornness about duty, and sent them home. the scene shows how sudden the occupation was — norway had until then tried to stay out of the war and was caught completely off guard. rolf hansen they hung a portrait, and the students threw it in the bin themselves the occupation did not go after the schools at first. after quisling's people became minister of church and education in the autumn of 1940, german-directed notices began piling up on headmasters' desks, one of them requiring schools to hang a portrait of quisling. one day, while hansen was teaching english grammar, a local quisling stormtrooper burst into the classroom, climbed onto a desk and nailed the portrait to the wall — and this man had once been his student. they carried on with the lesson as if the portrait did not exist. after class a girl stood up and said: "we can't let that picture stay here. father says quisling is a traitor, and a madman too." hansen said he would discuss it with the other teachers, and when he came back for the next lesson the portrait was gone; a few days later the janitor saw it in the rubbish bin. rolf hansen a propaganda speech was drowned out by the whole class laughing hansen never forgot the visit of quisling's county propaganda chief to address all the children about "the mess of our rotten democracy." the school had just been given a new headmaster, a little fool who had schemed his way into the post by getting the old headmaster put in prison. at the start of the speech he stood carefully at the back of the classroom, his eyes not yet clear from the previous night's revelry in the german canteen. when the propaganda chief bellowed, "we don't want rotten democracy, we want a leader, and our leader is a capable man, a strong man," the boys and girls spontaneously turned to look at the new headmaster, the speaker's voice drowned in laughter, and the assembly soon collapsed entirely. rolf hansen 12,000 teachers refused to join the nazi union in february 1942 quisling issued a decree ordering all norwegian teachers to join the quisling teachers' union and to assist the compulsory quisling youth service. of norway's 14,000 teachers, 12,000 flatly refused to have anything to do with the union. a month later, more than 1,000 teachers were beaten by german police in concentration camps, some were forced to labour for the german war machine in remote parts of norway and finland with with dividends reinvested, that's roughly 25% compounded annually over 45 years. it is the single best-performing stock in the s&p 500 from its listing date to today: $1,000 would become about $17 million, versus just $170,000 for the s&p 500 over the same period. david notes that who holds this equity is itself a key part of the company's strategy — early employee ownership and long-term share price growth are the same mechanism. ben / david home depot is not a price club clone what bernie set out to build was not a low-sku warehouse club but a warehouse where you buy everything for one job: price club carried only 4,000 skus, while home depot would stock 25,000 and deal with a huge number of suppliers. gross margin was set below the industry too — hardware retail's standard was 45% at the time, and they ran at 30%. the other fundamental difference is the nature of the goods: anyone buys toilet paper, but nobody is born knowing how to build a deck, hang shutters or lay flooring, so the store has to be staffed with people who have real expertise — and price club's org structure was never designed for that. ben / david big-box stores aren't the moat; service is in the 1980s a pile of capital rushed into the category: builders square, home club, home quarters warehouse, mr. how warehouse, all copying home depot, and today not one of them is left. david's explanation: home depot is not "costco for hardware." costco is general-merchandise retail where customers need no human help beyond the checkout lane; home depot is specialty retail, where price, selection and convenience — the "trinity" — aren't enough. you also have to offer something unique to the category, the way a tire shop has to mount tires, a beauty store has to let you try makeup, and apple has to have a genius bar. home depot essentially invented "serving the customer" in home improvement itself. david low margin rides on turns, not on margin rate home depot's warehouse model has two structural disadvantages: an extremely high sku count and an extremely large in-store service staff, which makes fast turns operationally hard, and per-store labor costs higher than the price-club model. ben says what holds it all up is "manufacturing buying frenzy" — with that many skus you have to give people a reason to buy across all of them. the key line: what feeds the company is not the gross margin percentage but gross margin dollars. so it needs enough volume and enough turns that the gross margin dollars add up to justify all that inventory in the store. once volume is there, it can place bigger orders with suppliers, demand lower prices, and pass the savings to customers, spinning the whole wheel faster. ben it invented the national chain, so no one could buy nationally home depot's early philosophy was radical decentralization, letting stores use local knowledge to decide what to stock and how much; h: the first public atheist was a country priest who didn't dare publish meslier wrote the testament denying god's existence but dared only to copy three manuscripts for posterity; bayle used skepticism to show that religious questions exceed reason, and therefore no one has the right to persecute others in the name of faith. this episode opens the series on the history of atheist philosophy. the information density is moderate, but bayle's argument for toleration is laid out in full and worth close attention. listeners interested in early modern atheism and the history of religious toleration, especially those who want to understand how bayle used skepticism to defend toleration. history of philosophy without any gaps history of philosophy without any gaps hop 499 beyond belief: bayle, toleration, and atheism atheism toleration early modern philosophy bayle meslier five hundred episodes without a single public atheist the show has reached nearly five hundred episodes without ever featuring a thinker who publicly declared himself an atheist. the ancients who were occasionally accused of atheism, on closer inspection, mostly held unorthodox views of the divine, like the epicureans. the only ancient case that really stands up is the sophist diagoras, but his writings are lost. the author therefore proposes: if there really is a clear history of atheist philosophy, its european starting point is probably around the turn of the eighteenth century. peter adamson a priest writes a manuscript denying god meslier (jean meslier) was an obscure country priest of blameless life, yet he left behind a testament that fiercely attacked christianity and denied god's existence. he said he had accepted holy orders only to please his parents, and had always loathed performing those idolatrous and superstitious masses. he dismantled the faith from several angles: there is no reason to prefer christianity to other religions; christians are required to believe absurd doctrines that other religions lack, such as the eucharist; the quarrels and violence among christians themselves show precisely the danger of blind faith; the old testament endorses animal sacrifice and absurdly claims that god chose the jews. peter adamson the problem of evil is his main weapon against god meslier was a rationalist, claiming his arguments relied only on the "light of natural reason," and that this light led him to the conclusion that god does not exist at all. his chief argument is the problem of evil: he says ironically that christians call god a father, yet this father abandons his children to every kind of suffering and evil. he has nothing but contempt for arguments for god's existence, especially against fénelon: if perfect things need a creator, then doesn't this perfect creator also need a creator, leading to an infinite regress; since the physical universe plainly exists, why not stop there instead of positing an invisible cause? peter adamson he didn't dare publish in his lifetime, only made three copies why has no one heard of this man, why wasn't he arrested or even executed? two questions, one answer: meslier was bold and fearless, but not bold enough to publish these heretical thoughts while alive. in his later years he copied three manuscripts of the testament for posterity, claiming he did not care about posthumous fame, and ended by writing that he was "almost nothing, and would soon be nothing." he did want to be read; the text often calls on readers to abandon superstition and to resist tyranny closely bound up with religion. he believed the idea of god was originally invented by rulers to oppress others more effectively. peter adamson religion and politics prop each other up, and he also advocated communism meslier wrote that religion supports political rule, however vicious it may be; political rule in turn supports religion, however false it may be. he went further and advocated communism, envisioning a society with all property held in common, modeled on plato's republic. thus the charges against him would include not only blasphemy and heresy but sedition. a few years after his death, copies began to circulate secretly; voltaire published excerpts in 1761, but avoided the most seditious parts. this cautious and incomplete reception meant meslier failed to spark the political and conscientious revolution he wanted. peter adamson his arguments were not new to contemporary readers the author suspects meslier's arguments would only shock readers, not shake their faith. for such anti-religious arguments had long been considered, if only to be refuted. what is special about the testament is the emotional intensity and its political agenda; but as for arguments about religion and god, it is a bit like a scholastic treatise that keeps only the hypothetical objections and deletes the responses. the theologians meslier despised, at least in their own view, would have had little difficulty meeting his challenge. peter adamson another anon

the second half is the real target of this episode: dismantling the lab-origin argument with numbers. listeners who want the argument can jump to 52 minutes. readers interested in viral evolution, the lab-origin debate, and deep-sequencing methodology; anyone who wants to see a controversy taken apart with quantitative data rather than rhetoric. this week in virology this week in virology twiv 1357: furin, naturally with paul bieinasz virology deep sequencing lab origin furin site coronavirus they changed the gfp sequence and the recombination rate went up the team first built an oc43 reverse-genetics system and made a pair of viruses: each carries a frameshifted gfp, so infection with either alone yields only fragments, but co-infection lets recombination stitch green fluorescent protein back together. they expected that changing the nucleotide sequence of one of the gfps would lower the recombination rate; instead it rose. paul says there is only a hypothesis for this, no data — one possibility is that once double-stranded rna forms, strand-transfer events during recombination become more likely because the duplex ‘breathes’. this counterintuitive result became the reagent starting point for the whole paper. paul bieniasz knock gfp out of frame and let insertions reveal themselves measuring insertions and deletions is far harder than measuring point mutations, because they were thought to be rare and sequencing depth was insufficient. their approach was to put the gfp gene into the viral genome and then deliberately knock it out of frame, preceded by a start-codon peptide that is in a different frame from gfp, so the virus does not glow green; it turns green only when that site acquires an insertion or deletion of a particular length that pulls gfp back into frame. this lets them both count event frequencies and pick out green viruses to sequence back and infer the mechanism. this is where figure 1 of the paper comes from. paul bieniasz knocking out nsp15 made insertions go down, not up the original hypothesis came from prior work suggesting that nsp15, a nuclease, affects deletion rates — when you think nuclease, you naturally think deletions, not insertions. but the experiment went the opposite way: viruses with nsp15 showed a greatly increased rate of acquiring insertions that pull gfp back into frame. paul says the deletion rate numbers were not good enough this time to quantify, but the insertion result was black and white, and they were very surprised at the time — it was this accidental result that opened up the entire line of research. paul bieniasz every base sequenced a million times before you talk frequency they moved from picking green viruses to brute-force sequencing: concentrate about 10 milliliters of virus down to 1 milliliter, load part of it onto a sequencing chip, and produce hundreds of millions of reads, so that every nucleotide in the genome is read at least a million times, with roughly 30 human genomes' or 3 million viral genomes' worth of data per virus stock. paul stresses that depth has to match the number of virions in the sample — sequencing hundreds of millions of times when there are only a thousand virions in the tube is meaningless; they calibrated to sequence roughly a few percent of the viruses in the sample. paul bieniasz eleven nucleotides is the threshold for calling an origin short insertions (three to six nucleotides) can arise randomly in a viral genome, so their origin cannot be determined, and they were excluded from the analysis. they calculated that if an 11-nucleotide stretch matches the viral genome perfectly, the probability of that being pure chance is below 5%, so they restricted the analysis to insertions of 11 nucleotides or more. the result: over 90% matched the viral genome perfectly or nearly perfectly, and in oc43 wild-type virus carried 87 times more insertions than the nsp15 mutant, most of them from the positive strand. paul bieniasz insertions aren't rare events — they're a few per thousand vincent says that for years he was told insertions are rare, but the data suggest this is happening all the time. paul responds that ‘rare’ is a relative term: one in a million is rare, but if you have ten million of them, it's common. the insertion frequency they give is a few genomes per thousand — roughly five to ten genomes carrying an insertion out of a thousand virions. that frequency is lower than the point-mutation rate, but not by much. the reason it seemed rare in the past is that the vast majority of insertions are harmful or even lethal to the virus and get purged at low multipl

fought a land battle. at the battle of mylae, the carthaginians clearly did not expect this, and took heavy losses. eve also cautions that the details of the corvus leave many unanswerable questions consequences nobody counted — antigravity equals free energy, hyperspace travel equals handing the technology to every alien civilization. the first half is live improv riffing; the second half — the roman telescope, robot babies, the falling-atom experiment on the chinese space station, and the verne details — is denser and worth skipping ahead for. for listeners who like science-fiction premise-building and progress in space telescopes and robot learning; founders can skip the first-half riffing and go straight to the technical details in the second half. the skeptics' guide to the universe skeptics guide the skeptics guide #1105 - sep 12 2026 physics laws space telescopes robot learning science fiction thought experiments changing a law of physics changes it for the whole universe the rule is hard: pick only one, and it has to be practical and feasible within the laws of physics — no perpetual-motion-style having it both ways. steven starts by handing most science-fiction premises a death sentence — warp drive, shields, phasers, artificial gravity, antigravity — either they violate physics or they fall under non-trivial: theoretically maybe possible, but never going to happen. the real fun of the whole discussion isn't in what you pick, it's in finding the consequences inside each wish that nobody counted. steven novella antigravity means free energy thrown in jay wants antigravity, on the grounds that transportation, construction and materials handling would all change. bob points out it's a twofer: if you could feasibly turn gravity off, you'd turn it on while the water wheel goes down and off while you haul it back up, and you'd have a perpetual motion machine. steven, as the buzzkill, patches it by force: the energy it costs to turn gravity off has to equal the energy you get out of it — no free lunch. the argument also incidentally kills science-fiction movies — single-stage-to-orbit is simply impossible in a 1g gravity well, and every shot of a ship reaching orbit in a minute is lying, because it assumes antigravity exists. jay novella hyperspace travel hands the technology to every alien civilization bob picks entering subspace/hyperspace: run ordinary engines over there, come out having crossed a far greater distance — essentially practical ftl. he argues there's no downside risk, because hyperspace is separate from real space and doesn't affect our universe. steven and jay immediately push back: changing a law of physics changes it for the whole universe, not just for you, and hostile civilizations could use it to colonize earth just as well. bob's answer is to hide — human radio signals dilute into noise a few light-years out, so in principle nobody could work backward to the conclusion that earth has life. jay offers a compromise, jump gates: both ends have to be built, so expansion can only be slow, and not every alien comes knocking. bob novella zero-point energy is too thin, and forcing it triggers a big rip steven's second choice is free energy, specifically zero-point energy. bob gives the objection: zero-point energy is observationally extremely thin, and lighting a single bulb might take several cubic light-years of space; and if you really injected that much energy into space, cosmic expansion would run away into a big rip that destroys all life. steven's response is that this is exactly why these aren't laws of physics — every wish, once it actually lands, brings catastrophic consequences, so the fun of the thought experiment is finding the loophole that dismantles the wish. julia adds her astrophysics-major perspective: if gravity had a knob, 90% of the observations used to infer stellar phenomena from gravity would all be wrecked. bob novella even a bucket of water can compute like a neural network the core of physical reservoir computing: any nonlinear system — a bucket of swirling water, time-varying mayonnaise — as long as you measure the right spot, its nonlinear interactions can be mapped onto an artificial neural network and made to ‘think’ for you. someone gave a talk saying, ‘we got mayonnaise to think very slowly.’ once that analogy holds, scale becomes a variable: if you had a nonlinear system the size of a nebula, you feed it input and measure output at the right point, and it can do the computation for you. the speaker himself admits this is a ‘wild idea’, but stresses that once you shrink physical constants down to something tiny, a pile of strange corollaries pops out. roman is a thousand times faster than hubble, but cast as a supporting player the nancy grace roman space telescope is a wide-field infrared telescope with a 3.4-meter primary mirror, the same size as hubble, but its design goal isn't ‘better than existing h: german cars lost to chinese evs, and afd's rise is just a symptom afd is not a german problem but a western one: people feel tomorrow won't be better, and the simultaneous loss of competitiveness in germany's proudest industries — cars, chemicals, rail — is the real fuel for the far right. the first half covers afd and german social mood; the second half is the substance: the ai value chain, the 80/20 intelligence split, and europe's real gap being a lack of people who can make the call. investors watching european politics and industrial competitiveness, founders building for or expanding into europe, and engineers who want to understand the geopolitics of the ai value chain. the good fight the good fight judith dada on the rise of the afd european tech afd ai value chain german autos venture capital afd is not a german disease, it's a western disease judith dada argues afd's rise is not a german phenomenon: the us, france, the netherlands and the uk all show the same tendency — people feel left behind, feel tomorrow won't be better than today or yesterday, and feel a melancholy for ‘the slower world of the past, where their value in their environment was clearer’. she stresses at the same time that afd is ‘the ugliest expression’ of this problem — among all far-right parties in europe it is one of the most extreme, in some respects with regrettable similarities to nazism. but she refuses to treat it as a fringe right-wing problem: in saxony-anhalt more than four in ten people voted for it, which shows the problem is societal and needs drastic political change, plus a vision of the future that can bring people along. judith dada the neighbour who votes afd is actually very friendly dada lives on the island of rügen in mecklenburg-vorpommern, and in daily life she has not encountered xenophobia; her neighbours are very friendly to her, her husband, her children and her darker-skinned nigerian father. but she notices her own fear growing: last weekend her father visited and the two walked around stralsund, the streets full of afd campaign posters, the occasional german flag hung in front of an apartment block or a parking lot, and she felt a kind of nausea, wondering ‘whether my father, whether i, am seen as not belonging here, as unwelcome’. she says if she saw a french flag in france she would not feel the same unease; but seeing a german flag in the country where she was born, she asks: is this because they love germany, or because they are far right. judith dada germany's last shred of face has been taken too dada says the german model ‘very clearly no longer works’: the economy has long been in stagflation, pillar industries like cars and chemicals have lost competitiveness because of high energy costs, and large numbers of jobs have been cut or moved away. she takes german cars as an example: germany completely misjudged the relevance of electrification and underestimated chinese automakers' ability to catch up — it used to be assumed chinese brands could never have the same prestige as german brands, but now go to markets like south africa, where german cars once sold at a premium, and you see byd and a crowd of chinese brands pouring in, and people no longer care whether it's a bmw or a mercedes. she says the last remnant of german pride — ‘nobody in china can build a high-end car brand’ — has now been taken away too. judith dada america's non-tech sectors are just as sick as germany's dada offers a comparison: the us has 150 companies with software revenue above a billion dollars, europe has only about 30. the mag 7 together are worth almost half of total global market cap, and economic growth is extremely concentrated in the single sector of tech. but she points out this is not just a european or german problem, it's a technology problem: america's existing non-tech industries are suffering exactly the same malaise as german and european industry, us economic growth is broadly driven by capex going into data centres, by the tech and ai boom, while non-tech sectors grow at the same rate as mature german and european industry. she stresses, however, that this does not remove a fact: in industries dense with technology and r&d innovation, europe simply does not have as strong an industry as the us. judith dada europe is absent from every layer of the ai value chain dada breaks the ai value stack into three layers: the chip and infrastructure layer (chips, and the data centres that host them and turn them into training and inference compute); the model layer (the models that actually produce intelligence); and the application layer (using that intelligence to build concrete applications that bring value to people's lives). she says europe plays too small a role at every layer, and the further down the stack you go, the starker the gap. she argues that without a structural answer to ‘what is american tech, what is chinese tech’, no amount of small anymore anish says that three years ago, if a company wanted to do something too grand, a16z would not invest; today it is the reverse — ideas that are too small, too local, they do not want to touch. the reason is that model capability has torn down the threshold of ‘can it be done’, and the remaining constraint is ambition itself. he calls this technology ‘unbundling skill from desire’: not only can productivity be amplified, the scale of what you want to do can be amplified too. anish acharya it is not recursive self-improvement, it is autocatalytic anish pushes back on the ‘fast takeoff’ narrative: the people in the labs who understand it best do not say rsi (recursive self-improvement), they say autocatalytic effects — using new technology to improve your own process, but not truly recursively. he gives two counterexamples: first, economic diffusion is extremely slow, and when he went back to his hometown he found people's lives had barely changed; second, many problems are simply not intelligence bound — give fedex or domino's a data center full of phds and it still will not make supply chains and pizza exponentially crush everything. anish acharya using ai and reorganizing around ai are two different things anish uses the diffusion of electricity as an analogy: from the invention of electricity to factories actually reorganizing took 40 years, and it meant burning down the old plants and rebuilding, not swapping coal for electricity. today the most aggressive companies redesign everything around models, while slower companies just grant permissions to existing roles and functions. he also cites the mexican used-car company kavak's jedi academy: a six-week course teaching everyone, including mechanics, to use the new tools, and at graduation each person delivers an agent in the production environment. anish acharya companies will become a series of nested loops anish's steel man: after prompt comes agent (a loop of model plus tools, memory, skill files), and after agent comes loop (a group of agents doing a task). coding got there first because the models are best, the users are the most technical, and a mature loop already existed — a bug report comes in, a reproduction is generated, it is fixed, high-risk changes get human confirmation, low-risk ones ship directly, and the customer may even get an automatic reply. above that there is loop per person, loop per job function, loops across business units, up to a loop that can run most of the company. anish acharya a loop only climbs to the local optimum and stops the growth team's version of the loop: every variant is generated automatically, measured automatically, and once it reaches statistical significance it converges and ships, with a long-term holdout left behind, and then the next experiment begins. but anish stresses that a loop will hit the local maximum and then plateau, and at that point you need out of distribution thinking and human intuition to land you at the foot of the next mountain. his example is telling claude ‘make me a million dollars, no mistakes allowed’ — it cannot do it, because the direction has to be set by a human. anish acharya frontier model pricing is actually irrational anish explains model choice with pareto efficiency: frontier models are ‘irrationally priced’ on the price-performance curve — one more iq point may cost 100 times more than opus. but for industries like drug discovery, where the upside is unbounded, that one extra iq point may be worth a trillion-dollar outcome, so paying that price is rational; whereas for work with bounded upside like law and finance, you just want pareto efficiency, using a cheap open-weight model that is good enough. the conclusion is that the two architectures will coexist, not one or the other. anish acharya people want to spend time, not save it anish says ‘loop, make me happier’ is the big opportunity: people say they want to be more h: copper grades have fallen from 2% to 0.4%, while ai's power demand is going to the moon global copper grades keep sliding, new mines take 35 years to permit, and an ai search uses 30x the power of a normal one — supply is shrinking, demand is exploding, and copper is becoming the new oil. robert friedland distills the copper supply-demand deadlock from 40 years in mining: falling grades, 8-year equipment lead times, sulfuric acid shortages. high information density, but the real goods only show up in the second half. investors and founders watching commodities, the energy transition and ai infrastructure; engineers who want to understand copper's structural supply-demand gap and supply chain bottlenecks. odd lots odd lots robert friedland on the world's monumental shortage of copper copper commodities ai power supply chain mining energy transition the next 18 years will require mining all the copper of the past 10,000 friedland offers an arithmetic that makes you squirm: humanity has mined 700 million metric tons of copper in all of history, and to recover all of it you would have to dismantle the us and europe back to the mammoth age to get back roughly 700 million tons. but at the current pace of the global economy, just sustaining 3% gdp growth — not even counting evs and data centers — means the next 18 years require mining the same amount of copper as the past 10,000 years. and people in the industry broadly think that's impossible, because the us has deindustrialized and hasn't built a single copper smelter or nuclear plant since. robert friedland the world's largest copper mine's grade is in freefall friedland dissects escondida: when this, the world's largest copper mine, was discovered a generation ago, its grade was close to 2%; today it's down to 0.8%, and within two years it will fall to 0.4%. falling grades mean crushing and grinding more rock to extract less metal, and crushing and grinding account for 4% to 5% of global energy consumption. the mine sits at 12,000 feet in the andes, in the atacama desert where it hasn't rained in 30,000 years, and it takes two cubic meters of water to crush one cubic meter of rock. they built a $4 billion desalination plant and spend $1 million a day on electricity pumping water from sea level up to 12,000 feet. the upshot: just keeping this one mine producing requires another $10 to $12 billion of investment. robert friedland an ai search uses 30x the power of a normal search friedland gives a concrete energy comparison: one google search consumes the electricity to light a 100-watt bulb for 12 seconds, while one ai search — he uses chatgpt4 and cloud — uses 30x that, equivalent to lighting a 100-watt bulb for two or three minutes. every five-year-old on the planet with an ipad is using ai search, and power demand ‘literally goes to infinity’. he also points out: nothing about the internet is inherently green, and this studio itself is copper-intensive and energy-intensive. robert friedland sulfuric acid prices rose more than sixfold in eight months about 25% of the world's copper requires sulfuric acid for leaching and extraction, and sulfuric acid comes mainly from middle eastern natural gas. after the strait of hormuz closed, sulfuric acid prices went from $150 a ton to over $1,000 a ton in eight months. russia and china have already banned sulfuric acid exports. friedland's company benefits, because it built africa's largest copper smelter where sulfuric acid is a byproduct — they sell the acid to fellow copper miners in congo, at ever higher prices. but he warns: without more sulfuric acid, global food prices will rise too, because sulfuric acid is also used to make fertilizer. robert friedland buying one large motor means waiting eight years friedland tells a supply chain story absurd in its specificity: building the oyu tolgoi copper-gold mine in mongolia's gobi, they needed large motors about 40 feet in diameter, and just the ring gear took four and a half years to arrive. today the same equipment takes eight to ten years, ‘if ever’. and hyperscalers trying to buy natural gas turbines face lead times of six to eight years. an even more extreme example: a congo copper mine flooded by an earthquake needed pumps to drain it, pumps moving 1,300 liters per second with a head three times the height of the eiffel tower. they called the us and germany, and neither could build them, because they couldn't get samarium-cobalt magnets. only china could build them within 30 days. at the time, the flooding was costing $15 million a day in lost revenue. robert friedland us miners earn $100 an hour; congo engineers earn $800 a month friedland directly compares cost structures: congo copper grades run 3% to 6%, the median age is 18.7, and a congo software engineer who knows ai earns $800 to $1,000 a month. mining copper in the us, by contrast, means the united steelworkers demand over $100 an hour for underground work, plus h: the oldest manuscript of the song of roland is actually an english performance copy the oxford digby 23 manuscript is written in anglo-norman, and scholars date it to between 1140 and 1170 by tracking dialect drift — the most complete version of this french epic was performed for the english. this is a members-only sample episode, medium information density, but it gets very concrete about how a manuscript gets read as "some minstrel's working copy" — good for listeners interested in manuscripts, oral epic and dialect reconstruction. listeners interested in medieval manuscripts, oral epic and dialect reconstruction; anyone who wants to see how a single manuscript gets reconstructed into a specific performance setting. the british history podcast british history podcast chansons de geste and 12th century performance sample medieval manuscripts epic dialect studies british history the most complete version is an english manuscript the song of roland is a french epic that took shape around the 12th century, belonging to the genre chanson de geste (songs of deeds), and it spread with 12th-century french cultural hegemony to regions including britain. but its most complete and oldest surviving version is not from france itself — it is an english manuscript, catalogued as oxford digby 23. this manuscript was originally bound together with a completely unrelated book by someone later, which is why it is called digby 23 b, and a is that "other book." nobody knows who bound them together; possibly some monk felt both were his favourite books. every stanza is a camera position the poem is organised in laisses (stanzas) of varying length, and each laisse is like a camera focus: when the scene or the mood shifts, you change laisse. the whole poem is in decasyllabic meter, cut into four plus six in performance: the first four syllables rise, then a dramatic pause, then the last six syllables fall, overall close to iambic turning into trochaic. recited over and over this becomes hypnotic, and the poem runs to four thousand lines — hours of recitation. at peak emotion, the same action is performed three times this kind of epic has a convention that is hard for any reteller to handle: when the action is especially intense or the emotion especially strong, it uses consecutive laisses to tell the same action from three angles, a kind of poetic slow motion. for example, roland's refusal to blow the oliphant is told three times, with almost no gap between them. this is also why it reads like an action film or a comic: scenes cut hard, with no softening transition — for instance, "roland dies, his soul ascends to heaven" is followed directly by "the emperor arrives at roncevaux." the performer's name is left at the end of the manuscript digby 23 is very likely a real minstrel's working copy. line 4002 of the poem, its final line, says roughly: "here ends the song of deeds; turoldus will not tell more." this line appears before charlemagne's lament, so it reads more like the performer saying: this is too sad, i cannot go on. the name turoldus does not appear in the poem, and he is not a known scribe, so scholars lean towards him being the owner of this manuscript, the performer of this performance. its pocket-book size gives away that it was for work the manuscript is only about six and a half inches by four and a half inches, a pocket book you could carry on your person, not a wealthy man's finely bound volume. it is itself heavily worn and not refined, and it contains some small annotations of unclear meaning. together these features point to a professional performer on the move: he might have travelled alone with an instrument, or been the lead singer or narrator in a troupe, with someone in front of him doing the physical performance. such people were jongleurs — the origin of the later word juggler. the dialect pins this performer to england the manuscript is not in the french of central france, nor continental french, but in anglo-norman, which suggests this performer was probably anglo-norman, performing in britain or at least in normandy. the dialect features are very specific: continental french o and ou are replaced by u, so roland becomes rulant, l'or becomes l'ur; anglo-norman french was also losing final soft e. these changes even begin to break the originally strict decasyllabic meter, leaving some lines with only nine syllables or swelling to eleven. accent drift alone can date a manuscript scholars' grasp of this dialect is fine enough that they can date the manuscript to between 1140 and 1170 based on the degree of accent drift. the method is similar to scholars reconstructing shakespearean pronunciation, tracking regular changes in syllables and sounds. poetry is especially suited to this kind of reconstruction, because meter and rhyme expose which sounds were dropped and which were added. for many jongleurs, french was a second language anyway, spoken with a dialect accent, and they spelled by sound. a french

h: americans suddenly fell in love with japan — not because it's cheap, because it's normal the real driver of japan's tourism explosion isn't the exchange rate, it's the functionality of public space — clean subways, on time, no trash. what american visitors experience in tokyo is a society where entropy has been paused. this episode uses expert interviews plus a listener survey to break "why is everyone going to japan" into six verifiable reasons; the back half, on japanese craft culture versus american dysfunction, is especially worth hearing. anyone curious about the japan tourism phenomenon, founders and investors making calls on consumer and cultural trends, and readers who want to understand the contrast with american social dysfunction. search engine search engine why’s everybody going to japan? japan tourism soft power cultural difference public space consumer trends an excel sheet of 119 visitors the questioner, lisa, is a japanese person living in tokyo. she made a visitor calendar from november 2022 to april 2026, with green cells marking days someone visited. she counted 119 people, 96 of them her own guests, averaging one person every five days, 20% of all her days. she says she spends all her free time helping visiting friends plan itineraries. this data visualization is itself evidence that the problem has spun out of control, and it's the starting point for the question this episode sets out to answer. lisa japan is poor in resources, rich in story roland kelts argues the first reason for american interest in japan isn't economic, it's story. he says japan has almost no natural resources, no oil, very little land, only small rice paddies, yet its story culture is astonishing. the world's first novel is japanese, the tale of genji, a thousand years old. through manga, anime and the internet, the whole world discovered this narrative capacity. this didn't start in the 1990s — roland says there were two earlier waves: japanism in late 19th-century europe, and the beats' and hippies' fascination with zen and buddhist concepts in the 50s and 60s. roland nozomu-kelts america used to fear japan david marks points out that for seventy years after world war ii, mainstream american feeling toward japan was fear, not affection. before 1945 japan was an enemy nation; afterward it was seen as a developing country rebuilding itself. in the 70s and 80s it became anxiety about japanese economic power, and michael crichton's rising sun cast japan as the villain. after the cold war ended there was even a cia position paper discussing whether japan should be the next enemy. when japan's economic bubble burst in the 90s, america actually felt a kind of relief. when david moved to japan in 2003, having a friend visit japan was the event of the year, because nobody came at all. w. david marks the government made japan cheap by hand the third wave was a government plan. in 2003 junichiro koizumi launched the visit japan campaign, aiming to raise the target from 5 million tourists a year to 10 million, with ads full of western stereotypes — geisha, cherry blossoms, temples. but what actually worked was shinzo abe deliberately weakening the yen in the 2010s; the intent was to help exports, and the result was making hotels and restaurants cheap for foreigners. roland says in tokyo you can eat a very good soba lunch for under $10, while in new york $10 won't even buy an apple and a banana. in 2013 abe relaxed visas for thailand and malaysia, then china and indonesia; asian tourists surged first, and european and american tourists followed. roland nozomu-kelts japan's functionality is the biggest draw roland says the most important reason is functionality. public space in many countries, especially the united states, has become disabled: parks are dirty and dangerous, rail systems are terrible, airports are a mess. in japan, things just work. pj adds that american ears hear complaints about poor public order and dirty subways as elitism, as rich people's complaints. but in japan, wanting a clean subway isn't elitism — it's the reverse: why shouldn't public things be good? on tokyo streets you see no trash, not even cigarette butts, and you don't smell urine or feces. pj says this isn't the reason people go the first time, but it may be the reason some people go again. roland nozomu-kelts japan reveres the people who make things, not the people who sell them the sixth reason is craft. the japanese word shokunin means artisan, someone who can make things extremely well, and such people are still respected in japan, a status traceable to the 17th-century edo period, when makers outranked merchants. roland tells of an animation industry person explaining the walmart model to him: in america, the company selling the goods ranks first, nobody cares who made it, and a $5 pillow was made by someone who knows nothing about pillows. but in japan, the person who makes a pillow extremely well is the most valuable. he took an america

h: emulating to the point where stock firmware runs — that's where the lie ends voxel squeezed an entire oxide rack into a mini pc in twelve weeks, but the real bar isn't getting it to boot — it's oxide: how faux can you go? emulation hardware internal tools llm open source the test environment is always twenty-seventh in line steve karam says anyone who's done software development or it knows the test environment usually isn't second fiddle — it's twenty-seventh fiddle, ahead only of education and enablement environments and documentation. and when your product is an entire rack, the problem gets especially hard: the rack itself, the fabric, the sleds, the switch zone, the sp, the root of trust — every layer needs one. so oxide has multiple fidelity tiers: dog food racks, the racklet mini rack, single-instance omicron (simulated or physical running on helios) — but it was missing a middle tier that's easier than a racklet yet higher fidelity than a single chassis. steve karam four by two compressed everything into boot time voxel's predecessor was called four by two, and it used a pile of shell scripts to define what the rack should look like, bringing up a virtual rack at boot with cargo bay, shared disks, networking and emulated networking. it did work — ipv6 and unnumbered bgp were first tested on four by two. but steve points out the fatal flaw: doing everything at boot time is a recipe for disaster — boot took forty minutes, it was hard to self-heal, and "you know it's going to crash in the last two minutes of that fortieth minute." so ryan goodfellow proposed a rewrite and came up with the name voxel: virtual oxide emulation labs. steve karam voxel splits build and deploy into two steps the biggest difference between voxel and four by two is the separation of build and deploy: give it an omicron commit, it clones, compiles, produces a perfectly formed sled image and snapshots it, then reuses that snapshot to play every sled and gimlet. the other big change is a full rewrite in rust, shedding shell scripts as much as possible. because one snapshot has to play six roles, something has to tell it what to be — voxel has a built-in agent written in rust, delivered at each sled's boot, telling it "you're the switch," "you're sled 1," "you're sled 2." steve karam llms are great at enumerating registers, bad at judging threads steve says llms are very strong at enumerating registers and finding the bits and pieces that make up a complete system, because nobody can hold an entire rack in their head; with rfds and design docs as context, the results get much clearer. but elsewhere it confidently reaches wrong conclusions: he once had the root of trust and the sp share a single thread for communication, and the llm said that was absolutely not a problem — after splitting them, performance improved 500x, and the rack could finally bring both up at once. steve karam don't touch the main software — that's voxel's bottom line steve says voxel has a creed it tries hard to hold: don't modify the main software. when he worked on multi rack, he stuffed all kinds of hacks into voxel to make voxel and omicron pretend multi-rack was already supported — for instance, creating a port that doesn't exist in omicron at all but magically exists in voxel. robert said on the company channel that you shouldn't create things that don't actually exist in omicron. steve admits he was right: it's putting the cart before the horse, and it's the trap you easily fall into when doing emulation — you start rewriting h: sugar on the cell surface isn't frosting — it's the brain's moat the mucins on the brain's vascular endothelium are like a redwood forest; with age the leaves fall off and the blood-brain barrier neurodegeneration bioorthogonal chemistry drug delivery glycobiology was abandoned by its tools in the 1960s and 70s, carbohydrates were taken as seriously as proteins, but once recombinant dna arrived, proteins could be cloned, expressed and studied — sugars could not. sugars are not a product of the central dogma; they are the output of enzymes encoded by hundreds of genes, and molecular biology techniques cannot manipulate them directly. so the field rushed toward whatever could be accelerated, and sugar science, technically hard, was left where it stood. bertozzi says this is not because sugars are unimportant, but because "just because you don't study an area doesn't mean it's not important." carolyn bertozzi she built the flashlight before talking biology when she started her lab at berkeley in 1996, sugar science was missing two things proteins had long had: sequencing (knowing which sugars exist) and live imaging (seeing where sugars are and how they move). her lab's initial goal was to fill exactly those two holes, and it took roughly a decade to develop bioorthogonal chemistry — a chemical reaction that can label sugars inside living cells and is now a general-purpose tool in the life sciences. with a flashlight, you can finally see places no one had looked before. carolyn bertozzi nobody had asked how sugars change with age tony wyss-coray's lab was studying transcriptomic and proteomic changes in brain endothelial cells as they age — standard practice — but nobody had asked about the glycome. sophia, a student who had rotated in bertozzi's lab, moved to tony's lab and brought the sugar imaging reagents with her to compare the vasculature of old and young mice. the result was "absolutely striking" — the sugar changes were far more dramatic than any phenotype observed in the transcriptome or proteome. carolyn bertozzi brain endothelial cells have mucins like a redwood forest mucins on the cell surface are like giant redwoods: tall, stiff, straight, projecting above everything else. the mucin forest on brain endothelial cells is far thicker than on the vasculature of heart, kidney or muscle — a landscape unique to the blood-brain barrier. with age this forest turns into winter: leaves gone, trees bare, you can see straight through. young mice are spring, dense with foliage. sophia found that the enzymes responsible for synthesizing these sugars drop in abundance in old mice; restoring the enzyme with a gene therapy vector restored the mucins, reduced blood-brain barrier leakage, and the mice got through the maze faster. carolyn bertozzi a reagent crossed the blood-brain barrier on its own sophia injected a mucin-binding reagent into mice and found hours later that it first bound the vasculature, then crossed the blood-brain barrier by itself into the brain parenchyma. textbooks say proteins cannot cross the blood-brain barrier alone, and this is the biggest pain point for biologics companies working on brain drugs. the accidental finding made the team realize it could serve as a shuttle carrier — a brain shuttle — delivering cargo into the brain. sophia now has her own lab at harvard, and she, bertozzi, tony and another student are spinning out a company to do brain shuttling. carolyn bertozzi only 15 cns biologics are approved more than 150 biologics have been approved to treat immune disease, and a similar number for cancer, but only 15 treat central nervous system disease — and most go in by intrathecal injection: a lumbar puncture, invasive, a whole day gone, hard to scale. if those drugs could be given as ordinary intravenous injections, it would be transformative for patients. the drug classes that could get into the brain include monoclonal antibodies, enzyme replacement therapies, sirna and antisense oligonucleotides, mrna lipid nanoparticles, and viral and non-viral gene therapy vectors. carolyn bertozzi cd22 is the brake on the brain's immune cells tony's lab found a courtyard house inside the city cost only a few hundred yuan per square meter, and people were unwilling to borrow from banks because they felt debt was shameful. fang yan was working at an ad agency at the time. to convince the market, he first had to convince the people around him, so in the office he fabricated the story of the chinese old lady who saved her whole life to buy a house and the american old lady who took out a loan, bought a house, and finished paying it off just before she died — then spread it through the media. once he believed it himself, he bought his first apartment in 2000, made a rule of buying one every year, and planned to retire at 40. the detail shows: many wealth beliefs treated as common sense trace back to a single marketing campaign. fang yan companies that sell advice can't go public fang yan ran an ad agency in his early years. his clients went public one after another, so he asked a securities firm whether they could take him public too. the answer: your kind of company is called a ‘people-based company’ — you sell ideas, and to come up with more ideas you have to hire more people. only a ‘capital-based company’ that pools money together generates enormous force, and only that is suited to going public. restaurants are the least suited to listing, because one location being delicious doesn't mean a hundred will be; they made money first, then chose to live the value-investing life. india's pabrai also sold his company, put a big pile in the bank, and waited for opportunities. the companion rule is ‘if you want to be a value investor, you have to live the value-investing life’: buffett keeps three to four hundred billion us dollars in cash in the bank, and has lived for over fifty years in a $30,000 house in a fourth-tier city. fang yan buffett's engine is 60 to 70 subsidiaries, not compounding fang yan breaks it down: over fifty years of doing business, buffett gained control of 60 to 70 wholly owned subsidiaries, and those subsidiaries in turn control several hundred grandchild companies. the ceos' job is to continuously generate free cash flow, but they have no right to allocate it; h: the failure of liberal democracy is not economic, it is the distribution of recognition fukuyama says liberalism flattened the human soul into a creature that wants only security and consumption, ignoring the longing to be seen and recognized; trump-style backlash and identity politics both grow from here. fukuyama himself restates the end of history, threading recognition, thumos and state capacity into a single line. information density is high, though the ai section in the back half is looser. founders, investors and policy researchers concerned with why democratic institutions are failing and with the roots of populism and identity politics — especially suited to anyone thinking about ai governance. the ezra klein show ezra klein show francis fukuyama on trump, china and the legacy of 9/11 political philosophy populism recognition politics state capacity ai governance the end of history is not the end of events fukuyama clarifies that the phrase comes from hegel: it means history has direction and a goal, and asks what objective endpoint the process is heading toward — not that big things stop happening. his observation in the late 1980s was that every systemic competitor had either self-destructed or been abandoned by its followers, so things would stop at liberal democracy plus capitalism, the second-to-last station. his challenge to opponents has not changed: can you point to a better alternative that leaves people ultimately happier and more complete. francis fukuyama the foundation of liberalism is not self-preservation, it is recognition fukuyama moves the philosophical basis of liberalism from hobbes and locke to hegel. hobbes and locke ask only for self-preservation and a decent material life; hegel saw deeper: humans also have thumos, an immaterial impulse demanding that others recognize their humanity. he coined two greek words: isothumia is the basic dignity everyone is born entitled to, cashed out through rights; megalothumia is the desire to be recognized as greater than others. the former is the base of a free society, the latter the engine of excellence, and you cannot do without either. francis fukuyama the pain of poverty is being unseen fukuyama cites adam smith: the rich are honored for their wealth, while the poor are invisible to their fellow citizens, and the real pain of poverty is this invisibility. he gives ralph ellison's invisible man as an example: the north had no legal segregation, but whites simply did not regard black people as fellow human beings, and this invisibility is the root of resentment and distrust. so material politics and recognition politics bleed into each other: you may have a decent income in a country, but if it makes you slide down the ladder of recognition, that is a serious harm. francis fukuyama the tech right's radicalization comes from a sense of humiliation fukuyama says politics in recent years is in some sense a collision of two ‘status-reversal’ demands. on the left, wokeness carries an impulse to treat white privilege and wealth as suspect and to demand you prove your innocence; on the right, an attack on journalists and cosmopolitans as the ‘chosen elites’. he singles out the radicalization of the tech right: we made money and built big companies by the rules of capitalism, and now you hate us. this feeling of being unjustly unrecognized, mixed with moral judgment, pushes people toward increasingly dangerous politics. francis fukuyama liberalism deliberately lowered the horizon of human aspiration fukuyama concedes that liberalism is necessarily pluralistic: born out of the 17th-century wars of religion, to stop people from killing each other over fine theological differences, it deliberately lowered the human horizon to survival — the right to life takes priority over the right to a good life. the cost is that modern america asks very little of its citizens — obey the law, pay your taxes, and that is enough; no sacrifice, no major risk required. but part of the human psyche longs for a life that stakes life, property and sacred honor on a cause, and that longing has no outlet in the existing society, so on january 6 the people in camouflage invented a cause for themselves. francis fukuyama the real consequence of 9/11 was the west's overreaction fukuyama does not think radical islamism genuinely challenged liberalism; it only took root in poor, loosely organized muslim societies and lacked the universal appeal of marxism-leninism. the real danger was the west's overreaction in afghanistan and iraq: the militarization of foreign policy, the embryonic surveillance state that america built out of fear, and the fact that neither war ended well, producing extreme cynicism about american power and directly giving rise to trump. he was a neoconservative who supported removing saddam at the time, but studying developing countries in the 1990s made him doubt whether america had the stamina to remake a heterogeneous society. francis fukuyama trump is r

but no one knows how many other agents are out there, the models labs are training now are stronger and more dangerous than astra, and this incident itself will be written into the next generation of models' training material. greg jensen the window into model reasoning is closing the previous generation of models at least reasoned in english, which let researchers see what it was doing and why — a critical safety window. but jensen says the newest models are dropping that constraint, because reasoning in english slows the model down. so we end up in a state where we have no idea what it is doing or why. he goes further: even if you ask the model directly why it did that, what it gives you is a story disconnected from the actual computation, like a person making up reasons for their own impulses. the difference is that you can interrogate the model almost infinitely — what if we change this condition, what if we change that one — and in that way circle close to its reasoning. he says this is how bridgewater tests a model's diagnosability, but even so it is only an approximation, because the model itself no longer knows what its real reasoning was. greg jensen bridgewater runs an ai controlled experiment with two funds bridgewater runs two production lines internally. one is "human intuition translated into algorithms, ai-assisted", corresponding to pure alpha; counterintuitive; but the comedy interludes eat up a fair amount of time, so the information density is middling. anyone who wants to understand the silver–opium–tea economic chain behind the opium siftings left over. yangwen says the british market drinks mainly these last two grades, packed into tea bags; china drinks whole leaves, with attention to leaf shape, body, and a complete ritual. her
