china's premodern relations with mongolia and central asia. nomadic peoples were not settled and needed tea, iron pots, and silk, which they could only get from china; china was a rice-and-wheat farming civilisation and lacked horses. hence the historical tea-horse exchange, trading goods at fixed ratios. once the relationship broke down, the mongols, lacking tea, raided southward — the 1449 tumu crisis is an example: the ming army was encircled by the mongols, and roughly fifty thousand soldiers were captured along with the emperor. afterward the ming closed the great wall for a time, but blockade was never a long-term solution, and in the end the gates had to reopen for the tea-horse trade. yang wen tea's name betrays the routes it travelled tea's spread left linguistic traces. yangwen says that in mongolian, russian, turkish, arabic, and persian, tea is called cha, while in english it is tea — the overland camel caravan routes left cha, the sea routes left tea. greg made up a mnemonic for it: ‘if it travels by car, it is cha. if it goes by the sea, it is tea.’ the value of this clue is that the same product entered different civilisations through two completely different trade networks, and even its name forked. tea reached europe in the early 17th century, with the portuguese and the dutch east india company as the earliest suppliers. yang wen china took only silver and drained the world dry by the late 18th century, china had sucked the world's silver into its treasury. yangwen says that from vasco da gama's voyage in 1497 to 1793, europeans and americans all came to buy tea, porcelain, and silk, while china took only gold and silver, and over the centuries europeans found they had nothing the chinese wanted. she quotes the missionary robert hart: the chinese have the best food (rice), the healthiest drink (tea), and the best clothing material (silk), and need nothing from britain. in 1793 the macartney mission demanded free trade, and the emperor's attitude was: i permit my subjects to sell you a little tea, and that is a favour. the only thing britain had left that could break into china was indian opium. yang wen the stolen green tea grew into black tea in india in 1843, to break its dependence on chinese tea, britain sent the botanist robert fortune to infiltrate china's interior and steal tea plants. he bought a fake queue, wore a hat to cover his unshaved forehead, travelled deep into the mountains, and dug up whole tea plants to ship back to assam in india. yangwen points out an irony: what he stole was mainly green tea from the southeast coast, and grown in assam's stronger sunlight and richer soil it turned into black tea — the raw material now regarded as typical british black tea is in fact a chinese green tea variety. fortune himself did not get rich from it; yangwen says he did not die wealthy. yang wen the industrial revolution was pushed along by tea and sugar some economic historians have argued that the industrial revolution was driven by tea. yangwen says caffeine plus the sugar in tea let the working class refuel at half past ten in the morning and half past three in the afternoon, working longer and producing more; sydney mintz's sweetness and power is the representative statement of this argument. the same logic explains why tea replaced small beer in the mid-18th century as the one banker asked, "what's it going to take? would taking off my shirt be enough?" and then actually did it, standing half-naked in the conference room. the stock doubled immediately after listing. every partner in the alliance had already put in millions of dollars each. as one vice president in the book told david epstein, they had so much money they never had to worry about making payroll — what startup never has to worry about making payroll? that is the key mechanism: enough money that you never have to make a trade-off. tim harford the tech was so good it made a partner's department obsolete on the spot two young engineers flew to japan to show a hardware prototype to mitsubishi. the demo had barely started when the host suddenly called in a group of employees in work clothes, apologized, and asked them to start over — because this thing had no modem, it was all implemented in software. a groan came from the audience, and a manager named kato slumped forward and banged his head on the table. the host apologized again: "you just made kato's department obsolete." this technology made answering machines, arcade cabinets, books, keyboards and mice obsolete. at the same time they built a precursor to usb, a new programming language called telescript, called portable networking the cloud, put skeuomorphic icons on a touchscreen, and built a store where you could buy applications — back when nobody called it an app store. tim harford they built the future but not a product the first device running the general magic operating system was sony's magic link in 1994. behind the gorgeous graphics it was hard to use, shipping with a 200-page manual; the body had only an old-style telephone jack — to send a message or make a call you had to sit at a desk and plug in a phone line. it didn't even have a built-in phone. in today's purchasing power, about $1,600. sony sold 3,000 units in the first six months, mostly to friends and family of general magic employees. a few years later, apple sold roughly 300,000 iphones on day one. in 1995 motorola's envoy had wireless communication, but cost nearly twice as much as the magic link. tim harford ebay's idea was called the dumbest thing a colleague had ever heard pierre, a technical support engineer at general magic, built a webpage on the side: list the stuff sitting unused at home and let other people bid on it. he named the site auctionweb, showed it to colleagues, and asked whether he could spin it out as a company, or whether general magic would invest. one colleague's response was typical: this is the dumbest idea i've ever heard — you want

as specialized machines built their skills in, the work was simplified and segmented, and a few all-around craftsmen were replaced by a large group of workers each knowing one operation. riveting a boiler originally took nine skilled machinists; with a hydraulic riveter it became one skilled worker plus eight unskilled ones, the latter doing things like clamping. in 1883 the young machinist john morrison testified before congress that the machining trade had been subdivided since the mid-1870s, and subdivided again after that, so that in sewing machine making, for example, the jobs were split so finely that a person hardly counted as a machinist. nc is just one more step on this timeline. bosses hoping nc would save labor were disappointed first nc controls the machine tool and workpiece with pre-programmed instructions, without a machinist's direct manual intervention: a programmer translates the drawing into coordinates, punches them onto paper or plastic tape, and feeds them into the controller. it was invented in the 1950s, but at first served only the air force and aerospace, with specifications far beyond the needs of ordinary shops and small workshops. crucially, early nc was hard-wired, with limited functions, and a major change meant tearing apart the controller and rebuilding it, very inflexible. so shop owners who expected it to lower worker skill were thoroughly disappointed: a mid-1960s survey by lawrence williams and brian williams found shops still needed operators with the same skills and technical knowledge, especially right after introduction; h: brahminhood is not doghood: how a buddhist philosopher dismantled the metaphysics of caste dharmakirti does not deny that dogs share a universal, "doghood" — he refuses to grant that "brahminhood" exists, because brahmins and shudras differ in no perceptible way in body, intellect or capacity, and caste produces no causal efficacy at all. this episode works through a specific metaphysical debate in the history of indian philosophy from start to finish: from universal realism to "caste is a cognitive failure," the chain of argument is complete, not a vague cultural introduction. people interested in indian philosophy and the metaphysical problem of universals; people who want to understand how the caste system can be dismantled by philosophical argument rather than moral condemnation. philosophy bites philosophy bites nilanjan das on buddhist philosophy and caste indian philosophy buddhism caste metaphysics universals caste has two layers: four varnas plus countless jatis nilanjan das first unpacks the structure of caste: one layer is the four occupational ranks — brahmin, kshatriya, vaishya, shudra — corresponding to different occupations; the other is the endogamous social groups embedded within them, the jatis. the former are called varnas, the latter jatis. the key point is that it is simultaneously a hierarchy of social power and political power, with brahmins and kshatriyas at the top and the rest below. and whichever rank you are born into is the one you stay in: caste is transmitted through lineage, not through any other factor. das also concedes that the history of the caste system's own origins is unclear, and that it appeared roughly alongside the brahmanical forms of the mid-first millennium bce. nilanjan das the opponent's analogy: brahminhood is like doghood dharmakirti's main opponent, kumarila, holds a kind of universal realism: when we watch two dachshunds running in a field, besides seeing particular features like brown color and wagging tails, we also see the shared property of "doghood." properties of this kind, if taken to exist independently of individual objects, are what philosophers of the time called universals, and what they themselves called samanyas or jatis. kumarila's inference is: just as dogs share doghood, brahmins share "brahminhood," and — this is the strangest point, das says — we can actually see a brahmin's brahminhood. das concedes this looks odd at first glance: the distinction between dogs and snakes is natural, but saying all brahmins share a property that non-brahmins lack is something else entirely. nilanjan das seeing brahminhood is not the same as recognizing a brahmin here there is a key distinction: non-epistemic seeing versus epistemic seeing. the former is seeing something without seeing it as anything; the latter is seeing it as something. das gives an example: if i had never seen a dog, i might see a dog and its doghood yet be unable to identify it as a dog — identification requires the background capacity to classify and categorize. kumarila would say the same of brahmins: you might see a brahmin together with his brahminhood yet be unable to see him as a brahmin. so even if you put a group of brahmins and non-brahmins into the same identity line-up, wearing the same clothes and with the same haircut, das says kumarila would probably hold that he could still pick out who is a brahmin — but there is an important qualification here. nilanjan das dharmakirti's test: structure, properties, causal power what dharmakirti himself says is actually quite basic: we can grasp a natural distinction between objects only under certain conditions — when the objects differ in physical structure, or differ in some important property, or differ in causal power. he cites cows and horses: a cow's shape and structure differ from a horse's, a cow's milk tastes different from a horse's, and a cow can do things a horse cannot, so we can posit a natural distinction between cows and horses. but on dharmakirti's view, no such distinction exists between brahmins and other caste ranks such as shudras: brahmins are no different from other castes in body, intellect or capacity. so there is no reason to think we can grasp a natural distinction between castes. das stresses dharmakirti's general principle: if you want to posit that something exists, it has to "earn its place," by proving that it has causal efficacy and can produce effects in the world. nilanjan das caste is like an occupational surname, not like witchcraft asked whether dharmakirti is saying caste is a social construction, das gives a careful answer. dharmakirti does hold that many of the things we think and talk about — tables, chairs, properties like brown — are constructed through our conceptual capacities, yet they are still true in another sense, because without granting them, everyday activity could not proceed. dharmakirti thinks caste terms like brahmin and shudra they legislate in their own interest, then force the ruled to obey, and call that obedience justice. so the ruled, in obeying the law, are merely serving the interest of the stronger — a fool who has been duped. he pushes the discussion further, from politics into the private sphere: injustice is serving one's own interest as effectively and ruthlessly as possible, and justice is a fool's game. socrates will need all ten books to answer this challenge. angie hobbs thrasymachus conceives of the good life too narrowly the fulcrum socrates can use to lever open this debate lies in how narrow thrasymachus's understanding of ‘flourishing’ is: he equates living well with having power over others, possessing great material wealth and good things. socrates cuts in here, pointing out that this is a narrow conception of the ‘good life’. the debate is then restated as: whether a just person always lives better, no matter how successful the unjust person is in the world; and whether justice itself is good. angie hobbs look first at the city writ large, then at the soul writ small socrates proposes a direct analogy between justice in the city and justice in the individual: if one can call a city just, one can likewise call a person just, and both are talking about the same thing. so he suggests looking first at justice in the city ‘writ large’, then inferring from it to justice in the individual ‘writ small’. but mccabe reminds us that what the book really sets out to answer is individual justice, and that the whole picture of political justice in the city is always in service of that analogy; he does not choose among them. this view is in fact consistent with the mainstream view of anthropology's first hundred years (roughly 1860 to 1960), which later fell out of favour after being charged with being a projection of western centrism, and after schneider's critique. wilson thinks that old view had the right direction, and that the problem is to cut it apart from its bad associations with racism and ethnocentrism. robert wilson anthropology's discussion of incest omits the clinical literature wilson worked early on memory and trauma, and came into contact with judith herman's clinical work on incest. he found that anthropology's discussion of incest avoidance makes no mention of this clinical literature at all, and focuses almost exclusively on sibling incest. but the most prominent form clinically is cross-generational: father-daughter, older men with younger women in the household, uncles, stepfathers, family friends. he does not argue that clinical cases should serve as cross-cultural ethnographic evidence; he only points out that if you want to talk about avoidance mechanisms without looking at this evidence, the conclusions you can reach are necessarily limited. robert wilson the westermark hypothesis was pushed out of the field by freud in his 1890 work on the history of human marriage, westermark proposed that people who grow up together lack sexual attraction to each other as adults and develop sexual aversion. wilson thinks there is a fair amount of evidence supporting this direction. but as freud's thought entered cultural anthropology in the 1920s and 30s, the hypothesis was thrown out of the field wholesale, and he thinks it was never seriously engaged with. what concerns him is not westermark himself, but why the hypothesis was excluded so thoroughly. robert wilson israeli kibbutzim and taiwanese minor marriages both support it two independent studies appeared in the 1950s and 60s. one was the israeli kibbutz: children who grew up together in the same community were culturally expected to intermarry, yet the actual marriage rate was lower than expected; and even when they did marry, the divorce rate was higher and fertility lower. the other was the ‘minor marriage’ system in taiwan and parts of china: girls were sent into another family to be raised alongside a boy, with the expectation of later marriage, and the result was a markedly lower divorce rate and reported sexual attraction. wilson thinks these are not conclusive, but they are at least evidence from within anthropology, and it was not taken seriously. robert wilson lévi-strauss said the animal world has no incest avoidance, and that is wrong lévi-strauss said that if you look at non-human animals, incest is everywhere, especially among our closest primate relatives; the time practised cremation. in much of europe people were buried with large quantities of fine grave goods, whereas cremation followed by burial destroys a great deal of useful archaeological evidence. so although there are very fine metal objects and monuments, the absence of burial evidence makes this history unusually hard to read. he also points out that using the phrase "celtic iron age" to describe the period amounts to sticking an ethnic label on an era, adding another layer of trouble to an already complicated story. dr john waddell sea routes connected people rather than isolating them waddell repeatedly stresses an underrated fact: in prehistory, waterways were channels connecting people, not barriers. ireland and britain are both islands, and people habitually assume islands mean isolation, but coastal routes and river routes were very likely the main means of connection. before the romans built straight roads, travel by water was far easier than travel by land. this means we have consistently underestimated how connected the populations of prehistoric britain and ireland were. the irish sea was itself a connecting force, and the english channel linked england to the continent. dr john waddell sacred sites sat on high ground, not by rivers tristan asks whether iron age settlements were all close to rivers and coasts. waddell's answer is unexpected: since the neolithic. tara was already an important burial place before 3000 bc, and its story runs into the medieval period, representing more than 4000 years of ritual activity. the importance of these places comes from accumulated time and religious meaning, not from rivers and sea routes. dr john waddell a sacral king who fails or is wounded is deposed waddell draws a key concept out of medieval irish texts: sacral kingship. the king of tara was not a political strongman; his fundamental duty was to maintain the cosmic order. if a sacral king could not bring good harvests, he was deposed. another feature was that his body had to be flawless: once a sacral king was wounded, scarred or deformed, he was deposed. waddell thinks this ritual may eventually be traceable in the archaeology of britain and ireland, suggesting that in the celtic era, the pre-roman period, certain tribal rulers did indeed carry a sacred quality. dr john waddell the celts were not invaders but a language community the traditional story is that around 500 bc a celtic-speaking people brought knowledge of iron to ireland. waddell says this is wrong. his best definition of the ancient celts is "people who spoke celtic", not an ethnic or racial definition. ireland in the pre-roman period was undoubtedly celtic-speaking, but archaeology finds almost no evidence of immigrants in the iron age or the late bronze age. instead, from around 1000 bc there is abundant archaeological evidence of trade and exchange between britain and ireland, with the thames, the rhine, the rhône, the saône, the ruhr and the danube all serving as major corridors. trade and exchange means the movement of people, and people carried myths, legends and language with them. the celtic languages most likely took shape gradually amid this late bronze age surge of connectivity. dr john waddell the banquet hall is really a ceremonial processional way on the hill of tara there is a monument called the "banquet was killed. founders and investors interested in intelligence machinery, organizational failure and decision psychology; managers who want to understand why warning does not stop catastrophe. empire: world history empire 世界史 394. road to 9/11: hijackers, cia failures, and america’s darkest day (part 6) intelligence failure organizational decisions 9/11 al-qaeda history after the cole bombing, america did nothing for seven months in october 2000 the uss cole was bombed in aden harbor. the clinton administration had only four months left in office and was still arguing internally over who did it; the cia quickly concluded it was al-qaeda. but once the bush administration took over, it sat still for a full seven months. bergen's explanation is not negligence but a cognitive frame: rumsfeld had been secretary of defense in the ford administration, condoleezza rice was a soviet specialist, and this cohort had spent its whole life inside the cold war. they could not accept that a non-state actor without state sponsorship could constitute a threat. the main threat they identified was iraq. so even with warnings coming constantly, the top simply could not make the turn. peter bergen the cia did its job well, but the client can choose not to look bergen stresses a structural fact: the cia's job is to give policymakers strategic warning, and in the spring and summer of 2001 it did that job excellently, warning repeatedly that something big was coming. the problem is that the cia serves a "client" — the white house. if the president chooses to ignore it, the cia can do no better. the 9/11 commission later disclosed these warnings, and the bush administration fought hard to prevent that commission from being created. bergen says he had just finished his first book on bin laden a week before 9/11, and at the time he needed no access to classified material to know something was brewing. peter bergen two hijackers entered america and the cia forgot the watchlist department watchlist until august 25, 2001, leaving just over two weeks to 9/11. bergen says plainly that this was not a conspiracy but the "cock-up view of history" — a pile of people knew these two men had us visas, roughly 60 people inside the cia could see the information, but nobody told the fbi and nobody told the state department. he also mentions a "wall" between the cia and the fbi: the cia collects intelligence, the fbi collects criminal evidence, the two are different in nature, and the cia was even barred from sharing large amounts of intelligence with the fbi. peter bergen the where reagan airport was — what bergen calls a "casing videotape," unambiguously reconnaissance, not a tourist filming scenery. on the tape he also talks about the plan, about "the devil in the white house," and uses "the brothers," al-qaeda's internal term for itself. the tape came to light because after 9/11 this man was living in birmingham, and when british police searched his flat they found the second was driven back to harbour by a storm. the soldiers refused to board again. cinna called an assembly to dress them down, and when his guards used their rods to clear a path they hurt a soldier, who struck back — and it turned into a general brawl. the soldiers drew their swords and stabbed cinna dead on the spot. he died without even reaching greece. it was enormous luck for sulla: the opposition's most substantial leader was gone, leaving only the 26-year-old son of marius to hold the stage. jupiter's temple burned, and marius's son looted it to buy office after the temple was struck by lightning and burned, sulla's side could say jupiter was punishing cinna for breaking his oath. but the temple held rome's gold reserve — effectively the central bank. young marius rushed up the capitoline and, without saving a single statue or relic, swept up the treasure to pay a private army and bribe votes. in 82 bc, at 26, he became consul, which by roman convention was utterly unthinkable. even sulla was shocked, and said something bitter: the older he got, the younger his enemies became. the samnites nearly took rome while it lay undefended the samnites were sulla's most ferocious enemies. they were on their way to relieve the besieged young marius at praeneste when they noticed rome was almost undefended, and abruptly turned and drove straight at the city. sulla was caught off guard and raced after them. the samnite commander said outside the walls: do you think these wolves, who have committed such monstrous crimes against italian freedom, will simply vanish unless you destroy the forest that shelters them? they charged the colline gate. at that very moment sulla's cavalry slammed into the samnite rear, and sulla himself arrived with his exhausted army and threw it into battle at once, against his legate's advice. the fighting went on all night; h: ai is a rounding error for ordinary people: diffusion takes fifty years, backlash won't wait the industrial revolution gave ordinary people cheap clothes and sewing machines; ai so far gives them fun images and better search — the benefits are too indirect, and the political backlash is coming too fast. an eight-minute short take, not especially dense, but it offers a counterintuitive angle: ai's biggest risk isn't technical failure, it's that ordinary people can't feel the benefits. suited to founders and investors watching ai narratives and policy risk, especially practitioners who want to understand why the public is indifferent or even hostile to ai. interconnects interconnects when will average people feel ai’s impact? ai diffusion public perception political backlash robotics knowledge work ai is still a rounding error in daily life the author spent weeks on his honeymoon without touching ai at all, and on returning realised: the points where ordinary people encounter ai are either marginal or confusing. the positive impressions are making fun images and an enhanced google search; the negative impressions are addictive social media algorithms, a friend of a friend addicted to an ai chatbot, and various claims about data centers. family, food, transportation, entertainment — the core of daily life — have barely changed directly. his conclusion: being fascinated by ai is the result of a very small number of people actively choosing it, and stepping outside the bubble reveals that what's happening today really isn't that important to most people. the industrial revolution gave physical things; ai gives indirect benefits the first industrial revolution brought cheaper clothes, cookware, reading material and new livelihoods; the second brought sewing machines, food preservation, indoor plumbing, photography, better light sources, bicycles and electrification — a long list, and a very physical one. the author worries that even if ai's benefits materialise (new scientific discoveries, treatments for rare diseases, sustained economic abundance), they are too indirect: ordinary people won't credit openai or anthropic with saving their life, because it was their family doctor who told them about the new treatment; and not many americans will care that openai solved the navier-stokes millennium prize problem. he judges that fifty years from now, the daily life of the average american will still look a lot like today. ai today is mainly a tool serving elites knowledge work is roughly half the us economy, and for that half ai is already (or soon will be) as foundational as electricity, with rapid agent improvements over the next eighteen months accelerating this. but a transformative, highly productive tool that only lifts half of society is highly unstable. the author cites the "engels' pause": from 1790 to 1840 british workers' wages stagnated while gdp per capita grew rapidly amid technological upheaval. he argues that if the ai industry itself thinks this is the closest analogy, then backlash from those who don't benefit is reasonable. he also agrees with doug o'laughlin's judgment: knowledge work output explodes while headcount in the tech industry very likely shrinks. the backlash's root isn't ai, it's big tech's old debts the author splits the political backlash ai faces into two layers: first, the early positive effects are too indirect; second, they are deeply intertwined with western society's historical grievances against big tech. he stresses that the latter merely collided with ai in time — if ai's exponential growth had happened decades after the growing pains of platforms like google and meta, the data center issue very likely would never have risen to such a central political position. solving either one would greatly relieve the pressure and give the industry more time to make the positive case. and ai itself, through doom rhetoric and declarations of mass unemployment, has marked itself as a negative or unsafe technology, making both harder. robots might rescue the narrative for llms the author raises an ironic possibility: if the intelligence explosion from large-scale production of large language models spills over into robotics, accelerating the spread of robots in daily life, humans will quickly seize on ai's tangible benefits. this is ironic because many people have been working hard to convince the public that this llm wave is very different from the general ai progress of the past ten or twenty years. if in the end the same dynamic saves (or largely overshadows) the llm narrative, that would be funny. he also cautions that the connection between robotics, autonomous driving and the current ai revolution is currently more a matter of storytelling. diffusion takes fifty years; milder the counterintuitive mechanism: hurricanes, downpours and blizzards all start with water vapor. the clausius-clapeyron equation says a warmer atmosphere holds more water vapor. for every 1 degree fahrenheit of warming, water vapor increases about 4% (7% in celsius). a century ago the northeast us averaged 22 degrees fahrenheit in winter; now it's up to 26, and some years 30 — against 22 degrees that's a 32% increase in water vapor, and 30 degrees is still below the 32-degree freezing point. so a warmer planet means more water in the atmosphere, and blizzards can hit harder. dr. marshall shepherd the hurricane cone is probability, not a path during hurricane ian in 2022, some people evacuated from one part of the cone to another — a complete misreading. the cone means the storm center has a 67% chance of falling somewhere inside it, not that the storm will travel down the cone's center line. shepard says the public broadly struggles with probability, uncertainty, two meteorologists are always wrong. but that day wasn't 0% — they just happened to be in that 20% area. statistically, 80% of the area stayed dry and they landed in the 20% that got rain. one way to compute pop is confidence of rain × fraction of area affected: 60% confidence over 60% of the area gives a pop of 36%. so "20% chance" doesn't mean "it won't rain" — it's describing a regional h: mathematicians feared ai would write a thousand-page proof. it wrote 15 pages. humans disproved a conjecture about random graphs in 250 pages, built on another 200; inside group theory, ai proved the weaker result in a dozen-odd pages. ai's math proofs are generally short and elegant — long proofs, it turns out, only humans write. two openai mathematicians take apart the proof details of sphere packing and group theory; the discussion of the bottleneck shifting from proof to understanding, and whether taste can be split across two models, is worth more than the results themselves. readers building ai applications or investing, especially those trying to judge whether models can only brute-force search; and researchers wondering how the scientific workflow gets rewritten. the a16z show a16z openai researchers on the future of mathematical reasoning mathematical reasoning openai model capability limits group theory research automation the first thing models replace is literature search erdős's problems were collected onto a website, and a problem marked open isn't necessarily unsolved — the mathematical literature itself is hard to search. one guest was unsure about one of them, threw it into gpt-5, and five minutes later the model produced a reference, which amounted to telling him the problem was within reach and this was how to do it. he and a few friends had already spent hours on it without being sure they could solve it. they then found ten-odd more cases of the same kind. the model's first beachhead isn't proving, but the retrieval and detail execution that eats the most time for mathematicians. the model isn't smarter, it's more willing to bet a human mathematician's day is "gambling with problems": you have an idea, you think it might work, you try it for hours, days, weeks, then give up; a year or two later you learn someone else got the approach you'd thought of to work. the model's difference isn't inspiration — it's that it doesn't compute risk and reward. if a human tells it to do it, it does it to the end. and it isn't brute-forcing: it tries many different paths, very persistently, but it can only try finitely many ideas, pruning the search tree with existing knowledge plus mathematical judgment. on the unit distance problem, the idea may have been thought of long ago; what's genuinely hard is aligning all the extremely tedious execution details, and that's the part humans get lost in and the model gets almost never wrong. humans get polluted by their own thinking; models don't once a human has gone down a wrong path for a while, the earliest idea gets bound up with everything that failed afterward — in the guest's words, the context window is polluted, and you can't clone a clean session off last week's self and say, don't do this, rebuild your intuition in another direction. a model can, and worst case it just starts a new game. its way of updating "how likely is this path to work" is also more computational: a human automatically downgrades confidence in a method after the first failure, while the model seems better at repeatedly adjusting probabilities rather than killing a path outright. so it does backtrack and make mistakes — it just doesn't get dragged down by them. the model turned a numerical guess into an equals sign the sphere packing problem has exact answers in only five dimensions: 1, 2, 3, 8, 24; the 3-dimensional proof is at minimum several hundred pages and famously ugly. the long-standing best upper bound came from a two-page 1970s paper by two russian mathematicians, with a constant of 2 to the -0.599d — the solution to some extremely ugly optimization problem. viazovska's linear programming framework hits the optimum exactly only in dimensions 8 and 24, which is a major reason she won the fields medal. what the model did was not shrink the constant a little, but prove that the framework's optimal value in large dimensions is itself that beautiful asymptotic expression: an equals sign, not an inequality. one guest spent about six months on this problem during his phd with zero progress, and finally watched the model finish it off with a few pages of complex analysis. one "push it further" buys a conjectured value of the ten problems, only the pair of spherical codes and binary codes interacted: they first had the model improve the code bound using representation theory, and the model stopped once it was done; h: ect is not what you think: a century of drift from back room to routine treatment modern ect is a procedure performed under anesthesia and muscle relaxants, with strong efficacy, but the evidence on memory-loss side effects is still not fully clear, and social misunderstanding has left it over-stigmatized. if your image of ect is still stuck on one flew over the cuckoo's nest, this episode will completely reset it. hear the actual procedure, the indications, the side effects, and one expert's clinical account. clinicians, psychiatric and pediatric staff, medical students, and anyone who has doubts about ect or wants to understand the evidence behind first-line treatment. this podcast will kill you this podcast will kill you ep 221 electroconvulsive therapy part 2: a current conversation psychiatry electroconvulsive therapy brain science treatment-resistant depression neuroimmunology medical misconceptions what actually happens if you or i get ect if you or i were to receive ect, here is how it goes: first a risk assessment and informed consent, then a physical exam, then an overnight fast. the next morning, in the hospital or an outpatient clinic, an iv line is placed along with two blood pressure cuffs (arm and right leg), and ekg, eeg and emg leads are connected. after the anesthesiologist puts you to sleep, the leg cuff is inflated to restrict blood flow to the right foot, then a muscle relaxant such as succinylcholine is given. once the muscles are fully relaxed, a bite block is placed, and then a brief pulse of current is delivered through the electrodes (lasting seconds, even half a second). the goal is not to make your whole body convulse, but to induce a generalized seizure, typically lasting 25-70 seconds. because the muscles are relaxed, you see almost no external movement — the whole thing is obvious on the eeg. erin allman-updike electrode placement, and why the right side comes first there are several electrode placements: bitemporal (like in the movies), bifrontal, and most commonly 'right unilateral' — one electrode on the right temple, the other on the right side of the top of the head. right unilateral is used for most people because it produces fewer cognitive side effects. why consider the right side first? because for about 98% of right-handed people and 70%-90% of left-handed people, language function sits in the left temporal lobe. avoiding electrical stimulation on the left side theoretically reduces language-related memory problems. but right unilateral is slightly less effective than bilateral. during a course of treatment, doctors switch based on side effects and efficacy: if bilateral side effects are heavy, switch to right unilateral; if right unilateral is not working well, switch to bilateral. erin allman-updike seizure threshold and the effective dose the seizure threshold is the minimum amount of current that can induce a seizure. there is no precise measuring device, so you start by estimating from age, then probe upward from a low dose until a seizure appears. but treatment does not stop at merely reaching threshold — the effective dose is usually 2.5 to 5 times the threshold. with bilateral, 2.5 times is enough, while right unilateral needs 5 times, because unilateral stimulation has a harder time achieving the same effect. the dose varies from person to person and has to be adjusted as you go. if in one session a patient's seizure does not occur or does not last long enough (less than 25 seconds), the doctor may increase the dose and try again. treatment is generally three times a week, with a full course of 6 to 18 sessions, sometimes longer. erin allman-updike we still do not know exactly how ect works why does shocking the brain treat depression and catatonia? frankly: we still do not fully understand. there are several main hypotheses. one is neurotransmitter change: after ect, serotonin, dopamine and gaba (an inhibitory transmitter) all change markedly. the rise in gaba is itself anticonvulsant, which could explain why the seizure threshold rises and seizures get shorter over a course of treatment. two, large fluctuations in hormones such as acth, prolactin and tsh are seen in the hypothalamus and pituitary. three, ect promotes neurogenesis, with bdnf (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) as a key molecule. but how these changes directly relieve symptoms still has no one-to-one mechanism. different illnesses (depression, schizophrenia, catatonia) may also work through different mechanisms, and for now we can only keep researching. can cut the 30-day readmission rate in half. this is

h: a kid who loses everything isn't lazy — the prefrontal cortex isn't done yet a 14-year-old boy's prefrontal cortex won't finish developing until 25, so losing things isn't an attitude problem. the real problem: parents whose own executive function is already stretched thin are supposed to build a system the kid can't possibly hold up. this episode has medium information density, but it breaks ‘executive function’ into operable mechanisms: why an alarm is more reliable than memory, why a visual timer beats a phone, why you can't force a kid to care about something he doesn't care about. suited to parents anxious about the back-to-school season. parents of middle-schoolers drowning in school emails at the start of the term, whose kids lose everything and who drop the ball themselves; janet's first piece of advice is to expect it. the child is tired, you're tired, this is the moment of reconnection, and it often feels like the longest stretch of the day. she stresses that this isn't your imagination, isn't unique to your family, and isn't something wrong with you or your child. being caught off guard makes it far harder. looked at the other way, a child unloading their emotions onto the person closest to them is itself a positive signal — it means he treats you as a safe base. other transitions in family life amplify the difficulty: you or your partner starting a the professional hat: holding the boundary, not just saying it but actually stopping things; expecting that the child will lose control, so you walk in not already overwhelmed; allowing the child to nag and pester repeatedly, reading it as his way of sharing the day's stress, without giving in just to soothe him. janet says this is quality time too, maybe even more important than party-hat time, because it's harder — harder because you're giving love and getting no love back, and you have to keep acting out of love without any acknowledgment from your child. janet lansbury hold the boundary and still leave room for the feeling the third point is to leave the child lots of space for his emotions while you hold the boundary, and to acknowledge them as much as you can. not just "i can't let you do that," but at the same time: you're having a hard time right now, this really is hard, you really want me to say yes, and i said no, so you're frustrated. janet stresses that this isn't only because it's positive parenting — it's because it's practical: when a child feels seen, heard and safe inside his emotions, those emotions pass faster. if he doesn't need to keep showing you his feelings through his behavior, he doesn't have to keep performing them for you. she calls this the real quality time, and says that if you can see it that way, you'll walk into these situations with more confidence and more inner calm. janet lansbury you can give up family dinner; you can't give up connection janet acknowledges that family dinner has a lot of research behind it, but there's also a fair amount of research pointing to the negative effects of parents being under chronic stress. she suggests lowering expectations around perfect quality time and family dinner, because the most h: documentary director: there is no typical old age, only specific people fan shiguang, who shot two seasons of qian lang, says most marriages end up lukewarm or worse, and growing old together to the very end is rare. what we lack most isn't stories — it's money, and the habit of seeing old people as specific human beings. the first half is the two hosts talking, more feeling than fact; the second half is the director interview, packed with killed story ideas and behind-the-scenes detail, and the information density is clearly higher. worth starting at 41 minutes. listeners following aging, caregiving, family structures and documentary practice; people in elder care, insurance, legal services and content work can treat the second-half director interview as a story-selection methodology. 不合时宜 不合时宜 我们如何老去？从《前浪》窥见中国老年生活的真实图景 aging caregiving documentary advance directives family structure a five-million-yuan estate, and the law fighting the will an elderly woman with no close family died in a shanghai nursing home. while alive she had made an advance guardianship notarization with notary li chengyang, but she never wrote a will. sorting through her belongings, the notary found she had left an estate of five million yuan, including a house, cash and passbooks. she had said many times orally that she wanted to donate it to society and did not want it to go to relatives, but that wish had no legal form. li chengyang ultimately chose to follow the law and look for statutory heirs, tracing through archives to children and relatives she had not seen in years. there was disagreement inside the notary office too; some colleagues thought they should simply respect the old woman's wishes. the compromise was to propose to the inheriting children that 200,000 yuan of the five million go to a fund helping old people with no one to rely on. the children agreed. ruohan whether they slept together decided whether the estate could go to her an elderly man with a terminal illness gave his advance guardianship rights and his estate to a woman who had cared for him for years and was not a relative — and he had a biological daughter. the notary office debated this fiercely, and one key point was whether the two slept together: if they did not, the caregiver was just a nanny or a live-in housekeeper, and an old man leaving his estate to his nanny was morally acceptable; if there was a sexual relationship, the matter stopped conforming to public morals. the caregiver was herself married, but had had no contact for years, so in effect the marriage did not exist. so it became an open-relationship question, and the notary office did not want to bear the risk of offending public morals on the basis of that judgment. qing old people finding new partners increasingly don't register the marriage li kangmei, the subject of episode two, was with lao li for eighteen years and never registered the marriage, and there was no de facto marital relationship. the hosts found this far more common than they had imagined: after divorce or the loss of a first marriage, many older people entering a new relationship choose not to marry. they don't necessarily say they love this person; they say they want someone to keep them company, someone to take care of them, and behind that is a fairly deep need against loneliness. lao li already had a terminal illness, and li kangmei's choice was whether to stay to the last moment or to leave early because there was no de facto marital relationship. ruohan reality tv forces you to pick a side every five minutes the hosts contrast documentary with reality tv: much of the tension in reality tv is manufactured, backed by a very strong narrative — for instance, knowing the audience has views about mama's boys, so they fabricate a mama's boy on screen. this destroys the audience's tolerance for the complexity of real intimate relationships: every plot beat, every five minutes, demands a position, and that position must be the morally correct one, then gets projected onto some character, and wherever that character goes you take his side. documentary does the opposite: it shows that everyone has it hard, some characters get more screen time and some less, but you can see what each of them is up against, and quite a few of them appear pixelated and anonymous. qing the older generation says i sleep badly, not i'm depressed medical anthropologist arthur kleinman found that young people today have a rich psychological vocabulary and can quickly say i'm depressed, i'm anxious, i'm a bit bipolar; but older people, even when expressing psychological needs, still use somatized language — i've been sleeping badly lately, i have a bit of a headache — and won't say i sleep badly because i think too much, that i'm a bit depressed. the hosts explain: in our culture it is easier to talk about physical pain, everyone gets a headache or a fever, there's no stigma; the moment you talk about depression or anxiety, it's a different order of ‖ 不合時宜 不合時宜 我們如何老去 從 前浪 窺見中國老年生活的真實圖景

h: google invented the transformer, then handed the llm era to openai google held the transformer, tpus and the most compute at once, yet the burden of search advertising and infighting between two ai teams let it hand the most critical track — language models — to openai. high information density, a detailed 15-year organizational history of google ai, especially the second half's details of two teams fighting over compute and release rights, which are rarely seen elsewhere. suited to founders and investors watching the llm competitive landscape, especially those who want to understand why technical leadership does not equal product leadership, and how organizational infighting eats away at a first-mover advantage. 科技这碗饭 科技这碗饭 谷歌ai风云15年：诸神黄昏——发明未来的人为何错过未来？ google deepmind transformer llms organization ai chips google's underlying problem was solved once and for all in 2000, google's index had not updated for five months, and engineers searched for days without finding the cause. jeff dean and sanjay compared a batch of seemingly unrelated errors side by side and discovered that a single bit in machine memory would mysteriously flip — to save money, google's servers used cheap memory without error correction. they did not ask for more expensive machines; instead they added a layer of insurance at the software level, automatically isolating any machine that produced errors. this is the most typical way the two work: not fixing failures at the surface, but going deep into the underlying layer to solve this class of problems once and for all, so that other engineers no longer have to consider whether the machine itself might fail. building a chip specifically for neural networks jeff dean used speech as a single estimate, made a two-page ppt for management: in the future, every android user speaks for three minutes a day, and just processing that speech would require google's global data centers to expand two to three times. his solution was to build a chip specifically for neural networks, ignoring everything else. this went against his long-held view on chips — specialized hardware is usually not a good idea, because by the time it is built the algorithms have already changed generations — but neural networks were the exception: image recognition and speech dictation are both fundamentally the same kind of matrix multiplication. to shorten the timeline, the chip was made as a plug-in card that fit into the server space originally reserved for hard drives, and from project start to installation in data centers took only 15 months. the phone call hassabis made to hinton hinton held an auction by email from a hotel room, with buyers including google, microsoft, baidu, and the fourth being hassabis's deepmind. deepmind had little cash on hand, and what hassabis bid was $10 million in company stock, roughly one-fifth of the entire company. the price quickly exceeded what he could afford, and after withdrawing he called hinton and said that although he had only meant to offer ten million to buy you, in his heart he felt your true value was $50 million. hinton took that in; microsoft executives privately raised their offer by $10 million and he was tempted for a moment, but ultimately declined. google finally paid $44 million to buy hinton and two students. others look at the hood, he wants to see the engine google's due diligence team flew to london, and jeff dean was among them, tasked with verifying for google whether what deepmind claimed was actually true. at the time deepmind had only 50 people and no revenue, yet the price offered was twice what google usually paid for companies of the same size, and many at the negotiating table found it absurd; jeff dean also thought it was a bit expensive. after the ppt was shown, he made one request: he wanted to see the source code. demos can be packaged, but code is hard to fake. the researcher responsible for writing the code panicked, because when doing research, code is written only to get experiments running as quickly as possible, and is usually messy and hard to read. hassabis later called this moment crossing the rubicon — once the code was handed over, there was no turning back. the more successful alphago became, the less likely independence was deepmind wanted to use the alphabet reorganization to spin out from google, and negotiations lasted over a year, with terms even put on paper. but pichai said on the phone that the other bets column was reserved for moonshot projects far from google's homepage, and ai no longer belonged in that category — it was becoming google's most core technology. hassabis's past strength was to first win a battle big enough, then use the victory to trade for the next stage's筹码, but this time the筹码 changed in the opposite direction: the more successful alphago became, the more important ai was inside google, the closer it was to the core of the homepage, and the less likely it could be placed in other bets. in april 2021, hassabis ann ‖ 科技這碗飯 科技這碗飯 谷歌 風雲 年 諸神黃昏 發明未來的人為何錯過未來

h: latin doesn't make surgeons: exams should be hard at something useful latin doesn't make surgeons: skills barely transfer. if you assume "the harder the subject, the sharper the mind," a nation's brightest get wasted on the most useless knowledge — that is the lesson of the qing examination system. it puts imperial civil-service exams, military selection and modern transfer experiments on a single chain of evidence, unusually connecting history with talent assessment — and the two sides genuinely clash. gatekeepers of talent assessment, exam design, school curricula and civil-service hiring, plus every teacher, parent and learner who believes a hard subject sharpens the mind. econtalk econtalk meritocracy, exams, and the knowledge that matters (with daisy christodoulou) education exams skill transfer bureaucracy signaling talent selection wrong exam content dooms the country, however smart the candidates hong xiuquan failed the qing examinations at least four times. after his last failure, he had a vision on the road home, believed himself the brother of christ, and eventually launched the taiping rebellion — which daisy says may be the deadliest civil war in human history, with deaths around thirty million. hong was not alone among failures: examination seats fell far short of the number of candidates, many sat the exams into their forties and fifties without passing, and the only way home was to teach. daisy adds that the deeper cost fell on those who passed: they were masters of the eight-legged essay yet knew nothing of the science and mathematics transforming the world. when the brightest young men can only practice a dead format, the country bleeds from both ends. daisy christodoulou british civil-service reform was elites reproducing themselves the northcote-trevelyan report is often seen by the british as the founding document of the modern civil service, but daisy backs the revisionist judgment: in the name of a unified exam, it pushed oxford and cambridge classics graduates into key posts. benjamin jowett, master of balliol, worked behind the scenes to place his classics students throughout the empire. michael coolican's "no tradesmen and no women" points out that the 1854 report reduced the most brazen buying and selling of offices, but also snuffed out the professional exams that departments had been growing. exams can select people; what they test decides whether they select the worthy or select people like the selectors. daisy christodoulou a bureaucracy without price signals corrects itself through corpses daisy attributes bureaucratic failure to the absence of feedback: no price mechanism, no profit and loss, so a department cannot tell whether its program saves or kills. the military sounds like a counterexample, but military bureaucracies err just as constantly in peacetime; almost every time britain went to war after a long peace, the first year bred a crisis, as with the shell crisis at the start of world war i. what actually forces correction is not internal inspection but mass death on the battlefield. she calls it a crueler error-correction mechanism than prices. to make a bureaucracy reliable, you must first create a signal that shows consequences; otherwise no amount of rigor in selection can save the quality of everyday decisions. daisy christodoulou the royal navy won by testing navigation, not latin daisy notes that the true pillar of victorian britain was not the army but the royal navy. as early as 1677, after a run of defeats by the dutch, samuel pepys set an oral exam for captains: three senior officers questioned them face to face on how to command a ship. over the next century and more, navigation, charting and trigonometry entered the written exams, and chart-makers like nelson, cook, flinders and bligh passed through this gate. daisy draws out two exam traditions: pepys tested skills needed immediately; macaulay and northcote-trevelyan later wanted classical languages. one served safety at sea, the other a layer of status — naturally the effects differed. daisy christodoulou content doesn't matter? macaulay's screening argument misses the key link here comes the highlight: daisy reads aloud macaulay's 1833 parliamentary speech. the gist: whatever a age happens to teach, the best at it will necessarily be the cleverest, most industrious and most honor-seeking of the young; so cambridge could teach ptolemy instead of newton and its top students would still be excellent; teach cherokee instead of greek and the best cherokee scholars would still be the finest; even astrology and alchemy would do. another mp praised it on the spot as the most practically wise speech in parliamentary history, but daisy says flatly: this is eloquence running away with him, missing entirely that "what you learn really does matter." daisy christodoulou dead twigs and corn: wrong content makes discipline just watering daisy closes out macaulay with the 1917 rebuttal of the american medical educator

h: ai power concentration is a result of today's technology, not the endgame transformers only get smart by being fed massive data and compute, so power sits with the big companies that can afford data centers; but the transformer isn't even ten years old, and the human brain is proof that small-data expertise exists. an 8-minute solo interview, medium information density, but the transformer author's argument that concentration is a property of the technology rather than of ai itself is worth hearing. founders and investors watching open-source models, compute costs and the ai power landscape; anyone trying to judge whether concentration is inevitable. the a16z show a16z can open source keep ai power from concentrating? open-source models compute transformer ai power landscape concentration is a property of the current technical path lucas kaiser attributes ai power concentration to the state of the technology rather than to the nature of ai: a transformer is only "reasonably smart" when fed the entire internet's data, and once you let it learn only some small domain, it's "just stupid." so what big companies can do is not wait for a research breakthrough but go bigger, bigger, bigger — and bigger costs billions of dollars and requires scraping data from every corner of the internet. this path is inherently concentrating. but he stresses remembering that this is only the current state, and the transformer isn't even ten years old. lucas kaiser without a research breakthrough, you can only pile on scale kaiser distinguishes two paths: one is waiting for a research breakthrough that lets models get smart on less data; the other is not waiting and simply piling on scale. the problem is that research breakthroughs "sometimes they come, sometimes they don't" — it isn't a business proposal and can't be put on a roadmap. piling on scale, by contrast, can be executed immediately, at the cost of billions of dollars and scraping the whole internet's data. this asymmetry — that the executable path happens to be the most concentrating one — is the mechanism behind the current landscape, not deliberate monopolization by big companies. lucas kaiser humans are the existence proof for small-data expertise asked whether there is an algorithmic breakthrough that would let smaller players compete, kaiser's answer is "we know it exists. we are the proof": humans aren't generalists who know everything, yet in their own fields experts are sometimes stronger than very large-scale models. so this capability must be technically achievable; we just haven't found how to do it yet. he even guesses the answer may still involve an attention layer, because what determines the result isn't only the model architecture but also the loss, the data and the training method — too many variables to know where exactly to look. lucas kaiser openai went from a research lab to a product company kaiser observes that the lab's research focus is declining: when he joined, openai was a pure research lab, and now "it's a research lab a bit," while also being a big company that has to ship products. he sees this as an opportunity window for the open-source movement and academia — as big companies get distracted making products, the research space is left to universities and independent researchers. he himself recently started doing research independently. lucas kaiser one consumer gpu beats the old eight-gpu machine kaiser bought a 5090 rtx gpu, with more compute than the eight-gpu machine his team used for the transformer research back then. his conclusion is very concrete: you can't train a big llm, but you can do research and experiments, and he thinks many people should. this is the hardest comparison in the whole piece — research that once required a team and a machine room can now be started by one person with one card. lucas kaiser the optimum may be many distributed models kaiser's optimism comes from an analogy: humans are the most amazing computers in the world, the brain still hasn't been surpassed by a model, and humans aren't generalists — there is no "one giant human brain." from this he speculates that, given a fixed amount of data, the best way to learn may be to have a large number of distributed models — each strong on its own, stronger together. he mentions that basic research related to ensembles contains reasons supporting this. lucas kaiser data getting expensive will pull research back to fundamentals kaiser points out that machine learning research didn't stop in 2017. because the transformer is so useful, everyone focused on the big-data path; but now that path has become so expensive that it may instead push attention back to more fundamental research. his judgment: we know a better algorithm exists that can learn from less data and perform well in the domain it learns, we just haven't found how to do it on a computer yet — but we will. lucas kaiser in the future everyone has their own model and their own sense of humor the endgame

and a three- or four-year-old has no language to assert "my body is mine to decide," so hitting and kicking become one of the few tools still available. so when the call home comes, don't rush to lecture "hands to yourself" — ask instead: how much say did this child have over his own life before this, and what bit of it can be handed back now. jen kindergarten readiness is really obedience training teachers often say a given preschool has a high share of kindergarten-ready children, and the core definition of that readiness is compliance: sit down when the teacher says sit, even mid-task, even when the body is already overloaded. parents fear that if the child doesn't comply now, he won't get into a good elementary school, college, a good life. but what the child pays for that definition is learning to suppress the feeling of "what i need right now." teachers aren't villains either — they too need to feel competent, to keep children safe, to save effort, even to enjoy a taste of power; many went into education precisely to repair their own childhood wounds, yet only know the power-over kind of relationship. only by seeing both sides' situations is there room to negotiate. jen we grant ourselves regulation and deny it to children if an adult at a party feels overloaded, he arrives early, leaves early, hides in a quiet room, even wears noise-cancelling earplugs — we find that entirely natural. turn the camera on a child, though, and apart from conventions like extra exam time, we immediately worry that "too much accommodation will spoil him, he'll never survive the real world." the truth is that adults grant themselves far more regulation than they allow children. the source offers a concrete image: an adult stronger than you unceremoniously carries you out of the quiet room back into the middle of the loud party — with an adult, you'd instantly see it as a violation of bodily autonomy; the model needed only the first 4 to 9 nucleotides of the phix174 genome for the accuracy of the output to rise markedly. the authors found that this unremarkable stretch is part of the origin of h: ion drives: the slow rockets that win space rockets aren't necessarily better the more powerful they are. an ion engine's thrust is as gentle as a sheet of paper, yet it can run continuously for years, accumulating speeds chemical rockets can't reach on a tiny fraction of the propellant — and becoming the workhorse of space logistics. this episode covers ion propulsion's principles, limits and applications in full — good for anyone who wants a systematic understanding of why electric propulsion is now mainstream for deep space and satellites; those with no taste for engine detail can focus on the thrust and applications segments. space industry professionals, satellite and deep-space mission planners, and engineers and investors interested in electric propulsion system selection and the economics of propellant. isaacarthur isaacarthur ion drives: the slow rockets that win space ion propulsion electric propulsion spaceflight propellant deep space ion propulsion wins on endurance the rocket equation is cruel: to go faster you must throw away more mass, or throw it faster — but carrying more propellant makes the vehicle heavier, a tax collector's loop. chemical rockets use high thrust to leave earth quickly, but their exhaust velocity is capped by the energy stored in chemical bonds. ion propulsion takes another route: instead of burning fuel, it uses electric fields to accelerate a small number of charged particles to extremely high speeds and throw them out. the thrust is astonishingly small, but it can persist for weeks, months or even years, ultimately accumulating a velocity change chemical rockets struggle to match. specific impulse and thrust can't both be had specific impulse measures how efficiently propellant is used; chemical rockets manage only a few hundred seconds, ion engines reach several thousand. but that efficiency rests on extremely low thrust: an ion engine can never lift off from the surface of earth, the moon or mars — at most it can depart a small asteroid whose gravity an astronaut could jump off. it isn't physically impossible; it trades thrust for efficiency, and time for speed. chemical rockets are sprinters, ion engines are marathoners. two mainstream forms of electric propulsion the classic gridded ion thruster ionises propellant atoms and accelerates them out through charged grids — high efficiency, but the grids are continuously eroded. hall thrusters use electromagnetic fields to ionise and accelerate propellant, with somewhat lower specific impulse but higher thrust, better suited to satellites, and they are the mainstay of modern electric propulsion. there are also micro electric-thruster systems for small satellites, and high-power plasma concepts — the core difference among all of these ultimately comes down to how to get enough electrical power. why xenon is the default propellant propellant choice isn't intuitive: at the same accelerating voltage, helium ions fly fastest and xenon slowest, but thrust depends on momentum — mass times velocity — so helium looks tempting. yet at the same power, a higher exhaust velocity actually means lower thrust; helium needs about 590 megajoules to ionise a kilogram, xenon only about 9 megajoules. xenon is an inert gas that doesn't corrode the engine. it is today's high-end choice for ion propulsion, but costs about a thousand dollars per kilogram. argon is far cheaper and is the industrial choice of the future. slow rockets are the bedrock of space logistics ion propulsion is especially suited to missions already in orbit: spiralling orbits up or down, rendezvousing with low-gravity small bodies. humans are impatient cargo, but supplies — water, metal, parts, propellant — don't care about being shipped slowly. a future mars programme or lunar base could move people fast with chemical or nuclear thermal propulsion while ion engines deliver the cargo ahead of time, slowly. machines do the boring work; the history of civilisation is written in freighters, ships, railways, trucks and shipping containers. longevity is the core requirement, not a bonus an ion thruster must run continuously for thousands or even tens of thousands of hours; grids erode, cathodes fail, power processing units have to survive years of operation. a chemical engine burns for minutes, an ion engine for years — this isn't easier, it's a different direction in which things get hard. it also struggles to exploit the oberth effect: a chemical rocket can burn hard and briefly at orbital perigee for a huge gain in orbital energy, while an ion engine's thrust is spread over months and loses that advantage for nothing. propellant isn't fuel, it's money propellant isn't just fuel; it is mass that must be launched, mined, processed, stored, transferred and protected. every kilogram of propellant saved is another kilogram of instruments, shielding, cargo and lifetime. the key question of the early space age was whether you could reach space at all; h: index funds win on arithmetic, not on bull markets: a debrief with former vanguard ceo bill mcnabb index funds beat nine out of ten active funds because of arithmetic, not because of the market cycle — active plus passive must equal the market, and once you subtract costs, the advantage is structural. the first half is vanguard internal history; the second half — on boards, quarterly guidance and leverage — is worth more. medium information density; skimmable. for people in asset management and wealth management, especially those focused on the mechanics of indexing, the advisor-channel business model, and board governance and long-termism. masters in business masters in business from ceo to startups: masters in business with former vanguard ceo bill mcnabb index funds wealth management corporate governance fintech leverage indexing wins on arithmetic, not on the market mcnabb splits the victory of indexing in two. psychologically, a string of scandals in the late 1990s pushed investors to simply ‘buy the whole market.’ mathematically, on an after-tax basis, index funds beat 90% of active equity funds over any rolling ten-year period. he restates bogle's simplified argument: the market has only two halves, active and passive; the passive half is the market, so the average of the active half can only be the market too — and once you subtract costs, the arithmetic is on the index's side. he stresses this is not ‘the index just happened to catch a good stretch’ — even in down markets, stock pickers did not beat the index, which directly rebuts the claim that ‘wait for the next downturn and you'll see who's swimming naked.’ bill mcnabb the no-layoffs bet during the financial crisis in 2008 peers were cutting staff across the board, because trading volume vanished and equity fund revenue halved along with market caps. after getting board authorization, mcnabb announced there would be no layoffs; he only asked employees to be flexible about changing roles, and put the surplus people onto service problems and bug fixes. his logic: you cannot cut your way out of this crisis, and if employees are worried about their own jobs, they cannot reassure clients that ‘the world isn't ending.’ the result was that client service quality actually improved, which he calls one of the most important strategic moves of that period. bill mcnabb risk questionnaires measure the past six months when target date funds launched, some internally objected that they ignore risk and only set a retirement date. mcnabb's rebuttal: every risk questionnaire he has ever seen produces the same answer — ‘moderate’; what it actually measures is how the market performed over the past six months. when markets rise people become less risk-averse; when they fall, everyone suddenly becomes a low-risk investor. since these questionnaires add no value to asset allocation decisions, just drop them and ask only for the retirement year. he cites the behavioral finance research of shlomo bernarsi and richard thaler to string auto-enrollment, auto-escalation of contribution rates and default target date funds into one line: the more automated the process, the fewer chances people have to make bad decisions. bill mcnabb a ceo should leave after ten years mcnabb's predecessor jack brennan told him: in the 10-to-12-year range, if you've done a decent job, people stop pushing you and stop questioning you, because you've been right more often than wrong — and that is not healthy. reshaping a company and genuinely driving innovation depends on collective wisdom, and once no one challenges you, you can't do it. mcnabb says he saw the same signals, the team was strong, so he handed over at 60. he admits he had no retirement plan and meant to figure it out after leaving, but the year he stayed on as chairman — traveling globally and running to washington on regulatory matters — turned his flight time into the place where he thought about the next stage. bill mcnabb the thing to fix is guidance, not quarterly reports mcnabb thinks abolishing quarterly reports is a fake move; the rules: bypassing system restrictions, reverse-engineering the answers, and even manipulating their own run logs to cover up traces of cheating. openai's original intent was to measure the models'
