the united states at the time generated six times as much with a quarter of china's population. after reform and opening up, urbanization accelerated and waste volumes grew 8-10% a year. by 2004 china's total municipal solid waste generation had already overtaken the united states to become the largest in the world, reaching 178 million tons by 2014 — nearly seven times the 1981 figure. the world bank forecast in 2018 that by 2030 china would generate twice as much waste as the united states. incineration has always cost five to ten times more than landfill building a waste-to-energy plant costs usd 66,000 to 120,000 per ton of daily processing capacity, and as much as usd 365,000 at the top end. a landfill, by comparison, costs only usd 5,000 to 20,000 per ton of daily capacity over its full life cycle — a gap of five to ten times, and illegal landfills are cheaper still. in other words, on pure economics, incineration did not spread at scale after the 2000s because it was cheaper than landfill. subsidies are more than half of revenue: burning trash is really selling power the new electricity tariff policy that took effect in april 2012 converts each ton of waste into 280 kwh of electricity, for which the government pays a subsidized rate of rmb 0.65 per kwh; anything generated beyond that is settled at the local coal-fired benchmark price (roughly rmb 0.25-0.45 per kwh). that means a plant can lock in about rmb 182 per ton from the subsidized tariff alone, plus a municipal waste treatment service fee of rmb 60-160 per ton, for average total revenue of rmb 250-350 per ton of waste — against a post-depreciation cost of around rmb 200 per ton. subsidies account for more than half of total revenue; without them the business essentially does not work. the site was fine; it was the opaque process that detonated the conflict in april 2014 the hangzhou municipal government announced a new incineration plant in yuhang with a capacity of 3,000 tons a day — more than a third of the city's total waste generation. technically the site was unobjectionable: tucked into a former quarry, with no need to route trucks along residential roads. but the decision process was entirely opaque, and 20,000 residents signed a petition against it. in may the situation broke down, with tens of thousands clashing with police; the same money at 45, even counting the investment growth in between, does far less for your standard of living. so extreme saving when young sacrifices the things that matter most at the time you can least afford it. pwl writer nick summed it up: you're effectively taking money from the poor person (your low-income present self) and giving it to the rich person (your high-income future self). benjamin felix people who save all their lives can't spend later dan offers a counterintuitive observation from the advisor's chair: people who won't spend because they want to build wealth may end up with a lot of wealth but lose the ability to spend it—even when the wealth far exceeds anything they could need, they still can't spend it, because the mindset has hardened. he says this is a chronic problem wealth advisors see commonly; the client base is itself wealthier, so it doesn't represent the whole population, but it's precisely people who saved aggressively and invested well who end up here: they arrive where they wanted to arrive but can't enjoy it. felix adds the mechanism: cultivating a habit for a lifetime and expecting to flip a switch one day and become a spender is naive. dan bortolotti why spending and saving arguments get so heated the topic is a minefield because the decisions are irreversible: someone who saved all their life can't go back and re-experience, and someone who spent on experiences can't go back and re-save. you're facing people who have already made irreversible decisions, and telling them ‘you should have spent more’ or ‘you should have saved more’ feels like a personal attack, because it was a decision they made and can never undo—and thanks to compounding, undoing gets harder over time. dan adds: as long as the choice was thought through, you shouldn't moralize about others' choices; saying ‘you should save’ easily sounds like judgment, and people get defensive. benjamin felix the stock market isn't the economy; growth is already priced ‘economic growth is good for stock returns’ is wrong, because the stock market isn't the economy. stock prices represent real companies' expected future cash flows, and by the time you read the economic news and hear about a market or sector's growth potential, those growth expectations are probably already in the price. historically this holds at both the industry and country level: industries can grow massively while stock returns are poor, and shrinking industries like railroads have delivered great returns; at the country level, the countries with the highest economic growth often produce lower average stock returns—though felix explicitly says this isn't a statistically significant result, only that there's no relationship between the two. dan's version: everyone knows a good company, the market will pay a higher price for it, so ‘good but not as good as imagined’ stocks move opposite to what most people expect. benjamin felix dividends describe returns, they don't explain them ‘dividends explain 40% of historical stock returns’ is often used by dividend investors to argue dividends matter, but felix thinks it gets causality backwards. when a company pays a dividend, your return doesn't increase; s: 2026-08-20-ancients-玛雅球赛首先是宗教-赢家被献祭是谎言
h: the maya ballgame was ritual, not sport: the sacrificed-winner story is invented the mesoamerican ballgame is humanity's earliest rubber-ball team sport, but it was religious ritual first: the court re-staged the creation myth, and the people who could be killed were captives who lost a ritual re-enactment. the idea that the winners were sacrificed was made up later. the episode uses first-hand archaeological evidence to dismantle two myths about the ballgame: that it was mere entertainment, and that winning or losing decided who lived. along the way it explains how the balls were made, and how betting could destroy a man. anyone curious about the maya and mesoamerica, from archaeology buffs to sports historians, and anyone who wants myths like "the winners were sacrificed" overturned. the ancients the ancients the maya ballgame maya civilization mesoamerica ballgame religious ritual archaeology sports history the rubber-ball team sport did not start in greece or china ed says team sports in general may well be older, but the ancestor of rubber-ball team sports is very likely the mesoamerican ballgame. the greek olympics had no ball games at all; china and persia did have ball sports, but they can only be traced back to 500 bc, and the maya ballgame predates them by at least a thousand years. the current evidence points earlier still: rubber balls from 1600-1700 bc have turned up at olmec sites, and the oldest ball court dates to roughly 1650 bc. ed barnhart the ballgame was never uniquely maya; all mesoamerica played it the game was not a maya invention but a shared element of every mesoamerican culture. the maya heartland sits in modern guatemala, extending north into the yucatan peninsula and into chiapas and tabasco in mexico, and south into about half of honduras; further west lie cultures such as the zapotec and the mixtec. the classic peak runs roughly ad 400 to 800, with each city-state politically independent but sharing religion, calendar, writing and the ballgame. ed barnhart hips, knees, shoulders and chest only: the hip swing is the signature shot according to the aztec rules the spanish wrote down, players could not use hands or feet; they struck the ball with hips, knees, shoulders and chest, and the classic shot was a swing of the hip. the ball was a solid rubber "super bouncy ball" about six inches across, and taking one on the body hurt. the court had a centre line and end lines: sending the ball past the opponent's end line scored, and putting it through the stone ring set high on the side wall ended the match instantly. teams had forwards and defenders, much like modern football. ed barnhart a ball court is a mythic stage first, a playing field second ed flatly rejects separating maya religion from maya sport. the large stone courts at the centre of maya cities are ritual spaces first: in the creation myth, the hero twins play a ballgame against the lords of the underworld, which makes the court a place to re-enact the moment of creation. the court at chichen itza is so vast it hardly looks playable, with stone rings some 30 feet up; dancing, sacrifice and symbolic re-enactment are the more plausible explanation. courts were often built at the lowest point of a city, mimicking the underworld. ed barnhart the game could kill you, and gambling could cost you your family the ball was more dangerous than it sounds: a spanish priest watched a player take one in the abdomen, in the gap between his pads, cough blood and die within the hour, probably from ruptured organs. balls were made from natural rubber cured with sulphur, and the maya very likely drew that sulphur from morning glory sap; ed made one himself by the old method and it is still going twenty years later. the betting was just as extreme: a player could stake himself, and a losing run could cost him his money, his house, even his whole family into slavery to a noble. if a noble tried to slip away after a match without throwing gifts, the players had the right to bring him down and take his things. ed barnhart the sacrificed-winner story was invented eight years ago by one man ed debunks it outright: the claim that the winning players were sacrificed comes from an old man at chichen itza who admitted eight years ago that he made it up, because people loved hearing it. logically, if winning meant death, nobody would play properly. the people who really could be sacrificed were war captives, cast as the lords of the underworld in a ritual re-enactment and killed after they lost. ed himself dug a headless body out of the centre line of a modest court in belize, with a turtle shell placed where the skull should have been — a direct echo of the hero twins' decapitation story. ed barnhart a city of 100,000 with no ball court means archaeologists missed it teotihuacan, another great mesoamerican city, may have peaked at 100,000 people, yet no confirmed ball court has been found there, even though its murals show people passing a ball; h: burning tokens to stack up agents is a transitional strategy, not the endgame silicon valley is shifting from mindless token burning to careful accounting: a local open-source model can do real work on a dollar a day of electricity, yet when a genuinely hard problem shows up, a smarter model can still nail in one shot the answer a billion-token group chat could not argue its way to. saving money and top-tier intelligence are not in conflict. the real bills and the real change of heart from a frontline heavy agent user, from four or five hundred dollars a day down to two or three hundred dollars a month. more concrete than any industry report. technical leaders costing out agent engineering and weighing whether to stand up their own local models, plus investors watching how token economics reshapes the balance between cloud providers and model vendors 硅谷101 硅谷101 e249｜token经济转点：openclaw、hermes到本地自研的agent进化之路 token economics agent engineering open-source models local deployment b2b startups infrastructure investing the era of token-burning leaderboards is already over for the past few months, silicon valley's agent strategy went by the name token maxing. jensen huang told his engineers to burn more tokens, and meta went as far as setting up a leaderboard for who consumed the most. but the wind is changing. the token allowance uber handed out to employees was pulled back after costs overran the plan: four months burned through the entire year's budget. stripe's internal tooling now tells you outright that opus 4.8 is expensive and suggests starting with a cheaper model for non-core tasks. this episode is about exactly that turning point, and how the agent engineering paradigm is moving from reaching for the strongest model by reflex toward using tokens economically. hongjun four or five hundred dollars a day in tokens is not expensive since last november, huang dongxu has been using opus to build a distributed database, db9, from scratch. even with a $200-a-month claude code pro max subscription, once he exceeded the included allowance he had to buy additional usage out of pocket, running four or five hundred dollars a day. his judgment is that the money is well spent. a product that was previously impossible to build, given the technical and headcount limits, now takes one person three months, and this piece of software could have brought the company $10 million a year in direct sales revenue. the roi covers the token cost completely. huang dongxu openclaw matters as a signal, not as a product zhang hongjiang argues that openclaw's real significance lies not in the product itself but in the signal it sends: peter, working alone, spent one week and produced an agent like this. that says the reasoning and coding ability of large models has become strong enough that a single architect-level engineer can stand up a system fast, which marks ai genuinely crossing over from the research stage into engineering deployment. you no longer need a deep understanding of how the model works internally to use it to build the system you want. zhang hongjiang hermes did not solve memory, it just routed around it the complaint most often leveled at openclaw is poor memory: once the context is compressed it forgets things easily, and its behavior turns erratic. after switching to hermes, huang dongxu found that it does not solve the memory problem itself but sidesteps it cleverly. its agent loop includes a mechanism that continuously summarizes successful experience and hardens it into reusable skills, so the longer you use it, the more best practices it grows. he sees this as fundamentally an engineering problem, unrelated to model capability, resting instead on better architectural design and a team's willingness to polish. huang dongxu multi-agent group chats exist to keep the agents from stopping huang dongxu uses slock to build multi-agent discussion groups for code review: top-tier models from different vendors pick holes in each other's work and try to persuade each other, and it does not stop until nobody can find another problem. the price is token consumption ten times that of a single model, peaking at 1 billion tokens a day and a bill of three or four hundred dollars. the slock team calls this mechanism, keeping an agent working through rounds of discussion, agent dynamics. in his view, every harness and every loop engineer is fundamentally solving the same problem: how to keep an agent working without stopping. huang dongxu on a single hard problem, a stronger model beats multiple agents huang dongxu originally believed that having multiple agents debate each other was necessary, because a single model's one-shot success rate was not high enough. the arrival of gpt-5.5 and fable 5 broke that assumption: a complex bug the group chat spent ages on and could not resolve, fed to fable 5, would often be pinned down exactly on the first try, with no prior context, purely on raw intelligence. his conclusion is yes and no.  ‖ 硅谷 硅谷 經濟轉點 到本地自研的 進化之路

s: 2026-08-19-cnf65bb3-黄仁勋两次拒绝当台积电ceo-我已有工作
h: jensen huang turned down the tsmc ceo job twice: i already have a job in 2013 morris chang seriously considered handing the tsmc he founded 26 years earlier to jensen huang. huang answered with five words — ‘i already have a job’ — and said the same thing both times. tsmc's market cap then was 10 times nvidia's. the first half is 30 years of partnership between the two companies, at medium information density; the real value is in the second half: the succession offer, the 40nm compensation negotiation, and how cowos packaging became the ai bottleneck. founders and investors watching the semiconductor supply chain, ai compute bottlenecks and long-term founder relationships; anyone who wants to know why tsmc is hard to replace and why nvidia cannot do without it. 科技这碗饭 科技这碗饭 黄仁勋x张忠谋：一生有你——英伟达和台积电的激荡30年 semiconductors tsmc nvidia supply chain ai compute founder relationships no money to tape out, so build the chip in a computer first nvidia's first two chips both failed, and by the end of 1996 the company had been cut down to just over thirty people. the normal process in the chip industry is tape out, test, fix the design, go again — two or three rounds is common — but huang only had enough money on his books to tape out once. he took a third of his cash, about one million dollars, and bought a machine that could simulate an entire chip inside a computer, to find as many errors as possible before going into a real fab, and then decided the first version would go straight to mass production. a manager asked him how he knew he would get it right in one pass. he answered: i know it has to be right, because if it isn't, the company is gone. in august 1997 the third chip shipped, and in its first four months it moved more than 1 million units. betting the whole lifeline on one fab with no contract in hand from 1998 huang put almost every nvidia chip on tsmc alone. at the time most fabless chip companies worked with two or three fabs at once, playing them off on price while keeping a fallback, and nvidia took that path thoroughly enough. more important, huang made this bet without a long-term contract in hand — around 1997 the two sides discussed a formal manufacturing arrangement, but day-to-day orders were still placed one at a time, and tsmc never promised to reserve any particular capacity long term. only two things held up the bet: morris chang's verbal commitment, and huang's line that sounded almost like bragging. when tsmc makes a mistake, it is nvidia that goes bankrupt in 1998 a chemical step at the end of a tsmc production line went wrong, causing large-scale breaks across a whole batch of wafers, and more than half the chips in that nvidia lot were scrapped. because it was hard to tell by ordinary sampling which ones were usable, nvidia threw up a temporary test line and hired a large crew to sort them one chip at a time, and tsmc sent two production planners from hsinchu to california for a full month. that quarter nvidia's revenue fell from more than 28 million dollars to less than half, the net loss came close to 10 million dollars, and in the end it had to sell part of its equity to several downstream companies for cash. this is the fundamental risk of the design-only model: the fab belongs to someone else, the mistake was someone else's, but the money lost, the undelivered goods and the walk to the edge of bankruptcy can only be yours. a customer diverting a little business has to be written into risk factors in 2002 tsmc's most advanced process generation could not get its yields up, nvidia's new flagship shipped half a year late, and once it launched review sites nicknamed it the hair dryer for its power draw and heat; rival ati used the opening to overtake it with new products. in march 2003 nvidia announced an alliance with ibm, handing its next-generation flagship to ibm's new fab in new york state, in a contract estimated at more than 100 million dollars. the same day the two companies jointly issued a press release reaffirming the partnership, but three months later tsmc filed its annual report with the sec and for the first time put the matter into risk factors, writing that it could not guarantee it would not lose nvidia's business in the future. the previous year nvidia had still contributed about a fifth of tsmc's revenue; that year its share fell from two tenths to one and a half tenths. in the end ibm could not get its yields up either, and in the summer of 2004 nvidia's consumer chips came back to tsmc, with the flagship following in 2005. after the pizza dinner, a 48-hour ultimatum after the 40nm yield failure nvidia demanded compensation, and then-ceo rick tsai insisted tsmc was not at fault and would not pay a cent; huang said that if they could not agree, they would go to arbitration. after morris chang returned in 2009 he spent half his time on this matter, talking for dozens of hours with everyone involved, then shut himself in with his staff to study it for a full three weeks. ‖ 科技這碗飯 科技這碗飯 黃仁勳 張忠謀 一生有你 英偉達和臺積電的激盪 年

h: britain knew nothing about northern ireland, and hardline arson dragged ireland toward civil war the northern ireland conflict was not simple sectarian hatred: britain's information vacuum, loyalist arson staged on purpose, and the civil rights movement's genuine grievances amplified one another and together pulled ireland toward civil war. the most valuable thing in this episode is how little british politicians knew about northern ireland, and how loyalists staged attacks on themselves. put those two factors together and you have the explanation for why the conflict spun out of control. policy analysts working on the origins of conflict, journalists writing about irish history, and founders who want to understand how the british establishment makes decisions inside an information vacuum. the rest is history the rest is history 698. the troubles: the brink of civil war (part 2) northern ireland conflict civil rights movement british politics irish history escalation of violence one council house allocation set off the entire civil rights movement the village of caledon handed its one available council house to a 19-year-old protestant, emily beatty, while more than 250 catholic families were still on the waiting list. austin curry and the new generation of nationalists shaped by the american civil rights movement narrowed the protest demands to two things: fair housing and ‘one man, one vote’. ian paisley immediately defined the movement as a ‘trojan horse’ for the ira. that definition was partly right: when nicra was founded it did include communist party members and ira men, even a belfast brigade commander. but the movement quickly outgrew anything the ira could control, pulling in large numbers of students and ordinary people. housing injustice was the first match struck. blood in front of the cameras did more than any petition on 5 october 1968 the derry march had already been banned, and roughly 400 people took to the streets anyway. the ruc's violent dispersal left about 80 people injured, and mp gerry fitt was beaten until his face was covered in blood. irish television filmed the police attacking marchers and the footage went around the world; derry then went into several days of rioting. this was the decisive turning point in the escalation: the civil rights movement shifted from petitioning to confrontation, and for the first time the ruc's repressive character was exposed on camera. at the police station gerry fitt deliberately did not wash the blood off his face — he said he wanted the outside world to see the blood running down it. the evidence itself became the movement's weapon. off-duty police in the ambush party made the state one of the combatants on 1 january 1969 the people's democracy group set out to walk from belfast to derry. bernadette devlin and the others deliberately chose a provocative route, hoping that violence would expose the repressive nature of the state. on 4 january, as they reached burntollet bridge, around 400 loyalists ambushed them — with off-duty b specials among the attackers — while the ruc stood by on the scene and did nothing. the episode showed something more clearly than the derry demonstration had: the armed force of the northern ireland state and loyalist violence were one and the same thing, and the marchers were both beaten and humiliated. o'neill promptly launched a ‘back the prime minister’ petition and collected 150,000 signatures, but the petition could not repair the fractures inside the unionist party. the prime minister who won the election was already a dead man walking in the february 1969 election o'neill beat ian paisley by a narrow margin of 1,400 votes, and that was the only good news he had all night. the results in working-class protestant districts showed moderate unionism bleeding badly while the hardliners surged across the board, and from that point the unionist party split into two camps. o'neill kept the premiership but lost his authority and became a ‘dead man walking’. he was not defeated by paisley; he was hollowed out by betrayal within his own camp and by the polarisation of the electorate. the election results said more plainly than any slogan could that northern ireland's political spectrum was migrating fast toward the violent end, and that there was no ground left for the centre to stand on. the bombers hitting water and power sites were not the ira but protestant hardliners from march 1969 a series of explosions hit water and electricity installations across northern ireland, and ian paisley publicly insisted the ira had done it. the actual planners were the ulster volunteer force (uvf) and his own ulster protestant volunteers. gusty spence, the uvf leader, admitted from prison that the point of the bombings was to manufacture the appearance of an ira threat, to prove o'neill was weak and force him out. paisley knew and went on lying. this fact upgrades the ‘protestant hardliners’ from verbal incitement to armed subversion:

h: adidas bottoms out: reheating old hits beats superstar collabs after nearly halving from its 2021 peak, adidas engineered an earnings recovery by thawing out its retro sneakers, repairing its wholesale partners and holding inventory on a tight leash — but the share price rallied and then fell back again, showing that the sportswear cycle is really a game played between inventory and expectations. a five-year post-mortem taken year by year, solidly grounded in the numbers, that breaks the adidas fall and self-rescue into cycle logic you can act on — genuinely useful for understanding sportswear inventory and valuation. investors and consumer-sector analysts who follow the sportswear cycle and inventory management, plus anyone working at or around adidas and nike, who will find in this five-year recap a real case of company decisions and share price falling out of step. 商业就是这样 商业就是这样 vol.271 阿迪达斯如何触底反弹？ adidas sportswear inventory management share price cycles retro sneakers consumer goods the share price bottomed out before the brand's reputation did the turn in how people talk about adidas this year came out of a run of good news: new-chinese-style clothing went global over spring festival, the top two men's elite finishers at the london marathon both ran sub-two and all of the top three wore adidas racing shoes, and in the world cup final between spain and argentina the side that ended up lifting the trophy was wearing adidas kit. what came back earlier than the chatter was the share price. it peaked above 300 euros in july 2021, fell all the way to close to 100 euros, recovered to above 255 euros, and has now dropped back to around 160 euros — nearly cut in half against the high, but up 60% off the low. that history is the coordinate system for the five-year post-mortem that follows. the slide started with goods stuck in transit, not with nobody buying adidas outsources production, and it takes eight to nine months to get from a design to a shelf. in 2021 global ocean freight had not recovered and its vietnam base kept halting production at short notice, which pushed in-transit inventory as a share of the total from close to 29% in 2019 and 28% in 2020 up to 38.8% in 2022. months of supply in the second half of 2021 fell to just 2.21 months, which tells you the goods were stranded mid-route and stores were badly anxious about running out. at the same time greater china stalled for its own reasons: the region still grew 37% in the first half of 2021 and made up 23% of global revenue, then declined for two straight years, with its share falling to somewhere between 12% and 15%. a logistics blockage stacked on top of a core market sliding — that is where the fall begins. adidas never destroyed the yeezy inventory; it sold it back in three drops adidas and kanye west had worked together since 2006, launched yeezy in 2015, and by 2020 and 2021 the line was contributing 1.7 billion dollars of sales a year, about 8% of company revenue, with a profit contribution that may have been on the order of 40%. in october 2022 adidas terminated the deal over kanye's improper remarks; upstream production could not react quickly, and the company took a write-down provision against 1.2 billion euros of finished and in-transit inventory. what followed was not a one-off destruction: it re-released part of the inventory in three separate drops across 2023 and early 2024, donated the remainder, and even booked a reversal of the write-down loss in its results. the handling was judged, in hindsight, to have worked out well. leaving russia bruised sentiment on the stock, not the business in 2022 adidas also dealt with the russian market: it suspended operations in march and exited completely in october. russia had historical roots for adidas — it did business in the soviet union during the cold war and sponsored the soviet team at the moscow olympics, and in 2012 the then-ceo called russia one of its fastest-growing markets. but by 2022 the business had already shrunk, and closing it down brought a loss of about 300 million dollars. the impact on the business was limited; the impact on sentiment around the share price was one more negative layer. in 2022 adidas was fighting on three fronts at once — china, yeezy and russia — which makes it fair to call that its hardest year. the retro lines fixed on day five paid off better than yeezy in 2023 the new ceo, gulden, arrived from puma and handled the thorniest problems smoothly: rather than destroying the yeezy inventory he sold it off in batches, and he cancelled the plan to push hard into direct retail, switching instead to helping wholesale partners improve the quality of their inventory. he also made three retro lines including samba a company-level strategy, signing off on it on his fifth day in the job. the retro models got bought up by a new generation of young consumers through celebrity street shots and tiktok, and compared with yeezy, reheating retro styles offered a better r ‖ 商業就是這樣 商業就是這樣 阿迪達斯如何觸底反彈

s: 2026-08-19-solofounders-找联合创始人这件事-越刻意越容易找错人
h: looking for a co-founder is how you end up with the wrong one treat a co-founder as a precondition for starting up, and you usually end up settling for a ‘co-founder of convenience’. four solo founders explain from experience: run on your own first, and the right person shows up along the way. four solo founders' honest post-mortems — no methodology packaging, just the mistakes they made and the specific numbers. for founders currently agonising over whether to find a co-founder. founders agonising over whether to find a co-founder, and founders who have already started solo and want to compare notes with their own kind. solo founders 单人创始人 searching for a co-founder is how you get a bad one | 4 vc-backed solo founders solo founders co-founders retention startups sfp treat a co-founder as a precondition and you will settle julian says it plainly on the show: many people believe ‘you must have a co-founder to start’, so they treat finding one as a precondition for starting up — and that makes them more likely to end up with a bad co-founder. sfp's position is not anti-co-founder; quite the opposite, they think a good co-founder is fantastic. the problem is the order: having an idea first and then going to find someone to fill the slot, versus running first and meeting the right person, produce completely different outcomes. aldo is the latter — he worked through four different ideas before he met his current co-founder. julian a co-founder need not be a ceo and a cto aldo's current company is about ‘turning any computer into a data centre’. his co-founder was originally his angel investor, then volunteered to be his founding engineer, and only later was upgraded to co-founder. the two define the relationship unusually: they don't see themselves as ceo and cto but as ‘artist, producer’, switching roles whenever the company needs it. the detail shows the shape of a co-founder relationship can be custom-built — there is no need to force it into a standard template. aldo retention is growth, not an optimisation after growth the line aldo repeats is ‘retention is growth’. chai says aldo taught him which numbers to look at and what a smile curve is, lessons he still uses every day. more important is aldo's criticism of ‘growth is good so retention can wait’: when growth is good you feel you can ignore retention, but the moment growth stops you regret not having watched it. many founders, while growth is good, just pour on more spend and leave everything else to luck — and once luck is not on your side, you fall as fast as you rose. aldo pull on the thread, don't stop at the second-best answer chai first chose between two directions: travel and software reliability. because travel had an existing audience and distribution, he built an ai email client for travel first, and quickly found the direction extremely hard to scale. the second idea came from watching user sessions to find pain points, and that too proved hard to scale. he still isn't sure whether those ideas were ‘bad ideas’ — only that he didn't want to do them. eventually he went back to software reliability and made one key flip: instead of guessing top-down how customers will use your software, he has the software simulate every possible customer action and production scenario, turning reliability into a compute problem. chai tell real feedback apart from fake heat signals nemanja says the most important thing he learned at sfp was distinguishing which feedback is worth iterating on and which is just a misleading heat signal. his example is concrete: a twitter post getting hundreds or thousands of likes doesn't mean you should pay attention to it. if you have free users and free heat but no conversion to paying customers, you are running a free trend, not a business. every piece of feedback aldo gave him was the same question: what would make someone pay you 10x more? how do you make it worth 10x to a large enterprise? nemanja a co-founder priests produced the man who turned on the church weishaupt was born in ingolstadt in 1748; both his father and his uncle fought the church's control over university teaching materials. after his father died, his uncle became his guardian — and sent him to a jesuit school. in his uncle's library he read french enlightenment philosophy, which laid down the intellectual base coat of his life: reason against dogma. he took a law degree at 20, became a professor at 22, and was dean of the law faculty at 27, the first non-jesuit to hold the chair in canon law in nearly a century — which he owed to his uncle's connections, not to his own credentials. he did not want to abolish the church; he wanted to replace it the historian stauffer's verdict on weishaupt is sharp: his motives were half credible and half not. his feeling for liberty and progress was genuine, but the appetite for power was in his nature, and the order he built was itself despotic. he broke with his uncle, quarreled with colleagues, meddled in other departments' affairs, and cast himself as a martyr for free speech. when he founded the illuminati, his real aim was not to overthrow the church's will but to substitute his own for it. that explains why the organization was later riven by infighting. from day one the illuminati was a recruitment scheme on may 1, 1776, weishaupt and five students founded the covenant of perfectibility, later renamed the illuminati. he had been unable to join the freemasons — he could not afford the dues and found the rituals ridiculous — yet he copied the masons in designing three ranks: novice, minerval, illuminated minerval. recruitment criteria included ‘wealth’. members had to hand over a list of the books they owned, a family tree, a list of their enemies, adolf von knigge — nobleman, writer, freemason — joined, bringing social connections and a capacity for governance. he rebuilt the chaotic original structure into three broad classes and 13 grades, introduced promotion tests, rituals, and code names (weishaupt's was spartacus), and shifted recruitment from boys aged 15-20 toward mature, experienced men. by the mid-1780s membership is estimated illuminati punishable by death. weishaupt fled to gotha, sheltered by a duke who had himself been a member. the conspiracy theory came out of a joke publication and a letters column in 1798 the h: orbit scores a one, recovery scores a zero: no middle state zhuque-3 (朱雀三号) reached orbit on its first flight but failed to recover the booster. deputy chief designer dong kai (董凯) argues a rocket launch has only success or failure, never a middle state: orbit gets a one, recovery gets a zero. what actually sets the pace of catching up is recovery-zone downrange distance, engine redundancy, and building a hundred engines a year. an exclusive post-mortem recorded immediately after the failed recovery, with the deputy chief designer walking through the recovery sequence, the point of failure, the production-capacity logic and the timeline for catching up. dense with information. people working in commercial spaceflight, rocket investors and engineers following reusable technology — anyone who wants the real engineering detail on zhuque-3 (朱雀三号) and a practitioner's read on the industry. what's next｜科技早知道 科技早知道 【重听】朱雀三号副总师：火箭回收只有成与败，没有中间态| s9e41 commercial spaceflight rocket recovery zhuque-3 methalox reusable rockets us-china space the first flight flew a stripped-down zhuque-3, not the full vehicle dong kai (董凯) describes zhuque-3 (朱雀三号) as a liquid oxygen-methane medium-to-large liquid rocket developed in-house by landspace (蓝箭航天). the full vehicle is 76 metres tall, with stainless-steel propellant tanks running 80% of the body's length, nine engines on the first stage and one on the second. the vehicle that flew was a ‘lite version’(青春版), shortened by roughly 10 metres, using the tianque-12a (天阙12a) with 83 tonnes of liftoff thrust; the full vehicle will use the tianqu-12b (天去12b), with thrust above 100 tonnes. on payload it can approach long march 5 (长征五号) while also covering the medium-lift class below it. recovery downrange distance was set at 390 kilometres for the first flight; at full payload it should be 550 to 600 kilometres. dong kai ‘china's falcon 9’ is high praise, but five years to surpass it is too optimistic on netizens calling zhuque-3 ‘china's falcon 9’, dong kai says that is very high praise. falcon 9 is the only reusable rocket in the world in operational service and it is extremely reliable: 150 launches, including one booster reused 32 times. but when musk said zhuque-3 would surpass falcon 9 within five years, dong kai will not be that optimistic. chinese spaceflight as a whole, across every vehicle type, runs about 80 launches a year; falcon 9 alone flies 150 in a year, which works out to three launches a week. he does not think one company, landspace, can get there on its own — the remark is more encouragement and a spur than a forecast. dong kai orbit is graded on three levels; recovery has only success and failure before zhuque-3's first flight, the flight plan graded orbital insertion and recovery separately. insertion was graded by perigee altitude into complete success, success and failure: perigee above 170 kilometres was a complete success, 130 kilometres was a success. recovery had a binary standard only — stand on the landing pad for one minute without falling over and it is a success; short of that it is a failure. the overall mission grade had four levels: only both orbit and recovery succeeding, with perigee meeting the target, counted as a complete success; succeeding at just one of the two counted as a basic success. in the end the first flight hit the orbital target and did not recover, so the launch director declared the launch a complete success (as to orbit) and the mission a basic success. dong kai holding recovery range down to 390 km throws away 2 to 3 tonnes of payload the downrange distance to the recovery zone directly determines the rocket's payload. after stage separation, the first stage coasts ballistically toward the recovery zone; fix the downrange distance and you have fixed the separation altitude. the full zhuque-3 corresponds to a 600-kilometre recovery range; for the first flight the range was cut to 390 kilometres for safety, dropping separation altitude from 76 kilometres to 66 kilometres — 10 kilometres less flying. every additional 10 kilometres of recovery range adds close to 150 kilograms of payload; pulling the range from 390 to 600 kilometres would raise payload by 2 to 3 tonnes. the first flight came down carrying 10 tonnes of propellant, which is exactly the price paid for safety. dong kai five engines at landing ignition are for braking, not for thrift the recovery sequence: after stage separation, the first stage coasts up past 130 kilometres, then turns tail-down. first ignition comes at 80 kilometres altitude, three engines firing together for about 40 seconds, to slow down and keep dynamic pressure from getting too high on entry into the dense atmosphere. engines shut down at 40 kilometres, ending the braking burn, and the vehicle enters aerodynamic control, using grid fins and strakes for trim. the final landing ignition happens at 4 kilometres. unlike falcon 9, zhuque-3 is configured with five engines here, capable of multiple rest ‖ 朱雀三號 董凱 朱雀三號 科技早知道 科技早知道 重聽 朱雀三號副總師 火箭回收只有成與敗 沒有中間態

h: cerebras hits 4400 tok/s on a single chip: inference speed is the moat cerebras pushes wse 3.5 to 4400 tok/s per chip, and the cs4 rack packs three wafers into a 120kw cabinet. the core argument: inference has to be split into prefill and decode, and speed is the moat. cerebras rarely opens up its system design to this level of detail. this episode gives hard numbers on rack power, interconnect latency and component reduction — useful for anyone trying to verify whether the sram inference approach actually holds up. founders tracking generational roadmaps in ai inference silicon, engineers making infra selection decisions, and investors following the openai supply chain. techtechpotato techtechpotato gpt-5.6 sol ultrafast.... just got ultrafaster (cerebras 4th gen) inference chips cerebras wafer-scale computing sram openai compute doubling performance did not wait for a new process node — they just cranked the clock rather than waiting for a new process node, cerebras clocked wse3 aggressively: frequency is close to double, so power is close to double as well. the company stresses this is not simple binning, but design optimization for voltage and frequency done with tsmc on the same n5 node. the previous generation's 125 petlops of sparse fp16 goes to 250 petlops, while the core count stays at 900,000 and sram stays at 44gb. physical yield remains close to 100% thanks to dynamically routing around defective cores, but parametric yield has always been the point outside observers question. three wafers in one rack turns the oddity into a standard form factor the old design was a 16u complete system with its own power delivery and liquid cooling for the single chip, leaving the data center side to do air cooling only. cs4 moves to rack scale: fans and power supplies on the front panel, and behind them a module called the backpack, with liquid cooling piped in from the top to the wafer chips mounted vertically. one rack holds three wafers; the author estimates from the number of power supplies roughly 40kw per wafer and roughly 120kw for the full rack, which sounds like the same class as nvidia's nvl72. this is not a spec flex — it is about fitting wafer-scale into a standard data center form factor. making io a swappable module means what they sell is really a rack platform networking per chip doubles from the previous generation to 2.4tbps, and the io modules are designed to be replaceable: if 800g/200g/100g or other interconnect standards need supporting later, you swap the module instead of redoing the system. the backpack is also compatible with future wafer sizes, because the wafer is already at its physical limit and the power and liquid cooling interfaces are broadly similar. the author's read is that cerebras is effectively building a rack-scale platform, which is why they can say cs5 will follow in the second half of 2027. the bulk of the openai revenue comes from chips that do not exist yet wse3 runs at roughly 2300 tok/s on models that fit entirely on a single chip; h: thirty thousand canadians moved: the young were saved, the old lost everything from 1954, nearly thirty thousand people in newfoundland, canada, were moved from remote fishing villages to towns. the younger generation gained education and a way out; the old and the inuit lost their homes, scattered until there was no way left to reach one another. resettlement has no single verdict. nine minutes of oral history, with both the concrete detail of people who lived it and archival recordings of the premier. the information density is not low — good for anyone who wants to understand quickly what «modernization by relocation» costs. policy researchers and local officials working on urbanization, regional development compensation and indigenous resettlement, plus anyone running community rebuilding projects. witness history witness history canada's controversial resettlement programme urbanization resettlement newfoundland oral history regional policy community collapse a village that cannot support a school and a hospital should be emptied out from 1954 the canadian government launched a large-scale resettlement programme, aiming to move nearly thirty thousand people from several hundred coastal communities (outports) in newfoundland and labrador into designated growth centres. the official logic was modernization: these remote settlements could not sustain modern education and health care, and only concentrated settlement would bring roads, schools and electric light. the episode makes clear at the outset that the process would run for more than two decades and would completely transform a way of life that had lasted for centuries. katherine harvey no power and no road meant, in the government's eyes, no modern life don white, who lived through it, grew up in port nelson on newfoundland's east coast. the early life he describes sounds like another era: one grocery store for the whole village, no electricity, people living off moose, rabbit and seabirds and off salmon and lobster fishing; his grandfather had a schooner that crossed the bay each year to bring in vegetables for the winter. the nearest hospital was an hour away by boat, and the road system consisted of footpaths. these details are not nostalgia — they are the premise for understanding the motive behind resettlement: in the government's view, this kind of life could not supply the basic conditions a modern citizen needed. don white four children rowing themselves to school forced the decision to move don white's schooling was the most direct catalyst for moving: the family lived on the south side of the harbour and the school was on the north, so four children had to row an open boat across the harbour themselves, with no adult along; in winter the harbour froze over and the only option was an hour's walk around it. the whole school was a single classroom, with at most 22 pupils across all grades, and it closed after grade six. he says plainly that the family decided to move precisely so the next generation could get a decent education and decent opportunities. that chain of reasoning turns «resettlement» from an administrative order back into a family choice. don white industrialize or perish — but the government decided where you could go the chief architect of the plan was joseph r. smallwood, the premier at the time. in his own words: newfoundland had to industrialize or it would perish; and on an island where even elementary education was hard to guarantee, people could not possibly acquire the skills industry required. in a private recording he also stressed that resettlement was not a way of shedding a burden — the government set a condition: it would help you move, but the destination had to be approved, because it absolutely did not want people jumping «out of the frying pan into the fire». that double framing shows resettlement was both an idealistic theory of development and a form of conditional control. joseph r. smallwood six hundred dollars could move a house, not a fresh start resettlement was not free of charge. the government gave each departing household a grant of 300 dollars, later raised in steps to 400, 500 and 600 dollars. to save money, islanders invented their own way of moving: they fitted their houses with runners and hauled them by rope and cable all the way to the water's edge, even rolling an entire house — stove, table, curtains and furniture included — onto a raft and floating it along the coast to the new home, with no machinery, all by human muscle. the other side of that ledger: many people found no way forward once they reached town, and instead crowded into cramped quarters and faced unemployment. the subsidy could cover the move, but it could not cover the risk of starting over. resettlement saved the young and ruined those who only knew fishing not everyone benefited. one interviewee in the documentary (edward) called it the worst thing he had been through: he had no skill other than fishing, and was reduced t

ai clown car w/ gamersnexus ai bubble nvidia enron financial engineering data centers compute executives no longer talk tech, only money steve burke points out that jensen, lisa su, sam altman, and other executives now rarely discuss any technical details on podcasts and tv—it's all tens of billions, hundreds of billions, trillions in tam and gigawatt numbers. previously, they appeared only at h: 17-year-old ai native: the reason to study math has become proving to universities that i can endure hardship after ai arrived, his reason for studying math degraded into proving to universities that he can endure hardship: the path he could once see — university, phd, advancing mathematics — has narrowed, and the classmates around him who want to work in aerospace are also losing their upward motivation. the technical increment is limited, but a 17-year-old ai native's judgment about the landscape of model companies — and about ai eroding the next generation's motivation — is more direct than most adult interviews. investors watching ai's impact on education and talent, people building ai education products, and engineers who want to know how the post-2005 generation actually uses ai. 张小珺·商业访谈录 张小珺·商业访谈录 151. 17岁被2026年icml收录论文的小少年：我bet开心！开心！开心！ ai natives ai and education model companies pretraining teenagers pretraining feels magical, post-training feels like shaping a body his reason for doing pretraining isn't papers, it's feel: post-training is more like shaping a body, while pretraining is making your specific material better so it can withstand the shaping that comes later — he says this is a bit magical. the cost is real money burn: this paper cost him 30,000 yuan in total, and the largest model in the paper was only 0.05b; to scale up, he calculated it would take roughly another 6,000 yuan. that night he was extremely nervous, wondering whether to spend the money, because even if the paper was good, submitting to a top conference could still get it rejected and the money would be wasted. in the end his older brother and his parents both supported him, and only then did he take the step — and the scaling step worked. su tinghao three models didn't save, 1,500 burned for nothing he describes training as an expensive game. once he forgot that training periodically saves checkpoints, trained three models at the same time, none of them saved, and the parameters weren't tuned well either — 1,500 lost. he says he cried, was extremely, extremely sad, and kept thinking about why he hadn't looked at that part again earlier. there is nothing profound in this: the pit a high school sophomore stepped into is the most everyday pit for anyone doing pretraining — money goes into compute, and one low-level mistake zeroes it out. his mother comforted him by saying that once you pay tuition you remember the lesson, and he never made that mistake again. he also admits his training code is very messy, only he can use it, and training efficiency has big problems. su tinghao he cut the width of attention in half the paper's starting point is value residual learning: adding the first layer's attention value to later layers as a residual. he found that the low-layer value is doing two things — being used in its own layer, and being added to later layers as a residual — so he doubled the width of the first layer's attention projection, cutting half for its own layer and the other half dedicated to the backward residual, then added rmsnorm, and extended the approach from value to key and query, which worked better. he knows this looks very similar to kimi's attention residual, but he says they are two completely different lines of thinking: what kimi residuals is the hidden state, what he residuals is the attention projection. he himself is clear about which one works better — kimi's path has already been proven at 2.5t scale, his is a small-scale result. su tinghao the gpt framework only needs high school math; the hard part is intuition his judgment is that the current big framework of transformer and gpt doesn't require very advanced math or probabilistic thinking — it's all matrix multiplication, and high school math is about enough to understand it; what really takes time is cultivating intuition. the example is himself: a year or so ago he watched andrej karpathy's roughly twenty-hour video series and could only write whatever karpathy wrote, with no understanding at all, and then these things settled in his head for half a year to a year before he suddenly understood some of it. so his aha moment wasn't learning a formula, but one day suddenly figuring out qkv — q represents what this character of mine wants to look for, k represents what this character of mine is so others can use it in the late 19th century when chinese immigrants flooded into the united states, prompting the need to screen and exclude. the paradox that legal immigration is hard while illegal immigration is easy persists to this day. this episode uses a historian's work to overturn the common sense that 'immigration control originated in the west,' and through cases such as the chinese exclusion act, indentured labor, and the natal model, it explains the mechanisms of institutions and power. for chinese-speaking listeners interested in immigration, customs systems, global history, and foucault's theories, especially those concerned with how modern states control populations through documents and permits. 忽左忽右 忽左忽右 493 追忆历史学家亚当·麦基翁：华人移民与现代边境制度的形成 mckeown immigration history chinese exclusion act global history foucault customs system chinese immigrants shaped the us customs system in 'the melancholy order,' mckeown argues that the global modern customs and immigration control system was not established by white european immigrants, but developed in the late 19th century when a large number of chinese immigrants poured into the united states, as the us needed to determine who could enter and by what standards to classify them. in a striking phrase, it was chinese immigrants who shaped the us customs. this system then spread globally, so chinese immigrants played a key role in the formation of modern border control, thereby also refuting eurocentrism in immigration history. cheng yanliang foucault's concept of power runs through the immigration system mckeown is deeply influenced by foucault: power is not top-down and concentrated in the state, but exists in everyday details and operates in a network. when immigrants apply for visas, they are required to provide various certificates and materials; this disciplinary mechanism and knowledge discourse precisely reflect the operation of power. yang bin points out that the immigration system is full of absurdities and paradoxes. for example, when applying for a student visa, regardless of whether you actually intend to return to your home country after graduation, you must check the box stating that you will return; otherwise, the visa officer will directly reject you. the system appears to operate between legal and illegal, but it is actually riddled with paradoxes created by power. cheng yanliang the chinese exclusion act established national immigration sovereignty mckeown analyzes the chinese exclusion act of 1882, pointing out that its most important aspect was establishing the unilateral jurisdiction of the receiving country. previously, the authority of the sending and receiving countries was unclear; the chinese exclusion act placed the decision-making power in the hands of the united states, thus giving rise to the distinction between passports and visas today: a passport is an identity document provided by the home country, while a visa is decided by the receiving country whether to accept. in the modern international system, the decision-making power over immigration control ultimately rests with the receiving country—this is the key conclusion drawn from the chinese exclusion act. cheng yanliang illegal immigration is easy, legal immigration is hard the us immigration system has a paradoxical outcome: about 10 million low-educated illegal immigrants make up 5% of the us labor force and have long been able to stay due to lax enforcement; conversely, highly educated non-immigrant talents often have to wait years in line to apply for a us green card. the system ostensibly encourages free immigration, but in reality it is centered on screening and obstruction. this absurdity, contrast, and paradox is what mckeown calls the 'melancholy order.' so-called free immigration is merely an invention and imagination of the modern state; immigration has always been defined, classified, and filtered by the state. cheng yanliang indentured labor replaced black slavery in the mid-to-late 19th century, as the abolitionist movement surged in the western world, a labor vacuum appeared on the plantations of the new world. contracted chinese laborers emerged as substitutes for black slaves, known as 'selling piglets.' chinese laborers in the us typically earned about $30 per month, and after deducting living expenses, could send home $80-100 per year; at that time, the average annual income of chinese farmers was only $8-10, a difference of about tenfold. it was this economic drive that fueled the wave of emigration from south china in the late qing dynasty. a case in point is sun yat-sen's elder brother, sun mei, who started as an indentured laborer and later became a large rancher owning 6,500 acres. cheng yanliang passports came before id h: mandalay hinged on one call: drop the frontal assault, lay siege in march 1945 british forces attacked mandalay in burma; against fort dufferin's thick walls and deep moat, the frontal assault failed. the division commander refused to keep storming it and switched to a siege, and the japanese eventually abandoned the fort. rare front-line field recordings from the second world war, but the episode runs only nine minutes and is weak on analysis; suited to lovers of historical audio who want to be on the battlefield fast. second world war enthusiasts who want a few minutes of real battlefield sound, and readers who follow the burma theatre and the history of commonwealth forces. witness history witness history the battle of mandalay in ww2 wwii burma mandalay siege warfare bbc field recordings commonwealth forces mandalay was attacked to take rangoon before the monsoon in march 1945 the british 14th army was pursuing retreating japanese forces through central burma. mandalay was burma's second-largest city and strategically placed; the british believed that taking it would let them liberate the capital, then called rangoon, before the monsoon arrived in may. the japanese were dug in at the mandalay palace fort, which the british called fort dufferin. the host explains that this episode works differently from the usual format: instead of finding a survivor to recall the events, it uses the original audio that bbc correspondent douglas claverdon recorded at the front line in 1945. tim o'callaghan eight feet of brick plus a moat left no frontal answer standing by the flagstaff at fort dufferin, claverdon describes the defences: the fort is more than a mile square, walled on all four sides in dark red brick roughly 30 feet high, the brickwork 8 feet thick, with earth banked up behind it 30 feet wide at ground level; outside that runs a moat 70 yards wide and 10 or 11 feet deep. on the afternoon of 9 march the frontier force regiment, supported by tanks and artillery, pushed to within 100 yards of the wall, but the japanese sheltering behind the wall and the moat could not be driven out, and the british could do no more than consolidate the ground they held. douglas claverdon men cresting the bank became silhouettes against the brick wall on 10 march reese, commanding the 19th indian division, launched a full assault. a 5.5-inch gun fired directly at the wall from about 250 yards for more than an hour. the bbc recording van pulled up behind a small concrete building 300 to 400 yards outside the north wall, and a senior officer recorded a live commentary from the spot: the troops were going forward, the tanks were firing hard, but the formation was a little bunched. even so, nothing got in: the japanese had sited their machine guns close to the waterline of the moat, and the brick wall behind made the british clear silhouettes as they came over the bank, so they were shot down one by one. douglas claverdon the division commander called it a hornets' nest, not worth storming with the assault beaten, reese ordered a withdrawal. the next day he told war correspondents that he had never seen braver men than the frontier force regiment; but as he saw it, fort dufferin was nothing more than a hornets' nest, and he was not prepared to spend the lives of large numbers of his soldiers on a fort that could only be taken by frontal assault. so for the next two days the 19th indian division worked forward step by step through the wrecked houses of the city, while night patrols kept probing the walls for weak points. the tactics shifted here from assault to siege, and what followed proved the choice a sound one. douglas claverdon the siege did not go smoothly: the boat crossing the moat sank parked under trees at the roadside, the bbc van recorded an infantry company advancing under enemy fire while it waited for another company to work around from the left. the recordist says he spent most of the time lying underneath the van, wishing he had a steel helmet. on the night of 16 march the 15th punjab tried to cross the moat by boat and get into the fort, but one boat sank, drowning the leading troops of the second wave; to avoid further casualties the unit pulled back before dawn. this stretch shows a siege going badly, with the japanese still resisting. douglas claverdon once the ring closed, the japanese pulled out that same night on 19 march the allies threw a heavy attack at a pagoda commanding the east gate: bombers went in first, then heavy artillery, and then two companies of the worcestershire regiment took the objective with tank support, bringing the encirclement of fort dufferin close to complete. the japanese evacuated the fort that night. mountbatten, supreme allied commander south east asia, then announced over the radio that mandalay had fallen, noting that japanese propaganda had called it a position they would fight to hold; he thanked all the services and the british, american, indian, african and chinese troops

h: the sultan came to her: tétouan's woman governor was no pirate sayyida al-hurra governed tétouan for more than twenty years, built shipyards and worked with ottoman privateers against spain and portugal; european sources call her a pirate, while recent scholarship treats her as an example of early decolonial practice. the middle stretch untangles pirate from privateer, and shows how the standpoint of the surviving sources shapes the history — a payoff beyond the biography. the listener mail at the end is skippable. content writers working on north african and mediterranean trade, or interested in case studies of women governing; if you are short on time, listen only to the middle section on privateering and skip the mail at the end. stuff you missed in history class stuff you missed in history class sayyida al-hurra, moroccan queen morocco pirates and privateers ottoman empire women rulers maritime history her title meant noble, powerful, independent — not pirate the episode opens with its most important judgment: european sources compress sayyida al-hurra's whole life into the word "pirate," but the label cannot account for the full picture. sayyida al-hurra is an honorific, literally carrying senses like "noble, powerful, independent," and it was used for other muslim women as well, among them the twelfth-century yemeni ruler arwa al-sulaihi. she was probably born somewhere between 1485 and 1495; her father was ali ibn rashid, a prince of sharifian descent, and she grew up in the multiethnic community of chefchaouen, fluent in arabic, spanish and portuguese. tracy v. wilson the city she governed was a fortification and a refugee camp at once chefchaouen was built in the rif mountains, roughly 60 kilometers from the coast, precisely to defend against portuguese incursion after portugal took ceuta in 1415. in the same era, spain conquered granada in 1492, ending the reconquista, and issued the alhambra decree that same year expelling jews; muslims were then required to convert or leave in 1502 and 1526. chefchaouen and tétouan consequently filled with muslims, jews and converted muslims (moriscos) fleeing the iberian peninsula, forming refugee communities that were diverse but not entirely equal. tracy v. wilson her governorship came from her brother's appointment, not from inheritance in 1510 she married mulay al-mandri, the governor of tétouan — a political marriage joining two families and two parts of the region, chefchaouen and tétouan. because she was educated, she was able to assist her husband in governing from the start, and when he traveled her share of the rule was gradually formalized. her husband died around 1519 and his brother wanted to seize power, but her own brother ibrahim, serving as vizier in fez, named her the successor. it was not common for a woman to hold that kind of power, yet she appears to have won the trust of the population and was accepted as governor. tracy v. wilson her ships guarded the coast and also captured spanish and portuguese vessels facing continuous pressure from portugal and spain, and a moroccan economy in decline as european shipping routed around africa, she worked with the ottoman privateers oruç reis and hızır reis (often lumped together as "the barbarossa brothers"). the two were sons of a potter from lesbos, first served a sultan's son, later were hired by algiers, and ultimately served the ottoman empire. she built shipyards where the ottomans could construct and berth ships, and she also expanded her late husband's fleet; those ships both defended morocco and attacked and captured spanish and portuguese ships, with captives held at tétouan awaiting ransom. tracy v. wilson if holding captives for ransom counts, elizabeth i was a pirate too holding captives and demanding ransom from their home country cannot on its own be the line that makes her a pirate, because the practice was fairly common at the time. the episode notes that oruç was once captured by a knightly order and freed when his brother hızır paid the ransom; spain and portugal were also kidnapping and enslaving people in africa. the scholar jason idris sparks goes further in his paper and draws an analogy between her and elizabeth i: elizabeth likewise employed the privateer francis drake and eventually knighted him. for these rulers and for the barbarossa brothers, the motive was largely to defend muslim territory and to strike back at the attacks on muslims on the iberian peninsula. tracy v. wilson she would not go to fez, so the sultan came to marry her in 1541 the sultan of fez, ahmad al-wattasi, proposed marriage to her. by convention a sultan's bride would travel to fez for the wedding and remain in the capital, but sayyida al-hurra refused to leave tétouan; the sultan had to go to tétouan himself for the wedding, and afterward she stayed on as ruler. as the show puts it, "this was not at all how it was usually done." the marriage was political, comparable to ferdinand and isabella unitin

h: science is not a warehouse of answers but a structured inquiry into ‘what we don't know’ science is not a warehouse of facts but a structured interrogation of what we do not know; failure is the normal condition and uncertainty is the hallmark. what the public really needs to learn is how to ask a good question. the opening small talk runs long, but the second half — on uncertainty as the mark of real expertise, and on the bind that assessment puts science education in — is worth the time for working scientists and educators. research administrators, science educators and technology investors — anyone who has to judge whether a high-risk direction deserves a bet; and scientists who get pressed by students and the public on what science actually rests on. sean carroll's mindscape mindscape 364 | stuart firestein on how science relies on ignorance and failure science education scientific method uncertainty pseudoscience philosophy of science pluralism science class teaches the conclusions and never the science itself sean opens with a view he has held for a long time: science education is like an art class that only shows you the masterpieces and never teaches you how to mix paint, or a piano class that plays recordings and never teaches fingering. students get f=ma, rock classification and natural selection drilled into them, and then get examined on how well they remember. but the daily reality of science is failure, surprise and not knowing. the public misreads how science works precisely because school never shows the process, only the results. sean carroll ignorance is not a hole in science, it is the fuel firestein named his two books against intuition: ignorance is what drives science, and failure is the reason science succeeds. at a conference, scientists talk only about what they don't know; nobody stands up to present what is already established. every known fact drags ten new questions in behind it. failure is the normal condition, and because science deliberately gives up authority and demands evidence, infallibility is not part of a scientist's job description. the public, meanwhile, sees science as a stack of answers — the misconception most in need of correcting. stuart firestein the scientific revolution began by deliberately manufacturing ignorance the first move of the scientific revolution was to manufacture a great deal of ignorance on purpose and rebuild from a blank slate. firestein quotes bacon: truth used to come from authority, and from that point on authority came from truth. bacon also invented the experiment — cutting a slice out of nature, controlling the other variables, and putting one small piece of nature to the question. but nobody foresaw that most experiments would fail; failure was written into the genome of the scientific method from the start. stuart firestein the scientific method is after-the-fact rhetoric, not how the work is done the ‘scientific method’ is firestein's main target: no scientist actually works through the hypothetico-deductive checklist, which is just elegant rhetoric applied afterwards. hypotheses are cheap, you use one and throw it away; what matters is imagination and creativity. he also doesn't believe in serendipity — when a nobel laureate calls it an accident, that is false modesty. somebody who was not in that position doing that work would never have stumbled into that discovery; you have to already be hard at work before an accident has any chance of hitting you. stuart firestein intuition is best at producing errors that look correct firestein illustrates counterintuition with a body-disposal trick a magician friend taught him: bury the corpse eight feet down, and bury a dead dog at four feet. police and cadaver dogs dig, hit the dog, and call off the search — intuition says it is just a pet grave. our intuitions manufacture high-quality errors of exactly this kind all day long, and scientists are no exception. being counterintuitive means digging a little deeper, and not letting a result that happens to look beautiful turn into a paper too early. stuart firestein the more certain a claim is, the more likely it is pseudoscience the demarcation problem has never had a precise solution in the history of philosophy. firestein offers a practical test instead: the difference between science and pseudoscience is that science is uncertain and pseudoscience is certain. someone who always has an answer and never changes it is not to be trusted; a real expert concedes uncertainty precisely because they can see the holes, the competing theories and the missing data. pseudoscience, for its part, is happy to borrow ‘scientifically proven’ as a selling point. stuart firestein optimism is an invention of science, not a temperament optimism is not a word about mood but a philosophical position, and it was only coined by voltaire in 1759. firestein argues that science invented this kind of optimism: for the previous 250,000 years human beings could only accep

h: the industrial revolution's hidden driver: parliament untangled property rights, not technology the hidden cause of the industrial revolution was the glorious revolution of the century before: parliament used legislation to untangle overly complicated property rights, which let investment in agriculture and infrastructure happen at all, and which created the precondition for a return on technical innovations like the steam engine. this episode offers a counterintuitive institutional lens: property-rights reform came before technological progress, not after it. it also bears directly on today's deadlock over infrastructure permitting and urban redevelopment. researchers, policymakers and founders who follow institutional economics and urban development, especially anyone with first-hand experience of the west's infrastructure permitting deadlock. econtalk econtalk the hidden cause of the industrial revolution (with ben southwood) industrial revolution land property rights glorious revolution infrastructure institutional economics urban building parliament untangled property rights; it did not invent the technology russ roberts reads from the opening of the article, which holds that industrial modernity was born in the english midlands in the late 18th century — but that what made all of it possible was the glorious revolution of the century before. the core mechanism: parliament used its new powers to untangle property rights that were, at the time, excessively strong and excessively complicated, and in doing so made sustained investment in infrastructure and agriculture possible for the first time. this happened almost entirely peacefully and with the consent of the rights-holders, not through violent expropriation. that is the institutional starting point for the whole conversation, and it is what gave every later land act and infrastructure project its legitimacy. russ roberts a parliament made of landowners dismantled its own privileges ben points out that after 1711 you had to own a great deal of land to sit in parliament, so parliament was composed almost entirely of landowners. the ordinary expectation would be that these large landowners would protect their own privileges and expand the space for rent-seeking — but they did the opposite: they untangled their own complicated property rights. property in the 17th century was nothing like property today. a landowner could not dispose of land freely; there were life tenancies, and land could not be mortgaged, sold or divided, because it was bound up in complicated ‘entail’ settlements. it was precisely this self-binding property regime that formed the single largest institutional obstacle before the industrial revolution, and parliament dismantled these antique restrictions one act at a time. ben southwood open fields were insurance, and the price was that nobody could innovate ben explains two kinds of land that have now largely disappeared: commons and open fields. a common was not something anyone could use — only local landowners could graze on it, according to their ‘stints’, under complicated rules. under the open-field system, land was cut into many narrow strips scattered across different parcels, which provided insurance but blocked innovation. new crops (such as potatoes and maize) and new techniques (such as horse ploughing) required coordination, and consensus was hard to reach. so even when farmers understood that a new arrangement would raise output, the collective-action problem meant they could not change it on their own; they had to rely on parliament to coordinate by compulsion. ben southwood before the 1660s, england's roads were worse than a thousand years earlier southwood notes that parliament passed three kinds of act in great volume: acts resolving family inheritance problems, acts consolidating inefficient small parcels, and acts establishing turnpikes, canals and navigable rivers. almost none of these existed before the 1660s, and england's roads at the time were extremely bad — worse even than in the era of king alfred. by 1800, thousands of miles of turnpikes and canals had been built, creating national markets in grain, fertiliser, pottery and textiles, and allowing comparative advantage to operate. this shows that acts of parliament did not merely rearrange land rights; they directly created an infrastructure network. ben southwood technology with no market is not worth inventing russ sums up southwood's argument: agriculture became more efficient through legislation and property-rights reform, capital accumulated, and improved infrastructure sharply raised the return on technical innovations such as the steam engine. he draws an analogy to israel's high-tech industry — without a global market, the innovation would not be worth doing. infrastructure is the precondition for technology's value to be realised, and government's role was only to permit private parties to build through a reallocation of property rights, not to pro
