h: the pain of frontier tech entrepreneurship: on ipo day, i felt i'd let down those 12 years li zhifei, founder of mobvoi, says that at the moment of the bell-ringing, he wasn't thinking of glory but of whether the outcome justified the 12 years of hardship — and it didn't. he sums up the fate of frontier tech startups as a block of ice that can melt at any moment. an ai entrepreneur who spent 12 years and just took his company public talks candidly about failure, depression, and strategic misjudgments. high information density; the second half is worth more than the first. founders building large models or ai applications, agonizing over whether to go all in, and investors who want to see the real financial and strategic dilemmas of ai companies. 张小珺·商业访谈录 张小珺·商业访谈录 66. 和李志飞聊ipo、gpt-4o和你不知道的前沿科技创业的痛 frontier tech entrepreneurship large models gpt-4o strategy ipo most frontier technologies eventually disappear li zhifei proposes a "funnel model": of 100 frontier technologies, only a tiny fraction can be packaged from a technology into a product, form a business model, and have the technology investment and commercial value match to a sustainable level. most technologies at that point in time cannot pass the funnel test. but that doesn't mean the technology is useless — it might come back 10 years later because the environment has changed, the technology has matured, demand has matured, or new demand has emerged, and the technology is pulled out and run through the funnel again. he cites google glass in 2013: at the time everyone literally saw the future, but the product quickly disappeared, and the entire ar and vr industry hasn't taken off in all these years; now gpt-4o and google have spawned glasses again, and you see the future again — it's back. li zhifei a vision without a path and rhythm plan is just耍流氓 li zhifei says it's easy to talk about a broad future — he said in 2014 that every company would have an ai department, and a normal person wouldn't be too far off with such a judgment. what really matters is the judgment of path and rhythm: what to do first, what to do second. he gives two competitive scenarios: if a giant and a startup reach a consensus at the same time, and that consensus is wrong, the startup will definitely die because it can't hold out; if the startup forms a cognition of the future half a year to a year ahead of the giant, and has a relatively precise plan, then there's a certain probability of success — provided you can use that one-year time gap to build some kind of barrier, otherwise the startup will also die. he adds: even if this thing looks hopeless, as long as there's an investor willing to give you a billion dollars, that can keep you alive. li zhifei the key to gpt-4o is unification plus end-to-end li zhifei first states, "we don't know either, because they didn't publish a paper; we're all guessing." he identifies two core points: first, it's a unified single model, with all modalities in the same model; second, it's most likely based on the gpt architecture, using a language model as the cognitive foundation, then adding other perceptual modalities. he uses the analogy of teaching a monkey to cook versus teaching a six-year-old child to cook — the child has built a cognitive model of the world, so you can just describe in language how to cook; the monkey has no cognitive foundation. why is it hard? you have to turn all modalities into tokens, just like text. he mentions that his own model workshop's voiceover model was trained last april by adding voice training on top of a language model, but the language model was too small, so it could only do voiceover, not q&a. gpt-4o, on the other hand, can do both speech generation and understanding, and its text cognitive ability hasn't declined — it's even stronger than gpt-4 on mmlu. li zhifei there is voice generation, but no video generation li zhifei noticed a detail: gpt-4o's assistant model does not include video generation; whether at google or openai, video generation is a separate model. he explains the reason is that sora is not an autoregressive architecture; it probably uses dit, a diffusion architecture. he repeatedly emphasizes his belief: a unified model should be based on autoregression, putting understanding and generation together. he guesses that someone inside openai must be working on this, but he's not sure if it's being treated as the all-in direction — "engineers have their own beliefs too; they feel autoregression is unhappy, they feel diffusion is happier." he also gives the order-of-magnitude difference in token length: text is a few characters per second, voice is dozens of tokens per second, video might be several hundred tokens per second, each is at least an order of magnitude increase, and token length directly determines the cost and speed of inference. li zhifei bytedance's big price cut is inevitable; s: 2024-04-17-zhangxiaojun-agi-是马拉松-物理硬件成了最大瓶颈
h: agi is a marathon: physical hardware has become the biggest bottleneck last year we thought adding gpus and data would get us to agi; this year we find that a single data center hits a wall at 32,000 cards, and us energy infrastructure was planned forty or fifty years ago—the agi timeline has been stretched out by the physical world. a frontline investor strings compute, energy, models, products and alliances into one agi infrastructure map, dense with numbers, suited to anyone who wants to quickly calibrate their judgment. founders, investors and engineers following agi progress, who want to use one episode to calibrate their judgment on compute, energy, models and products. 张小珺·商业访谈录 张小珺·商业访谈录 64. 和广密聊agi大基建时代：电+芯片=产出智能 agi compute infrastructure scaling law robotics agi has gone from a sprint to a marathon early last year everyone thought agi was a hundred-meter sprint and no one was prepared; this year it has become a marathon, and everyone has ample time to prepare. the change comes from a concrete discovery: last year we thought we could add gpus and data indefinitely to reach agi, but suddenly we found that gpu data centers and physical hardware are a huge bottleneck—a single data center now scales to 32,000 cards, and going beyond that requires breaking through many limits; us energy infrastructure was planned forty or fifty years ago, and the energy mix is very different, so suddenly adding a lot of electricity demand really can't keep up. so the biggest feeling this year is that physical hardware has become the biggest factor hindering the agi timeline. li guangmi the economy suddenly got two new taxes one judgment is: model companies may be where value accumulates most thickly, just as mobile internet value accumulated in device makers and advertising platforms. thus two taxes appear—jensen huang's gpus collect a compute tax, and models collect an intelligence tax, suddenly adding two taxes to the economy and society. but li guangmi also gives the counterargument: if large models are electricity, the light bulb isn't necessarily made by the power plant. he leans toward large model companies being a research lab for basic discoveries; some labs have commercial capability and will produce top applications, but that tests organizational capability. li guangmi gpt-4's entry ticket is 300 million dollars break training cost into electricity and cards: assume gpt-3.5 trains for 15 days on 500 h100s, about 250,000 kwh, which is 0.05% of the three gorges or shanghai's electricity consumption; gpt-4 trains for 100 days on 8,000 h100s, about 26 million kwh, which is 5% of the three gorges or shanghai's daily electricity consumption, and 2% of texas's; if gpt-5 trains for 100 days on 32,000 h100s, it would be about 20% of the three gorges or shanghai's daily electricity consumption. in money: each h100 sells for $30,000, plus peripheral equipment, 8,000 cards is over $300 million—$300 million is the entry ticket for gpt-4; a 32,000-card cluster means $1.2 to $1.3 billion. li guangmi the bottleneck for a 10,000-card cluster isn't money a 10,000-card cluster is standard, but money alone isn't enough. every card must be connected, interconnection is very difficult, and the network topology is not one layer but three. factors affecting difficulty include: finding land suitable for a gpu data center, stable and cheap electricity, interconnection and communication of data centers, and the reliability of cooling and operations. resources are increasingly concentrated and converging; few customers can build large clusters, and it will converge to only four or five major customers. things in the physical world are slower to transform than the digital world. li guangmi scaling law hasn't slowed; compute just hasn't been pushed enough gpt-4 publicly has 1.8t parameters, moe architecture, about 13t data, trained for 100 days on 25,000 a100s. assume the next generation has triple the parameters and triple the data, that's 9x compute; jensen huang's announced 32,000 h100 cluster plus optimization efficiency gains just matches; wanting 10x parameters and 10x data is 100x compute, clearly not enough. the conclusion is that scaling law has not slowed; if it seems slower, it's that compute and data haven't been pushed enough—gpt-3.5 to gpt-4 used roughly twenty to thirty times more compute, and from gpt-4 to the next generation we haven't yet pushed twenty to thirty times effective compute. li guangmi this year you must surpass gpt-4, or you're out 2024 is the year of convergence for large model companies. the technical life-or-death line is that within this year you must surpass gpt-4, which requires a very strong team behind it; second- and third-tier model companies, including domestic ones, must surpass the best open-source models, otherwise their commercial value is relatively small. on compute, this year you must use a 10,000-card cluster, and few companies can do a good job with a 10,000-card cluster. the next 12 mont ‖ 張小珺 商業訪談錄 張小珺 商業訪談錄 和廣密聊 大基建時代 電 芯片 產出智能

s: 2024-04-07-zhangxiaojun-430亿美元买先正达-中国买买买大时代的高潮与落幕
h: the $43 billion syngenta deal: the peak and end of china's buying spree the golden age of chinese overseas m&a began with an official signal in 2009 and ended with the 2017 turn against globalization; syngenta was both the peak and the endpoint. buying cheap matters less than buying right—integration is the key to success. a firsthand participant reviews the entire $43 billion acquisition, explaining the four stages of m&a, two sets of discourse systems, and integration challenges. high information density, suitable for listeners interested in overseas m&a. founders, investors, and engineers following chinese companies going global through m&a, and those who want to understand the full process of the $43 billion syngenta deal and m&a integration methodology. 张小珺·商业访谈录 张小珺·商业访谈录 63. 商业口述史：中资到海外买买买的大时代，以430亿美元并购先正达为最高潮 overseas m&a syngenta state-owned enterprises globalization integration the starting point of the era was an official statement people in the industry generally believe this wave of overseas m&a began in 2009 and ended in 2017. in july 2009, the global think tank summit was held in beijing. li rongrong, then director of the state-owned assets supervision and administration commission, said in his keynote speech that the economic strength of chinese enterprises had risen significantly, but their global share was still very limited and not commensurate with china's national power. china would create a more favorable environment to actively support and encourage enterprises, especially central soes, to go global and engage in cross-border m&a. wang wei said that before this there had been private moves in response to the wind, but they were not systematic. only after the official tone was set could everyone start doing this. wang wei four things lenovo and geely had in common wang wei believes these two deals are benchmarks no one can ignore. first, before the acquisitions, both companies were confined to the domestic market and lacked a prominent industry position; geely was not even a first-tier domestic brand before acquiring volvo. second, the acquired businesses themselves were not favored by the market: ibm's pc business had low margins, and volvo's passenger car unit had already been sold off by ford. third, at the time of the deals, neither was favored; people thought the purchase prices were high and might drag down existing businesses. fourth, integration took three to five years; lenovo completed its deal in 2004, but results only appeared in 2009. in the end, both became fortune global 500 companies. wang wei western buyers cut jobs first; chinese buyers keep management wang wei explains why overseas sellers welcome chinese buyers: when western companies acquire each other, the first thing they do is cut jobs and eliminate management, because synergies usually come from saving on salaries and costs, which can amount to hundreds of millions of dollars. the first thing chinese companies do is discuss management retention, because they are unfamiliar with overseas markets and face many challenges. this is also the reputation chinese buyers have earned: willing to pay, willing to invest, willing to retain management. wang wei there are no bad deals, only bad prices wang wei says there is a saying in investment circles: there are no bad deals, only bad prices. it is always about value for money; even junk can make money if it is cheap. but companies see things differently: a deal must serve a strategic purpose. first clarify the purpose, then decide the path; m&a is just a means. if the right price can exactly solve my problem, it is a good deal. he likes to compare m&a to marriage: only the two people know if they are right for each other. outsiders may see that the education levels do not match, but what i value might be her virtue. wang wei syngenta was once the jewel in the crown when wang wei first entered the industry in 2009, he looked at the syngenta deal, but at that time chinese companies could not afford it, and the company was hailed as the jewel in the crown of the industry, said to be untouchable and not for sale. there were six major proprietary agrochemical companies: syngenta, monsanto, dow agrosciences, dupont pioneer, bayer's agrochemical business, and basf's agrochemical business—all jewels in the crown. the second tier were generic drug companies, with gross margins dropping from around 40% to over 20%. he turned to look at non-patent agrochemical companies, such as australia's nufarm and maxi aggan, the latter renamed adama after being acquired by chemchina. wang wei four stages of m&a; execution is actually the easiest wang wei divides m&a into four stages: determining strategy (the original intention), screening targets, execution, and integration. the execution stage gets the most attention because all intermediaries come in—investment banks, accountants, lawyers, consultants. if you fail, everyone blames you; s: 2024-03-17-zhangxiaojun-王小川-理想上慢一步-落地上快三步
h: wang xiaochuan: slow by one step in ideals, fast by three in execution zhu xiaohu looks at reality, yang zhilin looks at technology, and wang xiaochuan says both are only touching one leg of the elephant. what he wants to do is build a person, and healthcare is the towering, grounded scenario. wang xiaochuan directly responds to zhu xiaohu's six challenges and explains why baichuan does both foundation models and the three scenarios of healthcare, entertainment, and creation. high information density, with the second half more valuable. founders, investors, and engineers following china's large-model startup paths, especially those wanting to understand why baichuan simultaneously does foundation models and healthcare and entertainment scenarios. 张小珺·商业访谈录 张小珺·商业访谈录 61. 和王小川聊再创业这一年：回应朱啸虎与中国agi第三种可能 large models agi startups healthcare scenario models slow by one step in ideals, fast by three in execution wang xiaochuan positions himself as the third voice in china's agi. zhu xiaohu talks applications and pmf, yang zhilin talks technology and unified modeling, and he thinks each sees one leg of the elephant. his strategy: the zero-to-one problem has already been solved in the us, and catching up is much less work than starting from zero—you can approach them with a tenth or even a hundredth of the consumption; but on applications you must have your own thinking. he repeatedly stresses 'slow by one step in ideals, fast by three in execution'—this is his positioning for doing large models in china. wang xiaochuan the application of agi is building a person, not a tool wang xiaochuan believes gpt has done two things that never happened before: first, it can use language—marx said the difference between humans and animals is that humans use language; second, it can make and use tools. so he thinks the application of agi is building a human-like new species, not a tool. he opposes talking only about productivity, and thinks the second thing is that it is like a person—an assistant, advisor, professional, like a doctor, lawyer, teacher. any knowledge-intensive industry that needs supply is the greatest prospect brought by gpt. wang xiaochuan three model buildings: entertainment, healthcare, creation wang xiaochuan divides the models to be built into three worlds. entertainment, using the term from dream of the red chamber, is the 'illusory realm'—the core is not sora or midjourney, but the story engine behind them; npcs are just the connection between the story engine and the outside world. healthcare is the life model, corresponding to the real world. the third is creation, helping people improve productivity. he stresses these are not vertical models, but part of the agi model, called 'scenario models.' the three worlds may eventually merge, but he must know what capabilities the application scenarios ultimately need. wang xiaochuan doctors are a towering, grounded scenario, so dare to bet on gpt-4 responding to zhu xiaohu's challenge 'do chinese companies dare to spend money on gpt-4 research?', wang xiaochuan says he is not at all intimidated. the reason is that the scenario is clear: in building a person, doctors are a towering, grounded scenario—grounded because it benefits service, towering because it demands a large model. he gives a judgment: today, when doing large models, small models cannot do well; the larger the model, the better, with no ceiling. so betting on large models has at least one pillar, ensuring that the model's technical capability will become the moat for the scenario. wang xiaochuan responding to zhu xiaohu point by point: before pmf, there is tpf wang xiaochuan focuses on responding to zhu xiaohu's challenges. on 'no scenario, no data,' he says those companies probably do not include baichuan. on the risk that if others open-source, betting on gpt-4 will lose everything, he says open source will not produce the best models, and healthcare scenarios cannot be done well with open source. on 'ten people cannot find pmf, a hundred people cannot either,' he thinks this is a deep prejudice, because the companies zhu xiaohu invested in found m with small compute, but healthcare's m cannot be achieved with small models. he proposes the core is tpf—what kind of product the technology fits, rather than talking about pmf first. wang xiaochuan a technical colleague wanted to do sora, and i shut it down wang xiaochuan says he rarely gets angry at the company; the last time was because a technical colleague wanted to do sora. his reason: sora is not consistent with gpt; the agi ideal must be built with language as the axis, language constructs the conceptual space, and it cannot be replaced by a model like sora; video needs to incorporate language to become an engine toward agi. from the agi perspective, sora is only a阶段性 product. he thinks the public is easily impressed by visual effects, but those in the tech circle know that the breakthrough in language is much greater than in vision. wang xiaoc ‖ 張小珺 商業訪談錄 張小珺 商業訪談錄 和王小川聊再創業這一年 回應朱嘯虎與中國 第三種可能

s: 2024-03-11-zhangxiaojun-sora-是-gpt-3-时刻-不是-chatgpt-时刻
h: sora is a gpt-3 moment, not a chatgpt moment what sora shows is an emergent capability, not a usable product; it pushes the large-model war to a new level, but catching up in a year is too optimistic, because between being able to do it and actually doing it lies a great deal of know how. two investors sampled a dozen-plus groups of people to piece together the puzzle of how sora is implemented, and also give their judgments on the large-model elimination race, the bubble, and applications. information density is high, but the second half is more valuable. investors watching the large-model battle, engineers working on video generation or multimodality, founders trying to judge the timeline for catching up to sora. 张小珺·商业访谈录 张小珺·商业访谈录 60. 与戴雨森和季逸超聊，一幅sora的信息拼图和大模型淘汰赛 sora large models multimodality investment bubble sora is a gpt-3 moment, not a chatgpt moment ji yichao likens sora to gpt-3: it is a model that has emerged with certain capabilities, not a product. chatgpt was a product innovation that aligned gpt into a chat form, letting users converse and generate more input and feedback; sora, by contrast, generates a video and then it's over, with no interaction with the user. so it still has a long way to go before becoming a product, and what emergence shows is only a spark. this distinction determines how to price sora: it proves that a known model architecture can produce sora, but that does not mean it can start making money right away. ji yichao model size is about 6b, compute one or two thousand h100s from the sampling, the model parameter count is roughly around 6b, based on the 4x and 16x compute scaling examples in the tech report and extrapolated from the dit paper as a baseline. training compute may be on the scale of one or two thousand h100s, that is, tens of millions of dollars, not something that requires a billion dollars to do. but running experiments and doing the final training run are two different things; openai's already-deployed cards are estimated at two hundred thousand plus, so it can run experiments in parallel with more cards. data is what everyone is most focused on now, because model size has not increased significantly, and progress generally lies in the data and how it is processed. ji yichao between being able to do it and actually doing it lies know how dai yusen thinks catching up to sora in 6 to 12 months is too optimistic. the general direction is known, but how to tune the specific parts is not, and that is exactly what has to be figured out. after gpt-4 came out last year, many companies said they would catch up by the end of the year; now it is 2024, and the only one that has truly reached gpt-4 level across the board may be google's gemini 1.5, and it has not yet been used in an actual product. ji yichao adds that openai's starting point is much higher than that of domestic companies; sora used dall·e 3's recaptioning, and the language conditioning part may have used gpt's weights, so even with sora here, it will still take a long time of investment to get close. dai yusen sora pushes the war to a new level, and invites regulation the impact of sora's release on the global large-model battle is, first of all, to push this war to a new level. first-tier companies all knew multimodality would see a breakthrough like this, it is just that the timing came earlier, and many original plans will have to change. unlike chatgpt, it is not an interactive model; as a pure generative model, what happens after generation is still unknown. but it presents such a good video so intuitively that the impact on startups, application companies, the entertainment and film industries, and government departments is huge, and it will also invite more worries about ai regulation; departments such as the broadcasting regulator are paying very close attention to sora's appearance. dai yusen world simulators have three layers: physical, social, long-duration ji yichao divides world simulation into different layers: the first stage is relatively static scenery like aerial empty shots; the second stage is physical causality, such as a cup filled with water falling and shattering, but sora's result on this example is very poor, the cup does not know how to shatter; the next layer is social causality, such as a shark appearing on a beach causing surprise, a dolphin causing cuteness, a crocodile causing flight, or a baby punching its father versus a strong man punching a thin person meaning completely different things; further still is the echo between the beginning and end of a film. he believes what sora shows now is still an emergent capability, and it will take quite a long time before it is truly usable. ji yichao a unified model has not yet found a viable path language is discrete, while images and audio are natural continuous signals, and putting all different inputs into one feature space is itself a difficulty. what is harder is the training objective: language models predict the next w ‖ 張小珺 商業訪談錄 張小珺 商業訪談錄 與戴雨森和季逸超聊 一幅 的信息拼圖和大模型淘汰賽

s: 2024-01-27-zhangxiaojun-繁花-里的宝瀛大战-原型是一场违规收购
h: the bao-ying battle in blossoms shanghai was based on an illegal takeover in 1993, shenzhen bao'an used three subsidiaries to each buy 4.5% of yanzhong industrial, only disclosing when the combined stake hit 16%, evading the 5% announcement threshold. the csrc fined them 1 million yuan but still ruled the takeover valid—yanzhong industrial was truly bought out. liang jie of shanghai university of finance and economics, with the dual perspective of a local and an economist, compares the show's bao-ying battle, mr. a, and uncle to real history one by one. the institutional details are harder than the plot. people who watched blossoms shanghai and want to know what is historical fact, and investors and practitioners interested in the early institutional evolution of china's securities market. 张小珺·商业访谈录 张小珺·商业访谈录 57. 《繁花》真实版上海90年代：充满危险气息的黄河路和股市 shanghai stock market blossoms shanghai m&a 1990s institutional history when the exchange reopened, there were only eight stocks shanghai closed its stock exchange in 1949 and issued its first stock in 1984, but there was nowhere to trade it. in 1986, a dozen-square-meter storefront on nanjing road west and xikang road—said to have been a barbershop—was converted into an icbc trading point, with a blackboard showing the day's prices for just two stocks. the shanghai stock exchange was officially restored in 1990, with only eight stocks. people from all over the country had to come to shanghai to buy stocks. there was even fierce debate over whether stocks should be paper certificates or electronic—many felt uneasy without a piece of paper in hand. liang jie t+3 was forced by manually counting stock certificates initially, settlement was t+3: after selling a stock, you had to wait three days to get your money, because the certificates had to be counted daily—whether a thousand or ten thousand, they had to be counted one by one, and without an accurate count, payment couldn't be made. later, they found there were too many certificates; forget t+3, even t+13 wouldn't be enough. working overtime every night, they still couldn't finish counting. the exchange leadership then decided to switch to online, paperless trading. at the time, computers were just emerging, and many were skeptical. price limits weren't there from the start either; initially they were stricter than now, but later they found the limits too tight and people had no incentive to buy. after 1993, they were temporarily abolished, causing extreme price volatility, and were reinstated after 1996. liang jie almost all the earliest stock market entrants were washed out in the show, bao zong was born in the french concession area around sinan road and gaolan road, a descendant of capitalists, who entered the market to prove himself after his first love xue zhi thought he had no future. but in reality, the first wave of people who made money in the stock market from the late 1980s to early 1990s were a mixed bag: not-too-busy traditional chinese medicine doctors, university teachers who weren't so busy in the early 1990s, well-connected journalists, and vocational school teachers of finance and business. liang jie points out that what the tv series cannot fully show is that this group was largely washed out by the late 1990s, going bankrupt, disappearing, or even committing suicide for various reasons. almost no one could stand firm in the stock market for decades. liang jie yang baiwan only kept his money by buying real estate yang baiwan was a representative figure who made a lot of money by trading treasury bonds early on and then entered the stock market. in the 1980s, being a "ten-thousand-yuan household" was already considered well-off; he had a million, which was impressive in the early 1990s. but after ups and downs, he wasn't very successful in the stock market later on. fortunately, he used his earnings to buy real estate, and when he died in his seventies, he might have had tens of millions. liang jie says this is still a happy ending, but he recalls that many friends and colleagues who struggled in the stock market together quickly disappeared from the market in the 1990s or early 2000s for various reasons. liang jie the bao-ying battle is based on the bao-yan incident the heavily featured bao-ying battle in the show is based on yanzhong industrial, one of shanghai's old eight stocks, which shenzhen bao'an group wanted to acquire. the 1993 provisional regulations on the administration of stock issuance and trading stipulated that acquiring 5% of a target's shares directly or indirectly required a public announcement, and each additional 2% required another announcement with a mandatory interval. but the bao'an group had three subsidiaries each buy 4.5% and 4.8%, which together far exceeded 5%, and only disclosed when the total reached 16%. yanzhong industrial then discovered that its largest shareholder had become bao'an and immediately complained to regulators about a hostile takeover. liang jie fined 1 ‖ 張小珺 商業訪談錄 張小珺 商業訪談錄 繁花 真實版上海 年代 充滿危險氣息的黃河路和股市

h: miniso's overseas push isn't selling goods, it's an overflow of operating capability phone makers go abroad on manufacturing strength; miniso goes abroad on brand and operating capability. it runs direct-operated stores in the us and partners with a family conglomerate in the philippines, because wherever the traffic gateway is, that's where the strategy has to be. the first stretch on research methodology runs long, but the back half — overseas strategy, consumption tiering, the nature of luxury — is dense with sharp judgments. worth starting at 36 minutes. founders and investors in overseas expansion, retail and consumer investing, especially teams torn between direct operation and agency, or between extreme value-for-money and trading up. 张小珺·商业访谈录 张小珺·商业访谈录 56. 拼多多、名创优品崛起，是消费降级胜利吗？漫谈名创全球化之路 overseas expansion retail consumption tiering miniso brand retail has no siphon effect; it runs on ordinary people enduring hardship shen shuaibo sees miniso as ‘a victory of a bunch of ordinary people’: retail, unlike the internet, doesn't expand through resource-based, matthew-effect-style growth. its employees aren't recruited from the best schools, but their capacity for hardship is far higher than many better-educated people. the picture he paints: a miniso store selling over a hundred thousand a day, shelves empty by daytime, and the whole night spent restocking and re-merchandising. faking it for the occasional day is doable; sustaining it long-term is very hard. so retail also depends on luck, but not that much on luck, and not that much on the accumulation of innate resources. shen shuaibo the less technical difficulty something has, the higher its operating difficulty shen shuaibo's judgment: the less difficult something is from a manufacturing standpoint, the higher its operating difficulty, because everyone thinks they can do it. he uses bottled water as an analogy — so simple you just pump the water up and bottle it, so in the early years there were ten thousand drinking water companies, every region had its no-name brands, and in the end only a few like nongfu spring survived. evergrande couldn't pull it off; it's not something money alone can build. miniso faces the same with small commodities: low technical barrier, but an extreme test of management, channels, marketing and overall capability. reaching super-large scale is far harder than people imagine. shen shuaibo globalisation in the past was roughly equivalent to westernisation in malls in india and egypt, shen shuaibo saw that although these are arab countries, what he saw was still dove, head & shoulders, pantene — just with a string of arabic added under the english logo. his explanation: the industrialisation of southeast asia, south america, the middle east, south asia and africa was castrated. without a supply chain you can never enter brand competition, so the only brands that can appear are western ones. china's biggest overseas push in recent years was phones — xiaomi, huawei, transsion, lenovo, hisense, haier — which is essentially ‘mid-range scarce supply sold there at a lower price’. the high-end market is still samsung and apple. shen shuaibo phone overseas expansion is manufacturing strength; miniso is an overflow of operating capability shen shuaibo divides overseas expansion into two types: phones and new-energy vehicles are overseas expansion of manufacturing strength — few players, rigid demand, and once you get the general agency rights you can coast in the early days. miniso is overseas expansion of brand plus operating capability, selling spray bottles, hairbands, power banks, dolls, slippers, facing global competition. his picture: dump a pile of bottles, jars and dolls into a store on new york's times square and still have to sell several million to tens of millions a month to survive — the operating pressure is enormous. 7-eleven and familymart can open across the globe because they export management, supply chain and organisational capability in full. shen shuaibo retail doesn't sell products, it sells the store format shen shuaibo breaks miniso's development into stages: stage 0.5 is getting the store format working, because for a company that becomes a big chain, the most important product is that store format, not the individual products inside it; 1.0 is finding ‘the greatest common denominator of consumption’ — a starbucks reserve store of several thousand square metres can only open in the top locations of five top cities, so it's not the greatest common denominator; luckin's and miniso's store formats are. after that comes rapid expansion through an iron-army team of extreme management — the operations chief is a veteran who leads everyone in morning exercises, because managing an unlimited number of stores demands extreme execution. shen shuaibo franchisees get paid daily; s: 2023-12-31-zhangxiaojun-复刻-gpt-4-的只有三家-2024-年窗口就关了
h: only three companies have replicated gpt-4, and the window closes in 2024 globally only openai, anthropic and google have produced gpt-4-level models, and how 2024 plays out basically decides the long-term landscape — if you can't catch up in the next 12 months, it's very hard to flip the board afterwards. an investor who spent the whole year physically in silicon valley and backed two overseas large-model companies lays out financing, talent, cost, camps and endgame predictions as one continuous line. information density is high, but the second half is worth more than the first. founders, investors and engineers tracking the large-model race, especially anyone trying to understand the 2024 landscape window, the endgame for model companies, and the cost curve. 张小珺·商业访谈录 张小珺·商业访谈录 54. 口述全球大模型这一年：人类千亿科学豪赌与参差的中美景观 large models silicon valley financing scaling law agi there is only one core secret: data and tokenizer asked what the single most core secret is at openai, anthropic and google, the answer is that in the short term it's data — the mix of pre-training data, how the tokenizer is built; and if you could keep only one capability, it would be reasoning. this judgment pulls the ‘model race’ back from a compute narrative to data engineering: globally only two or three hundred people actually know gpt-4's data secret, almost all of them at the top few model companies, and any other company trying to figure it out needs at least several hundred, even several thousand, sufficient experiments — a few tens of thousands of gpus is a necessary condition. li guangmi the final circle for replicating gpt-4 has only three players taking replication of gpt-4 as the threshold for entering the final circle, globally only openai, anthropic and google have produced gpt-4-level models. on the timeline: openai did gpt-4 a year ago, anthropic half a year ago, google can only deliver next month, and other teams worldwide may need another 6 to 12 months. google threw the whole company at it for a year and only barely got close. three high-potential dark horses were named: musk's xai, character built by norm, a core contributor to transformer, and bidance. li guangmi only two or three hundred geniuses can build large models the talent barrier in large models is extremely high; globally the genius researchers who can actually make a real, major contribution to large models may number only two or three hundred, of whom over a hundred are at openai, twenty or thirty at google, and meta, aws and nvidia may have none. and the clustering effect is strong — these kinds of people and this kind of culture matter enormously, which is why there's less optimism that other giants can do large models well on their own. the test isn't the ceo, it's whether the model company has at least one genius scientist: openai has ilya, anthropic has dario, and the ctos of runway, ideogram and pika labs are all key figures in their respective directions. li guangmi next-generation training cost jumps from two or three hundred million to a billion if the training cost of claude 3 and gpt-4.5 is 200 to 300 million dollars, then the next generation in 2025 and 2026 could cost at least 1 billion dollars, even 3 to 5 billion. training cost splits into two parts: three quarters goes to experiments (repeated trial and error on small-scale models), one quarter to the final big training run — like a rocket launch. the publicly rumored figure for gpt-4 was 22,000 a100s training for 100 days, with the pure big-training cost at roughly 80 million dollars, but the biggest cost is the earlier experiments. 70 billion parameters is a dividing line: below it you can tolerate many errors, above it every step up makes training difficulty rise exponentially. li guangmi once 2024 plays out, the landscape is set how 2024 plays out basically decides the rough landscape; the window may be the next 12 months, and if you can't catch up in the next 12 months, it's very hard to flip the board afterwards. the most idealized landscape is that probably only one company remains — the most advanced model is also the cheapest, so there's no reason to use a second one; but because of camp rivalry, in practice it may be two or three. the camps: microsoft and openai on one side, amazon and google together backing anthropic on another, google as its own camp, and apple and tesla representing the device camp. meta isn't necessarily a large-model company; it's a company using ai to do its own business well. li guangmi cost is the overlooked invisible competitive edge large models going forward have two main threads: the visible line is rising intelligence capability, and each increment unlocks some new applications; the invisible line is falling cost — model training cost fell 4 to 5 times over the past 18 months, inference cost fell by a factor of 10 over the past 18 months, and another two or three rounds of optimization shouldn't be a problem. these two threads determine the scale of the ai ‖ 張小珺 商業訪談錄 張小珺 商業訪談錄 口述全球大模型這一年 人類千億科學豪賭與參差的中美景觀

s: 2023-12-15-zhangxiaojun-嫉妒无法被消除-只会换个地方重新长出来
h: envy can't be eliminated, it just grows back somewhere else you erase one source of envy, and people immediately invent another — because envy is rooted in hierarchy, and hierarchy is animal and cannot be erased. a good organization doesn't eliminate envy; it redirects the energy of pulling others down into pulling yourself up. wang yajun moves from animal nature and a four-element framework to cubicles, elevators and ab teams, offering actionable judgments rather than platitudes. information density is medium-high; the second half is worth more than the first. founders, ceos, hr heads, and professionals agonizing over year-end performance reviews or whether to join a particular company. 张小珺·商业访谈录 张小珺·商业访谈录 52.【职场人性】论嫉妒：人类最禁忌的情感，在职场里暗涌 workplace psychology organization management corporate culture envy decision-making erase one bias and people will invent the next the medium of envy can be eliminated; envy itself cannot. once cars, houses and luxury goods are all the same, people look at cubicle size, whether the office has a window, how close you sit to the chairman. level those too, and they look at how much hair you have, whether it's black or white, whether your skin glows. wang yajun's explanation: behind envy is hierarchy, and hierarchy determines the ability to acquire resources. that comes from the animal part of the human mind, so people will always create new things that separate themselves from others. the implication for managers: don't expect to cure envy by flattening one difference. you can only decide what the next invented difference will be. wang yajun the bigger the gap, the less envy; the more alike, the more envy the intensity of envy is inversely proportional to distance. two people far apart generally won't envy each other. close together, or even formerly peers, one year-end review separates them, and next year a new position opens and one becomes the other's superior — that is the most awkward way to work together. so some companies require that when several people compete for ceo, once one wins, the other two or three must leave. ge did exactly that, on the logic that "i don't quite believe people can still work together calmly after something like that happens." wang yajun distinguishes this from mckinsey's up-or-out: the latter is more a matter of ability, the former a matter of human nature. wang yajun envy itself is vitality; the question is where it goes wang yajun doesn't treat envy as purely negative: at bottom it's about securing a higher probability for one's own survival and the transmission of one's dna — a manifestation of vitality. imagine a world without envy, where everyone feels it's all the same whether others are better or worse than them, and no one wants to change the current situation. that world wouldn't move forward; it would become static. so the key isn't whether envy exists, but which path it takes once it does — pull others down, or lift yourself up. the six-pack example: one option is to make sure he doesn't have one; the other is for me to go train. the starting point is about the same; the action and the result are completely different. wang yajun luxury goods sell not function but stratification wang yajun says he used to find it hard to understand why one hermès bag costs so much more than another bag that's unknown, or even somewhat known — a bit more expensive makes sense, but that much more is unreasonable. then he figured it out: what you're ultimately buying isn't its function of holding things, but its function of stratification — telling others i have the money to buy this. same with luxury cars. school uniforms are the reverse operation: make everyone dress alike, so kids from very wealthy families and ordinary families wear the same thing and don't generate pointless envy. but even then, some kid will find a small way to be different. same in companies: everything else is about the same, but the watch has to be very expensive. wang yajun if your rating is low, don't fight it within one cycle performance evaluation is an abstract standard; the higher up you go, the more it resembles an ideal — perhaps no one exactly matches the a or a+ profile. those being rated feel it's unfair, which is essentially a form of envy, just usually called unfairness. wang yajun's advice is to look at procedural fairness: if you believe the company has rationality and fairness in how it handles such matters, stay another cycle and see what happens next time. the reason is that information can never be perfectly symmetric; there will always be error, but a good system, given two or three tries, will most likely regress to the mean — this time it pulled you down, next time it may be better; this time it pushed you up, next time it will pull you down. conversely, if every time you feel you deserve an a but every time you get a b+, you need to figure out whether it's systematic targeting or a bias in your self-perception. ask several people; don't keep it bottled up. ‖ 張小珺 商業訪談錄 張小珺 商業訪談錄 職場人性 論嫉妒 人類最禁忌的情感 在職場裡暗湧

s: 2023-12-11-zhangxiaojun-中国汽车出口第一-但日本车企的出海课还没上完
h: china is now the world's top car exporter, but its automakers haven't finished learning japan's overseas playbook china exported 4.41 million vehicles in 2023 to take the global top spot, yet from 2012 to 2020 its total exports were stuck at around 1 million units a year for eight straight years. japanese automakers' first overseas push into the us in the 1950s was a fiasco; they only turned it around thanks to the oil crisis of the 1970s — a crisis is an opportunity, but political risk matters as much as economic risk. it uses 60 years of japanese automakers' overseas history as a mirror for china today. the details of toyota's and honda's failures and turnarounds are concrete, and offer a direct reference for understanding the political risks chinese automakers face going abroad. founders and investors watching chinese auto exports, geopolitical risk and the globalization of manufacturing, plus industry researchers who want to understand how japanese automakers rose. 张小珺·商业访谈录 张小珺·商业访谈录 51. 地缘政治与大国汽车：中国跃居第一出口国？别浪费大危机 auto exports geopolitics japanese automakers new energy globalization eight years stuck at 1 million units is a geopolitical problem, not a product problem from 2012 to 2020, china's total vehicle exports — including both fuel-burning and new-energy vehicles — hovered around 1 million units. zhang junyi breaks out three reasons. first, export destinations were concentrated: iran was once the largest overseas market for chinese automakers, and after the us sanctioned iran, in 2019 china exported almost no cars to iran at all, causing a major decline. second, european and american regulations and technical requirements are complex and certification cycles are long. third, sea and land transport capacity was limited, with tight slots and high prices — at one point tesla booked entire ro-ro ships, leaving other automakers with orders they could not ship. earlier still, in 2005 a chinese model scored zero in a german crash test, which directly caused the first overseas push to fail. zhang junyi the pandemic interrupted international supply, and chinese cars filled the gap after the pandemic began in 2020, international supply was disrupted and many overseas markets struggled to deliver vehicles. chinese models, accepted by consumers for their practical and applied value, became a major supplement to local markets. at the same time, transport capacity problems were gradually resolved and export certifications completed, so exports scaled up naturally. in 2021 they suddenly broke 2 million units, overtaking south korea to become the world's third-largest vehicle exporter after japan and germany; in 2022 they broke 3 million to overtake germany; in 2023 they overtook japan. zhang junyi repeatedly stresses one line: never waste a good crisis. zhang junyi secure the home front first: an unstable domestic base means overseas setbacks zhang junyi says the phrasing may not be quite right, but the meaning is this: for a company to live well and survive, it must do so as a whole, and overseas business is always attached to the domestic business. if the domestic base is unstable, overseas development will also suffer setbacks. he gives two counterexamples: aiways exported a fair number of cars early on, but after its domestic business stumbled, its international business gradually changed too; great wall, unable to sell domestically at the time because it could not obtain a license, instead developed in places like russia and then turned back to the domestic market. but new-energy vehicles are a scale-competition market, and the gap between leaders and laggards keeps widening — going straight overseas without a certain base volume is a huge challenge. zhang junyi toyota's first us push: ugly, expensive cars nobody bought in the 1950s toyota's first attempt to export to the us met with a major setback. japanese cars were compact, small and durable, completely at odds with the flashy, large, powerful and gas-guzzling design of american cars, and americans found them ugly and unsuitable. zhang junyi breaks out the specific reasons: the us wanted large-displacement, large-body cars, while japanese cars had insufficient horsepower and were small; japanese roads were poor at the time, so vehicle designs targeted japanese road conditions; on price, a toyota model cost nearly $2,000, equivalent to 67% of the average american wage at the time, so americans could not afford it either; and more critically, the overseas strategy was simply immature — neither the sales nor the repair and maintenance market was in place, and with no parts supply nobody dared buy. zhang junyi the oil crisis gave small-displacement japanese cars their opening during the oil crisis of the 1970s, american cars were powerful but burned fuel heavily — they were gas guzzlers — and both sales and profits were hit hard. in the two crises gm's profit fell 50% and revenue fell 30%; ford's profit contracted threefold, turning from positive to negativ ‖ 張小珺 商業訪談錄 張小珺 商業訪談錄 地緣政治與大國汽車 中國躍居第一齣口國 別浪費大危機

s: 2023-12-07-zhangxiaojun-95后创业者把马斯克值拉满-但偶像其实是毛主席
h: post-95 founders max out their musk score, but their idol is actually mao what drives this wave of young founders isn't money, it's "this thing is badass, so let's build it first"; they don't write bps, don't chase leaderboards, don't do pr on their own initiative, and only accumulate reputation within the circles they care about. a founder born in 1997 gives his first interview, laying out clearly the real differences between this new generation of founders and the last one in drive, idols and management style, with concrete detail. founders and investors watching ai startups, aigc applications and 3d generation, and anyone who wants to understand the real state of post-95 and post-00 founders. 张小珺·商业访谈录 张小珺·商业访谈录 50. 95后、00后创业者怎么样了？他们的生猛、高马斯克值与现实 ai startups aigc 3d generation new-gen founders team management ai 1.0 was tuning parameters, 2.0 is general models song yacheng draws the difference between sensetime and minimax very clearly: the ai 1.0 era was a large number of scientists using hand-tuned parameters to solve long-tail problems one by one — face recognition, ocr, vehicle recognition, illegal dumping, one algorithm per scenario. by ai 2.0, it's the brute-force aesthetics of data driven, using one general large model to solve general problems, then growing segmented applications on top of the model. his judgment is that "it's a very black-box thing" — not covering the long tail with small algorithms plus a technical architecture, but optimizing one very general model. song yacheng six months without pay, 30-plus people held on they started the company at the end of last year, right at the point when the us was raising rates, russia and ukraine were at war, and everything that should have blown up and shouldn't have blown up had blown up. ask any fa and they'd say vcs might barely invest at all in 2023. song yacheng put his own money in, and the company only formally started paying salaries in june; before that there were six months with no pay for anyone, and the team of roughly thirty-plus people kept going the whole time. he says this is a trait of post-95 and post-00 founders — "we are a group of very faithful people." song yacheng the musk score is demanding that essential thing to the death song yacheng's definition of the "musk score": knowing very clearly what i want, then i want these one, two, three things, and no matter what method i'll get there; if someone comes along who can help me get there, we get there, and if they can't, i swap them out. his example is going to siggraph this august to give a keynote — the top graphics conference's fiftieth anniversary, fifty or sixty thousand attendees, with nvidia's jensen huang, ibm, unity and sony each speaking for an hour, and them too. never in history had a chinese person given a keynote at siggraph. the organizing committee at one point suspected they were a shell company; they asked partners like blender's ceo to write recommendation letters proving the company really existed, went through two or three rounds of interviews, and in the end what he went up and said was "i'm actually not here to talk about technology." song yacheng 3d data is scarce, so they scraped together 11 million entries he breaks ai into three things: the horse trainer (algorithms), the racetrack (compute), and the fodder (data). 3d is an extremely data-scarce field — most people have written weibo posts, posted to moments, shot videos, but never k-ed a 3d model. at the time openai's private dataset was 2 million, nvidia's 1 million, and other big companies around 700,000. as a startup, they spent huge amounts of time working with games, animation, film and tv, model communities and databases, pestering and trading on face, and in the end got 11 million high-quality entries — 3d native data hand-k-ed one by one by people in games, animation and film. a single model costing tens or hundreds of dollars is normal; buying it was out of the question. song yacheng his startup idol is mao, not musk song yacheng says the first answer from people around him for a startup idol is basically always elon musk, but he's a bit different — his idol is chairman mao. the reason is that he cares a lot about faith: the soul of a company lies in having faith, and things done out of faith don't need you telling someone every day, they'll go do it themselves. he observes that most post-80 founders didn't go abroad in middle school but went abroad for a master's, and their idols are generally jobs types; his generation went out earlier, and their idols are different instead. he distinguishes jobs from musk: jobs pulled an mp4 out of his pocket as a kid, while what musk makes is a sci-fi experience, "dragging nine strips and needing to run faster than nine strips." song yacheng two completely opposite kinds of people live inside an aigc company the technical people are relatively rational, more i-type, a bit socially anxious, don't like team building, each managing their own module like an a ‖ 張小珺 商業訪談錄 張小珺 商業訪談錄 後 後創業者怎麼樣了 他們的生猛 高馬斯克值與現實

s: 2023-11-21-zhangxiaojun-openai-政变-非营利董事会为何能踢走-ceo
h: the openai coup: how a nonprofit board could fire its ceo a 700-person company less than five years old, a six-member nonprofit board that exercised its power once and pulled off a coup — and its largest shareholder, microsoft, isn't even on the board. luo yihang has long been based in silicon valley and has had direct contact with sam altman. he explains the ins and outs of openai's power mechanism and how silicon valley elite politics actually works — this is not a retelling of the news. founders and investors watching ai corporate governance, founder control, and how overseas teams handle american-style politics; engineers who want to understand how openai's board mechanism came to be. 张小珺·商业访谈录 张小珺·商业访谈录 48. openai的权力游戏：脸谱、硅谷精英政治与讽刺意味 openai corporate governance silicon valley elite politics founder control a 700-person company set off a global uproar luo yihang judges this unprecedented: twitter was chaotic internally in its early years too, but that was a matter for a small silicon valley circle — it didn't get the whole world discussing and snacking on gossip. openai as a company has existed for only a bit over 4 years, nearly 5, with a headcount of 700-plus, yet it caused this kind of storm, which is very rare. this contrast is itself the episode's question: why can a single board vote at such a small company become a global event. luo yihang the means were political; the motive wasn't necessarily a conspiracy luo yihang repeatedly stresses: the coup happened very politically, but political things don't necessarily have bad motives — political is a characteristic and a means. the real cause is still a fairly large divergence in philosophy — when gpts and the gpts store launched on november 6, he personally was excited and shocked, feeling they had taken a very radical step. he also reminds us that any decision, especially one by an outstanding figure, is often mixed with very strong personal values and private interests — the two can't be separated. luo yihang on safety, they say one thing and do another luo yihang heard from people in the circle in silicon valley this may that sam altman actually says one thing and does another on alignment, safety, and governance — he is in fact very radical. this source is indirect, coming from an intermediary who is an ai entrepreneur, not directly from someone inside openai. by contrast, ilya has spoken in multiple interviews about three things: caring whether ai can possess human love, worrying about superintelligent ai in relation to human ethical order and safety, and that the most important thing he pushes internally is alignment. luo yihang the most prestigious independent directors all left the board list was originally long, 9 people, and they dropped out one after another: elon musk exited in '18 or '19 over philosophical differences — at the time he opposed openai becoming a nonprofit, and luo yihang believes that idea was genuine then; elon musk's ex-wife also exited a few months ago; most critically, linkedin founder reid hoffman, whose reason for leaving was that he was preparing to do similar startups and investments. luo yihang says, if reid hoffman were still on the board, would this matter have been less hard to wind down in the end — because this person is especially constructive, and is good friends with many people whose relationships are extremely opposed. of the three remaining, he feels ‘the prestigious people have all left.’ luo yihang they exercised power once, and it actually worked luo yihang says two things shocked him. first, the company's key decisions were actually all made by these three people; the directors were neither informed, nor had they fully exercised power in the past — and then they exercised power once, and this thing actually got done. second, 700 people signed in support — does this company have internal strife or not? it's practically a solid block. he believes ilya later joining the signatories was a very important trigger for getting those 700-plus people to sign. luo yihang a nonprofit controls a for-profit the mechanism was built like this: openai started as a nonprofit, and the people on the board held no shares, only voting rights, representing the public in supervising and managing the institution. in 2019 the situation changed — they were already using the transformer architecture for training, burning money heavily, and the directors who had promised donations only put in money without taking shares — elon musk promised 100 million, reid hoffman promised several hundred million, and the money came in bit by bit. so openai inc was set up as the nonprofit, and openai lp as the limited-partnership for-profit vehicle to raise funds. the result: openai lp has no board of its own — its board is the board of openai inc. luo yihang microsoft holds 49% but isn't on the board microsoft changed enormously that year, deciding on a route: ai goes toward artificial general intelligence, in partnership with openai. luo yi ‖ 張小珺 商業訪談錄 張小珺 商業訪談錄 的權力遊戲 臉譜 硅谷精英政治與諷刺意味

s: 2023-11-16-zhangxiaojun-真格交接-徐小平退场后-合伙人收不了年轻人的税
h: zhenfund's handover: after xu xiaoping steps back, partners can't tax the young zhenfund fights the erosion of its first-generation edge with all-hands sourcing and per-project individual ownership — every logo hangs under one name, and partners can't coast on decision-making. high information density, heavy on mechanism detail: how the ic votes, why partners can't levy a tax, why executive founders are dangerous. suited to anyone curious about vc organizational design. founders, investors and fund lps curious about vc organizational design and handover mechanisms, especially those watching generational succession in chinese venture capital. 张小珺·商业访谈录 张小珺·商业访谈录 47. 接班百亿基金的琐碎小事：徐小平和他的门徒 venture capital zhenfund org design succession investment methodology xu xiaoping's exit was schrödinger-style in 2018 xu xiaoping began attending only half of the investment committee meetings, but no one knew which half — fang aizhi's phrasing is "you might see teacher xu today, you might not." by 2020 he took no part in any deal-level discussion, not even the weekly meeting. liuyan says this exit was "really thorough," and not improvised: from very early on, xu xiaoping and wang qiang repeatedly said "after another couple of funds, this fund is yours." liuyan says he heard it for eight years. this kind of handover — planned years ahead, phased out step by step — has almost no precedent among china's top-tier funds. listener mail zhenfund's ic doesn't decide by partner vote count at nearly every chinese vc the ic is made up of partners and only partners vote; liuyan calls zhenfund "the only outlier": analysts through partners all take part, each person gets one vote, and votes aren't counted. the decision method is to see who holds a strong opinion about the project — if both anna and yusen think it's good, they invest; if one thinks it's good and one doesn't, they look at other colleagues; if everyone thinks it's bad, it depends on how strong the conviction of the colleague pushing the project is. someone will say "i won't invest, but i also won't block this project." only recently did they start using anonymous feishu voting, but only to keep track, not as a decision criterion. listener mail partners can't levy a tax on the young from day one zhenfund has insisted partners source deals themselves: every month each person has to submit a table of the projects they sourced, and anna has to write one and tick the boxes too. a colleague said straight out in a meeting that anna hadn't looked at many projects this month and surely didn't know this track very well. back when xu xiaoping was still around he said that if one day zhenfund's partners only made decisions and let the young people go find projects, "zhenfund is finished." liuyan's summary is "you partners can't levy a tax on the young" — levying a tax means degeneration. the old partner zhaoyu complained before leaving: if you can't levy a tax and you always have to find projects, then what's the point of being a partner. listener mail each project hangs under only one name on zhenfund's website and in its fundraising decks, every project has only one person's ownership, occasionally two, but eighty or ninety percent are one person — no matter whether that person is an analyst, an investment manager or a partner. xiaohongshu is anna's, party animals is yusen's, a certain mendan is liuyan's. tianjie, whom liuyan recruited, invested in a partnership biology project; liuyan invested in it too, but "his project is his, my project is mine" — liuyan never knew the data on tianjie's project. this structure lets young colleagues truly own a deal, and it also means partners can't skim a cut off the young. listener mail zhenfund's methodology is incompatible with other funds liuyan says zhenfund's core philosophy of judging people is actually hard for someone trained at another fund to agree with — everyone else looks at how big the market is, compares how many companies are in the industry, who's number one; zhenfund isn't that line of thinking. someone from sequoia can go to idg or hillhouse and adapt quickly, but zhenfund's methodology may be fundamentally at odds with those. the philosophical split at the bottom is: is your judgment of the market more accurate, or is a good founder's judgment of the market more accurate. so zhenfund tends to cultivate people from a blank sheet; xu xiaoping's slogan is "faith makes it work" — believe in the founder, and internally you also have to believe in this business of betting on people. in ten years only three colleagues went to another fund. listener mail professors who don't found full-time do better zhenfund studied all chinese listed companies and companies founded successfully by professors, sorting professors into categories: those who served as ceo themselves, those with a phd as ceo, and those merely lending their name. the conclusion overturns the received view: the most successful projects aren't professors founding full-time ‖ 張小珺 商業訪談錄 張小珺 商業訪談錄 接班百億基金的瑣碎小事 徐小平和他的門徒

h: double 11 without xiaoyaozi: platforms split the cake, merchants eat the loss double 11's complexity wasn't designed — it accreted as dozens of industry lines each piled their own playbook onto one app; the platform takes roughly half, and a merchant with a multi-billion-yuan annual business is left with a few million in profit. zhao yuanyuan (赵圆圆), former head of taobao live, gives the internal battle details and the platform's revenue split; the mechanics and numbers in the back half are worth more than the anecdotes in the front half. e-commerce practitioners, brand operators, livestream mcns, and investors watching the platform economy — especially anyone who wants to know how platforms, streamers, and merchants divide the money. 张小珺·商业访谈录 张小珺·商业访谈录 46. 失去逍遥子的第一个双十一：诡计、大混战与小阳谋 e-commerce double 11 livestream selling platform economy consumption big merchants shout no discounts, then discount anyway the most fractured scene on the merchant side this double 11: a group of big merchants declared ‘i'm definitely making money this double 11, i won't break price,’ small and mid-sized merchants believed them and narrowed their discounts, offering only free gifts. then the moment double 11 opened, the merchants who'd made the declaration slashed prices like crazy, and the small and mid-sized merchants were all stunned. zhao yuanyuan calls this ‘plain and unadorned commercial warfare’ — the big guy normally sets the industry standard price at 300, and everyone below can sell at 268 or 199 and still make money; the big guy suddenly goes to 99, and everyone collapses with him. so this year's double 11 has this character: some things really are cheap, some things aren't, depending on whose goods you're buying. zhao yuanyuan double 11's complexity was stacked up by the org, not designed why are there so many double 11 playbooks that even women can't stand it? zhao yuanyuan's explanation is ‘the inevitability of departmentalism’: the apparel industry line thought up a new playbook this year and stuffed it in, the food industry line thought up a new playbook and stuffed it in, livestream, short video, and juhuasuan each had to stuff theirs in too. even the central double 11 project team doesn't know how many playbooks are inside. users want to buy clothes, buy food, buy cosmetics, and every time they have to relearn the rules — the learning cost is extremely high. the bosses know it's complex too, but they can't solve it — if it were unified into a flat 50% off across the board, what would each line's people write in their weekly reports, what would they write in their annual reviews, how would they get promoted and get raises. it's a dead loop. zhao yuanyuan super-head streamers are the platform's math, not operations' doing taobao formed a super-head ecosystem like li jiaqi and viya, while douyin's fortunes rotate — zhao yuanyuan argues this isn't a difference in operational capability, it's users voting with their feet. the platform's math is: with the same ten thousand people online, split across 100 livestream rooms, total gmv just isn't as high as when they're all camped in one super-head's room, and the return rate may be lower too. but douyin later became ‘a bit anti-super-head’ — because once the tools matured, supporting merchants' own livestreams became more cost-effective: a merchant is thrilled to hit 1:2.5 to 1:3 roi, and on 100 yuan of goods sold the platform can take over 30 yuan, far faster than letting a streamer take the big cut and then skimming six points. zhao yuanyuan the threshold for a super-head streamer is 20 million per session zhao yuanyuan gives a concrete bar: a single session reaching 20 million or more counts as a super-head streamer. when super-heads run into trouble it's usually in two places — first, personal life: once they enter a revenge state they can't handle the wealth, and a pack of scammers suddenly appears around them; second, team management and operations can't keep up. his weighting: a super-head streamer's personal factor accounts for only about 30% of success factors, 70% depends on operations, goods, the surrounding service team, and partners. decline isn't suddenly vanishing the next day — because the cash flow is so large and the fault tolerance so high, the slide is slow, lasting at least half a year, and it repeats. zhao yuanyuan video accounts may break 500 billion this year, equal to pinduoduo five years ago one platform barely mentioned in the whole episode that zhao yuanyuan thinks could be the future e-commerce giant: video accounts. his judgment is that this year's scale should break around 500 billion, versus only one to two hundred billion last year, doubling every year; by next year and the year after it's trillion-level, i.e. the tier of the cat-dog-pin first-tier club. the key point is that with overall internet consumption not growing that much, this slice of cake is being quietly cut away by video accounts. his reflection: years ago everyone thought e ‖ 趙圓圓 張小珺 商業訪談錄 張小珺 商業訪談錄 失去逍遙子的第一個雙十一 詭計 大混戰與小陽謀

s: 2023-11-06-zhangxiaojun-宝洁没有爆品思维-它是一支德国军团-不是游击队
h: p&g has no hit-product mentality: it's a german army, not a guerrilla force p&g doesn't rely on creativity or hit products. instead, every 30 to 40 years, across a major cycle, it uses brand management plus category management to twist user research, supply chain, and brands into one rope. a chinese executive who ran pringles in the us for p&g explains the talent principles, methodology, and the decade this 186-year-old company missed in china. founders and investors in consumer goods, brands, or channels, especially those who want to understand p&g's methodology, multi-brand playbook, and chinese consumer going global. 张小珺·商业访谈录 张小珺·商业访谈录 45. 漫谈宝洁：隐藏在186年消费品王国里的规则和秘密 consumer goods brand management p&g organizational culture going global p&g has only two principles, and the second is up or out p&g has just two principles: promotion from within, only promoting from inside; up or out, leave if you don't get promoted. on day one, new hires are told, you are a class, and if you don't get promoted twice a year, you know it's time to go. no one will say congratulations. that cohort included people from harvard business school, a navy captain, northwestern's business school, and cornell, but only one or two of you will survive. the elimination cycle is 6 to 12 months. aile says today's talk of 996 or 007 is just about hours; p&g's hours aren't as long, but the competition is unbelievable. those who were eliminated are all doing very well today; some went to johnson & johnson to run the olympic team, managing tens of billions of dollars. aile he beat everyone by going to focus groups every week aile made brand manager in two and a half years, when the average was five. his method wasn't knowing american culture better—he didn't understand baseball or football—but knowing users better than anyone. p&g ran focus groups across the us every week, and the schedule was posted on the internal community, but few brand people actually went. he applied to go every week, running nonstop for half a year, sitting behind soundproof glass watching midwestern housewives buy snacks, watching their tone and speech when they were at a loss, impatient, or genuinely pleased. after six months, he had basically become the user; on any question, his answer matched the users'. he says this is the same as ‘go out, the answers are all in the field’. aile p&g was built by german immigrants on the ohio river proctor and gamble were two german families who moved from the rhine to america. when they reached the ohio river, it felt like home, so they stopped heading west and settled in cincinnati. they had made industrial goods in germany, were asked to make gunpowder during the war, and after the war discovered that compressing the powder could make soap, giving rise to their first hit product, ivory soap. the lesson of ivory soap: purity is hard to express, but ‘pure means light’—it floats on water. lightness must be demoed. aile says p&g inherited the german spirit of striving for perfection, so the company is a bit clumsy, but it endures. aile when attacked, first tell if it's a shell or a barrage p&g has a theory: when attacked, you must distinguish whether it's a shell that can destroy you or a barrage that you can survive by hiding in your fortifications—germans are especially good at building fortifications. aile uses this framework to look at anta's acquisition of maya active: that company was founded in 2016, reached 100 to 300 million in the first four years, then did poorly for four years, and the founder probably didn't want to keep going. anta said, i won't retrace your old path, and directly acquired it; on the day of the acquisition, the stock rose 12%. from the longer cycle of a big company, being attacked once is nothing; it wants a certain segment of your doing well or poorly, a good time for it to enter. p&g has gone through five or six major risks in 190 years, basically one every 30 to 40 years. aile p&g is not a flexible force, it's a german army p&g doesn't have much hit-product thinking; the products it sells are not very stunning, but when a housewife sits down and does the math, she finds it still has the best value for money. it's not good at capturing users' fleeting moods, not great at incredible packaging, not great at playing with channels and traffic. you can't see it as a flexible force; it's a german army. it comes with 1,000 tanks and 100 planes, overwhelming. you are a guerrilla; you might win the first battle, but it wins the second, it wins the third, and you can't survive. it wins on overall cost—production cost, channel cost, marketing cost bundled together, others can't beat it; and it runs saturation attacks like bidding for cctv prime time all day long, with twenty or thirty brands constantly bombing. aile brand, supply chain, and r&d teams mix, but brand is heard p&g places great importance on the combined capability of brand, supply chain, and r&d. when aile was a brand manager, he had to spend sever ‖ 張小珺 商業訪談錄 張小珺 商業訪談錄 漫談寶潔 隱藏在 年消費品王國裡的規則和秘密
